Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What can I do to convince my mom I can mess with the computer? She keeps telling me to join classes unrelated to computer engineering like STEM where they learn about mechanical stuff or Computer Science where it's just coding.
Answer: I’m not sure what you mean by “mess with the computer,” but you stand a decent chance of breaking something and/or electrocuting yourself if you poke around the physical guts of a computer. Been there, did that. In this day and age, I wouldn’t poke around anything assembled by someone else. I don’t know what you mean by “classes unrelated to computer engineering like STEM.” As Professor Joshua Gross states, far more computer engineering graduates do only coding, rather than anything that has to do with designing hardware. Including myself. Someone has to write the software to control the hardware, and the CS graduates often don’t have the knowledge to do it. If you want to learn more about computers, I would get your mother to buy you the pieces to assemble a Raspberry Pi system and find/create some projects to add pieces, do interesting stuff, etc. It’s a lot cheaper than classes if you’re in the U.S. (maybe $100 U.S.) and you’ll probably learn a lot more than by sitting in a lecture. But you should definitely be on top of your math and science classes until you are done with school.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: In what ways is Silicon Valley culture most commonly misunderstood?
Answer: In general, most people who haven’t lived in Silicon Valley for years are deluded in their impressions. Which is not any different from most of the other big metro areas. NYC is not all bankers, LA is not all actors. The difference is that Silicon Valley is a suburbia, so people’s delusions don’t hit them in the face the way a real city does. First, San Francisco is not Silicon Valley. Yes, there are some people who live up there and work down here. They are not representative of the bulk of the people. Other than workplace, I have little in common with such people. Second, Silicon Valley is not a single culture, and I’m not even talking about the 2/3 of the population that doesn’t work for a tech company. For example, I have little in common with the folks in the house next door, other than living on the same street. We work for different companies in different subindustries: we wouldn’t be hired by the other’s employer. Add to that different food, different languages, different schools for our kids, different sports we follow. We’ve got nothing to talk about other than our properties and neighborhood security. Third, regular folks, even if they work for a tech company, are squeezed, hard. Normal jobs, even at tech companies, can’t make ends meet. That’s Silicon Valley culture too. Fourth, a large portion of people present in Silicon Valley at any given time are transients. I’m not talking homeless, but people who come from somewhere else and think they’re going to make millions with their big idea. They epitomize the delusions people have of this place, and usually get washed out quickly. Incidentally, I’m ethnic Korean. And there are parallels with the situation in the Republic of Korea (South). You get deluded children in western countries who want to move to the RoK because they saw something on Netflix or YouTube. However, many people who were actually born, raised, and live in the RoK call it “Hell Chosun” (Chosun being the name for the old kingdom) and are trying to leave because the competition and pressure are insanely high. Even by my standards as a Silicon Valley worker. Only the rich can have it good, and most people have a snowball’s chance in hell of becoming rich. For most people, either Silicon Valley or the Republic of Korea would be hell. Don’t delude yourself into thinking it’s otherwise.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What is the average salary of a CEO in the heart of Silicon Valley?
Answer: Silicon Valley has no heart. Literally (geographic) or figuratively (emotional). “Average” is a meaningless statistic. You can have CEOs drawing a single dollar of salary, and CEOs drawing many millions of dollars when they’re laying off thousands of workers who are much more vital to the business. The former tend to be founders and major shareholders, and the latter are leeches.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Can I do my masters in engineering if I have a bachelors in computer science with a minor in either statistics/physics?
Answer: You don’t say which country you live in. In the U.S., probably not. If you want to do engineering in the U.S., start it in undergrad. There may be schools which will take you, but I wouldn’t count on an engineering job afterwards.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I'm thinking about pursuing a dual degree because I want to become an entrepreneur. Is this a good idea?
Answer: No, it’s an irrational idea. It’s like the South Park Underpants Gnomes. How do two degrees make you an entrepreneur? There is no logical connection between the two. Assuming you are a woman, Aisha, it would make more sense to say you wanted a gender change because most successful entrepreneurs are men. (Which is both irrational and doesn’t improve your chances, so please don’t do that.) How are you defining “entrepreneur?” There are lots of business owners in the U.S. It does not take a bachelor’s degree to be a business owner. Almost half of U.S. business owners do not have a bachelor’s degree. And if you don’t need a bachelor’s degree, having two seems like a waste of time. In fact, I know someone who has three bachelor’s degrees and runs her own business. The first two degrees are useless to her business. The third (nursing) makes sure that she can do the work when the labor calls in sick or gets lazy. Get one bachelor’s degree. No one cares if you have more than one.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: How prestigious is Georgia Tech among job recruiters?
Answer: I am not a “recruiter,” but I do select and interview candidates. Georgia Tech is prestigious enough in computer science/engineering that if you look like a good candidate, there’s no problem with you being from Georgia Tech. That’s also true for a host of other schools. If you’ve been out of school for several years, I barely care what school you went to. Your work experience and achievements of the last four years matters a lot more than four years in the distant past. I need someone to do specific kinds of work, and if you haven’t been doing something close to that specific work, I’m not hiring you. If you haven’t been a software engineer, even if you have the CS or CompE education, your resume probably won’t pass the initial screen that someone else does. No school provides enough prestige that having attended a school is going to invalidate negative issues for any employer that has choices. I’ve rejected candidates from every top ranked school.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What big tech company is best to join paywise?
Answer: Depends on the person being paid. Possibly none of them. In general, big tech companies assign people a “level.” A site like levels.fyi will tell you what people make at particular levels. The same names don’t always mean the same thing at different companies, especially since different geographic locations will have different pay scales: you have to consider that companies based mostly outside the SF Bay Area or Seattle (e.g. Intel or Qualcomm) will pay less. But the levels will give you an idea. More broadly speaking, everyone has different skills. The question is who is going to pay you the most for the skills that you have. Taking myself as an example and the so-called “FAANG” companies: Netflix has absolutely no need for me and wouldn’t bother interviewing me. Apple’s core business needs people like me. The other companies lie somewhere in between, with most of their employees and recruiters treating me as useless (I’m talking about you, Facebook and Google) unless my resume got routed to a few very specific teams. The point is that different companies value people differently. What companies are willing to pay me will be affected by: That first thing can cause a split in what companies offer. At this point in my career, my best overall compensation often comes in from startups and the like due to those effects. Actually getting that compensation is reliant on the startup succeeding, but I try (and so far succeeded) to choose startups that will succeed. In addition, most large tech companies have been having layoffs recently, so the odds of getting hired by them right now is low.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: As an Iranian immigrant with a America finance degree, is it possible for me to find employment in the United States? I have seen information suggesting that securing a job in the business and finance sectors may be more challenging for immigrants.
Answer: What’s your immigration status? If you don’t have the unrestricted right to work in the U.S., it’s going to be next to impossible to find a job: you need a work visa and we must have a shortage of people in the job for you to be eligible. We have no shortage of finance people. If you have the unrestricted right to work (permanent resident or naturalized citizen), then it’s no different from being a natural born citizen. But finance isn’t an easy place to get a job in general.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Does studying MIS over CS hurt my chances of employment or possible future prospects academically and professionally?
Answer: What’s your goal? If you’re trying to get a software engineering position, the MIS degree programs I’ve investigated aren’t sufficient to prepare you. But I’ve only looked into MIS at UIUC and one or two other schools (for my own education). If you’re targeting something else, maybe the MIS degree sufficient. I don’t know which positions those would be, so I can’t give you useful information there.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I will be done with my degree in 4 months and I don't think I will be able to find a job yet. Should I take a loan and continue grad school?
Answer: No. It’s a very bad idea. You should already have some job experience at this point. If you don’t, that is a problem you need to fix, immediately. Burying your head in the sand/school only makes the problem worse.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What tech areas are the most exciting to work in?
Answer: “Exciting” is entirely subjective. I’ve never looked for “excitement.” My priorities have been: 1. Impact/change. 2. Money. 3. Education and future-proofing. Not necessarily in that order.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: In your job today as a software engineer, what are some courses (maybe 5-10) you offered in the university/college that you find to be among the most important or most used (in hierarchy if possible)?
Answer: Note that I have a computer engineering education, rather than computer science. I generally work on compilers for specialized and/or high performance computing systems. I don’t use all the circuits and E&M I learned in school.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: How can I choose between dentistry and entrepreneurship?
Answer: I don’t know where you live, but here in the U.S., every dentistry practice I’ve been to is a small business. Dentistry is entrepreneurship. As Paul’s answer similarly states, “entrepreneurship” isn’t a job. You start a business to do something. Produce a product, provide a service, etc. As a past or current employee of four tech startups, and as a small business owner, my experience is that people who say they want to get into “entrepreneurship” have no idea what they’re doing and no idea what they’re getting themselves into. I work really damn hard, but I have not yet started a company by myself, because it’s a hell lot harder than my PhD or anything else I’ve done so far in life.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Does school prestige matter in the field of engineering? If so, to what extent?
Answer: Yes, but mostly when you are a recruiter looking at fresh grads. Significantly less so when you are the recruitee, and school “prestige” does not directly matter several years out of school. “Prestige” is a subjective amalgam of admission selectivity and the impressions one gets from a school’s graduates. When the school’s acceptance rate is under 10% and the typical graduate is very sharp, I’d call it prestigious. When recruiters are choosing how to spend their time, they will select for higher (or lower) prestige to maximize the use of their time. One of my former VPs recruited at only four schools: UC Berkeley, Stanford, CMU, and MIT. He said only those schools were worth his time. He did not deny that other schools had excellent students and graduates, but he wasn’t going to recruit at those schools, because his hit rate was lower. If a kid goes to a less prestigious school, they may not hear of certain companies (since the companies didn’t come to the school’s career fairs) and otherwise miss opportunities for awareness and connections. But the Internet makes this gap far smaller than it’s historically been. The important point is that prestige is a generalization used for filtering and maybe some calibration for grades. But graduate schools and employers don’t hire generalizations: they choose individuals. Once you pass those recruiting filters, school doesn’t matter compared to your personal performance and area of interest fitting with the job. For example, I recently hired a fresh grad out of a school ranked outside the top 15: his school provides a very solid education, his grades were excellent, he communicated well, and he has a strong interest in what we do. He hasn’t disappointed me so far. Several years out of school, or fresh out of grad school, it’s about work history, and if it sucks, you’re done for. I know several graduates of MIT and other top engineering schools who have been unemployed for years. In the U.S., we have ABET, which accredits engineering programs. Accreditation ensures an engineering program meets a minimum, and I can rely on a good graduate of such a program to know the basics. Unaccredited programs might be glorified technician programs: their graduates generally don’t measure up. Note that there may be schools or specific programs at certain schools (often computer science) that don’t bother, for various reasons. In addition, people attend particular schools for more reasons than just prestige, with cost being a major factor. Particularly for U.S. engineering, which has historically been dominated by recent immigrants and people trying to move up to the middle class. Few students in those boats can afford to spend $60k+/year when their flagship state university is less than 1/4 of the cost, and sometimes ranked just as high or even higher (e.g. UC Berkeley, UIUC, Georgia Tech, U-Michigan, Purdue, UT-Austin, and so on). As I mention in the answer below, one friend graduated from a school ranked lower than #100 in the U.S. That didn’t stop him from accomplishing great things so far. Undergrad study is just four years, and while it has an effect on the rest of your life, especially in the networks you form, I’d say it pales in comparison to both earlier education/life and the personal decisions you make in life and career.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: My sophomore year of Computer Science is approaching. Should I be mentally prepared for all-nighters?
Answer: Maybe. But needing to pull an all-nighter indicates at least one of three things: I pulled one all-nighter for a course in undergrad. Effectively everyone in that class did so, which puts it in the second category.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is computer engineering worth studying? I've heard it has a high income. but I'm afraid because it has become bold nowadays and I'm afraid everyone will study it and they will make it so crowded that it turns to a useless and cheap career.
Answer: “Bold?” I’m assuming English isn’t your first language, “Winter Blossom.” That word doesn’t make sense in this question. You haven’t mentioned where you live, and computer engineering opportunities vary significantly between countries. I’ve only operated in the U.S. and with a handful of partners in other countries. “Average” computer engineering graduates in the U.S. are already screwed today. As one professor mentions on another answer, a graduate degree (and the undergraduate performance implied) is about the norm in computer engineering jobs in the U.S. If you want to make big money, those teams often have a lot of PhDs from top schools. If you are good and work hard, you will be fine and make a good living. If you are not good or don’t work hard, you will not have a computer engineering job ten years after graduation.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What is the average salary in the US for an engineer? Is it a good salary?
Answer: Go look at the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics if you want statistics. The overall average is meaningless for most people because engineering disciplines vary significantly in compensation and engineers generally cannot jump from one discipline to another without reeducation. If you are a foreigner in a traditional engineering field, you may not be allowed to practice in the U.S. without further education or accreditation. Furthermore, the deviation in salaries for subfield and ability is significant. Many engineers leave their fields within 5–7 years because they either suck or don’t like the work. Those that excel can become spectacularly rich.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I am currently studying bachelor of business administration, but I think it's getting nowhere and I don't learn anything specific. Do you think it’s better to change my major to computer engineering?
Answer: Hard to say. I’d make that choice, but that’s easy for me to say in hindsight. The questions I have are: If your answers to these question are affirmative, then maybe you should consider switching. I would talk to the advising staff at your school about what they recommend. Generally, you should take a course or two in computer engineering to ensure you are prepared and can do the work.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What are the eligibility requirements for a Master's Degree scholarship in the USA? How can one secure a full scholarship for a Master's Degree in the USA?
Answer: This question has been asked thousands of times before. Master’s degrees were created to be cash cows for universities. Compared to the number of master’s students, there are effectively no scholarships for master’s students. The only supported master’s students I’ve known were on teaching or research assistantships, and PhD students have priority for those.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Does undergraduate school matter for engineering?
Answer: I only have significant experience in the U.S., so my answer is for there. Yes, the school “matters,” but not in the way most high schoolers think. A U.S. engineering school should be ABET-accredited: graduating from such a school means you should have the minimum needed to make yourself a successful engineer. After that, who you are is the primary determinant of your engineering career. Most of the prestige and reputation of a school at the undergraduate level have far more to do with the input (students) than the school itself. As my former professor likes to say to the MIT applicants he interviews, “who you are is much more important than the school.” Schools like MIT, Stanford, and CMU get the most smart, driven, and prepared students to apply, which is strongly (but not perfectly) correlated with the quality of output. You can look at the “middle 50%” of admits at schools to see what the data look like. When the lower 25% of a school like MIT beats the 75% mark of most other schools by a large margin, it’s clearly getting the better students. However, distributions of hundreds or thousands of admits say effectively nothing about a single graduate within that distribution. That individual may be around average, or may be at one of the extremes. Some specifics: Engineering graduate programs will consider students from any reasonable, accredited school. So if you are concerned about the quality or reputation of your undergraduate education, simply apply to a more reputed graduate school. Effectively no one cares about your undergraduate institution once you have a graduate degree, which indicates that the undergraduate institution is not important when there are other, better signals. In one extreme case, I know a guy who went to an undergraduate program ranked lower than #100 in the U.S., an effectively nameless school in Ohio. It was his local school. However, he was very, very sharp. And he decided to pursue a PhD at UIUC (ranked #2 at the time), which is where I first met him. Then he decided to work at a government lab, and later tried an idea for a startup: a handheld ultrasound device that would cost a few thousand dollars, instead of hundreds of thousands like most devices in hospitals at the time. The guy is definitely not hurting for money at this point, and I doubt anyone cares where he got his undergraduate. He’s the primary reason I don’t make snap assumptions about people from their undergraduate institution. Even if a diamond isn’t fully polished in undergrad, it’s still a diamond, and there’s 40+ years of career and continued education to improve in the future. Conversely, you can’t polish a turd to gemstone quality no matter what polishing/schools you subject it to (although the Mythbusters episode on the topic is amusing). The school can only do so much to/for the student.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Many people argue that pursuing a PhD is an unworthwhile endeavor for *most* people in the world. But is this notion really true? Doesn’t holding a PhD confer a tremendous social status benefits in Asia - and Asia represents most of the world?
Answer: In summary: people who are impressed by degrees are usually not the people who can do anything for you. I’m ethnic Asian, and I have a PhD. During the rare times I meet an Asia-born homemaker since earning my PhD, usually one of my mother’s friends, she’s always very impressed with my PhD. However, they’re usually more impressed with any degree from an Ivy League or similarly expensive private school, including ones that are ranked quite low. Their opinions are literally worthless to me: they don’t bring me any benefit. My PhD almost never comes up when I interview for a job. It’s about what I can do for the employer. And plenty of PhDs can’t do much. The rare times it does come up at a workplace, it’s usually at a startup, on a slide to investors, describing the background of the technical team. Maybe my PhD would have more cachet among managers and executives in Asia. But I don’t work in Asia, and I would claim that the companies I’ve worked for in Silicon Valley are superior in their fields. Which would imply that not inflating the prestige of PhDs is better for industry performance.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is a PhD in computer science worth it financially?
Answer: For most people, compared to the alternatives, no. There are PhDs who are probably doing as well as if they didn’t do the PhD. Common characteristics I see: It begs the question of whether they would have done as well or better if they stopped at the master’s. I suspect most of them would have done just as well without the PhD, although industrial research would have been closed off to them. As I have said in many other answers, do not expect a graduate degree to “fix” anything regarding jobs. People should pursue PhDs to do the jobs that require a PhD. Those jobs (professor) may not have higher pay.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: As a PhD student, if you intend to drop out and pursue job opportunities, should you leave out your PhD from your resume because someone currently pursuing a PhD may be less likely to get job offers due to their commitment to studies?
Answer: First, always keep in mind that a resume is about communication. You are constructing a profile in the reader’s mind, and you don’t want it to lead to something detrimental to yourself. Second: since you’re presumably still in school, you wouldn’t know this, but the biggest red flag for people reading resumes of otherwise qualified people is big gaps. That’s why it’s been brought up in several prior answers. Across many fields, justified or not (e.g. maternity leave), the big gap is the career killer. No matter how negative you think the PhD might be in the recruiter’s or hiring manager’s mind, a big gap is much, much worse. So don’t “leave out” the PhD if it introduces a big gap in your resume. I don’t think having pursued a PhD, especially when you’re withdrawing, would be less likely to get offers. I’m presuming you’re an engineer from your other questions: engineering work is very reliant on being good in our studies. I wouldn’t want to be crossing a bridge or staying in a building designed with someone who barely passed their classes, for example. What would be a negative is the inability to communicate clearly, either written or verbally, and some people who spent their entire lives in school are like that. So don’t be like that. So just communicate clearly on the resume that you started a PhD program and withdrew. When you get interviews, communicate verbally in a clear and unawkward manner. Your education is only a part of your profile fresh out of school, and it drops off significantly afterwards.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Would a doctorate in engineering be worth it? Why don’t I see them much? What does it look like?
Answer: Are you referring to a PhD in engineering, or an explicit Doctor of Engineering (EngD, Dr Ing for the Germans)? Why you don’t see one or the other depends on your personal circumstances: country, engineering field, and workplace. I see PhDs in engineering every work day, because I work in teams and companies where it’s a common credential. If you’re asking about EngDs: different countries and fields vary in their standards and different schools may or may not offer them. In computer engineering, the top U.S. programs do not offer EngDs, so of course I don’t see them. Mechanical engineering programs do offer the degree, and incidentally the most common reference I see of EngDs is overwhelmingly Dr. Ing. h.c. F. Porsche AG. As for whether a EngD would be worthwhile and what does it look like, I can’t provide any useful information there, since the degree generally isn’t awarded in my field. A PhD in computer engineering, assuming we’re not talking about academia, is only worthwhile for people who work on realistic problems that have applicability to industry. I can’t speak for other engineering fields.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: How is UCSD's computer science education better than UCI's?
Answer: The phrasing of both the original and modified question assumes that UCSD’s computer science education is better than UCI’s, and I don’t think that assumption is necessarily true, nor has it been consistently demonstrated. The admission standards of UCSD are slightly higher than UCI’s, and I suspect any perceived superiority of UCSD grads is mostly dependent on that fact: the “quality” of the input is the first order determinant of the quality of output. Similarly, MIT has one of the highest admissions standards of any school offering CS degrees, which is why it’s usually at the top. I did not attend any of the aforementioned schools, although I’ve worked with grads of all of them.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is it worth it to spend an extra 1 year getting an MEng if I just want to level up fast in Google/FANG?
Answer: A2A. Short answer: no. First, as Chris Clark’s answer states, you had better temper your expectations. I don’t know where you go to school or how good you think you are, but even if you were the top of your class at the #1 school in your country, you are far more likely to be rejected than accepted at any of those companies. I earned my degrees from a program ranked #2–5 in the U.S., depending on the year, and was in the top 5% for undergrad, but I was completely unexceptional in my teams at those companies. Top companies get a lot of very smart, hard working people. Second, advanced degrees do nothing to get you promoted faster by themselves. They might help get you the job by giving you rare knowledge or by signaling, but people in industry do not get promoted for their credentials. They get promoted for what they produce, with the expectation that promoting them will get even more out of them. On that topic, when graduate degrees are valued, a MEng will be treated as it is, which is an extended undergraduate. There is generally no research component. Taking more classes does not guarantee good work product. (Not that research does either, but at least it’s not just classes.) So no, the MEng does nothing to “level up fast.” Do it because you want to be armed with more knowledge, and don’t expect it to do anything for you beyond that.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I chose biotechnology as my major. What is the future of this major (career opportunities, detailed directions, etc.)? What other skills do I need besides a university diploma?
Answer: The degree programs I looked at seem to be aimed towards work in industries where some kind of life process, e.g. fermentation (alcoholic beverage production), is involved. Some include animal husbandry: they’re basically agricultural programs. There appears to be a significant range of content between schools: it’s not as standardized as the “pure’ sciences. So it’s harder to draw generalizations. If the program is rigorous and has connections with relevant industries, they will teach you useful knowledge for those industries. For any college degree, you want to be doing internships and other work experiences well before you graduate. The degree is insufficient if you want any reliability of having a job soon after graduation.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is it easy or difficult for international students in the United States to find a job after graduation?
Answer: A job in the U.S., or a job in another country? Short term, or long term? For the U.S., it’s effectively impossible for most international students to find a long term job in the U.S., which is why most go home after graduation. You can work for a short time (1 year for most) via the Optional Practical Training (OPT) for your F-1 student visa. For certain fields, that period can be extended, with certain STEM fields going to 3 years. There is a hard limit for everyone. For long term employment, the prevalent mechanism is the H-1B work visa. In order to qualify: Most college graduates do not qualify. The bulk of such people are technical workers with engineering and computer science degrees.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I did reasonably well in my engineering Master's, but given my struggles understanding research articles, limited relevant coursework options, lack of field knowledge, and limited passion for research, should I pursue a PhD for better job prospects?
Answer: A2A. No, because the PhD will probably not give you “better” job prospects. I know engineering PhDs, even from top schools such as MIT, who are unemployed or underemployed. A PhD does not improve your job prospects unless you work on the hottest new technology (meaning that there is no labor supply other than PhDs) and companies are pounding on your door. Like GPUs in 2008–10, or machine learning a decade ago. Those are still in demand, but labor has mostly caught up with supply. You don’t mention what engineering area you study, so I can only tell you what I see in computer engineering/science. The PhD is usually a net loss to one’s engineering career and earnings compared to ending at the master’s, and is almost certain to be so in your case.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Question for Senior software Developers: If you were 18 again and had to choose a 4-year degree to start in 2024, would you still do CS or something different?
Answer: I didn’t do CS. I was a EE major with a CS minor, which gave me full coverage of the CompE graduation requirements. My performance in software courses was below my (A) average. I did not get competent until graduate school and work. I still would not do CS, at least not in the way it was generally taught when I started undergrad. Starting with programming, particularly a language that isn’t “close to metal,” isn’t the best way for me and many other people to learn about computers. The right way for me is to learn about the hardware, then learn assembly language, then learn older, “lower level” programming languages like C. Basically in chronological order, because those things arose in that order for good reason. My eldest child (at age 11) has already shown better ability at programming than I did when I was 18, so she might be able to do the CS route. But I still wouldn’t go that route.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Why is artificial intelligence so reliable?
Answer: What do you mean by “reliable,” Pechi Wang? By my standards, it’s not reliable. If AI is “reliable” by your standards, I would say that’s because humans are notoriously unreliable.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Why is Samsung considered the world's best employer?
Answer: Apparently Forbes did the ranking that claims Samsung is first, and since Forbes hyped Theranos and their “30 under 30” list has lost more money via fraud than it raised, I’m very skeptical of anything Forbes reports. What I do know is that Samsung Electronics (the division most relevant to me) runs about a 3.8 on Glassdoor. Not bad, but Amazon, Apple, Google, Meta, and Microsoft are all higher. I’ve also known a lot of ethnic Koreans who left Samsung. Samsung is a very prestigious employer in the RoK (South Korea), and that affects how people see the company there. However, people who work in other countries know their alternatives and often prefer them. Apple and Google had a decent number of ex-Samsung, and most of the ones I know personally said they will never go back. So whatever Forbes claims, I have little desire to join Samsung at this time, and I have one more reason to distrust Forbes.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I saw an answer regarding completing an engineering program in less than 4 years. How does it work?
Answer: Before I talk about anything else: No one who matters will care how long it took you to get an engineering degree. That fact is true for both undergrad or graduate, and the only exception is when you take so long that people are questioning whether you’re even trying (and whether you’ll do the same thing at work). Don’t delude yourself into thinking otherwise. People care about other things. The vast majority of people take four or more years to finish an engineering undergraduate degree in the U.S. More than four is very common these days, and taking longer is advisable if you are doing it for “co-ops” (cooperative work-study where you work a semester). Many employers find summer internships to be too short, while a semester is much better. And as I said above, work experience is vital. You need to obtain credits outside of the ”regular” path to graduate faster. Common methods include: Examples of some real people: The point of these examples is that graduating faster doesn’t matter, and the people who graduate early and end up in a good situation are usually heading into graduate school (where you get paid to go to school). Most of my potential employers don’t even care that I have a PhD, let alone how long any of my degrees took. They don’t pay me to have degrees or to have gotten then within a certain amount of time. They pay me for what I can do for them now and in the future. Focus on what you can do and how well you can do it. Any idiot can produce garbage in a hurry.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What major do you recommend that has little to no math and has a high demand and good salary, preferably a business major?
Answer: You’re asking for something that does not exist. Salary is determined by supply and demand. Business majors and majors that do not require math are in high supply. Majors that do not require math are in low demand. Thus, you cannot find a “good salary” with that combination.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: If you own a car sold in California that still has the warning sticker on your driver-side window blocking your view, why haven't you removed it? Like 1 in 20 cars still have this sticker in the window, and I would like to know your reason. Thx.
Answer: I’ve left it for more than a few days because it doesn’t block my view of anything useful. Who’s going to look back and down while driving? The only situation I can conceive of is a toddler on a tricycle. But there’s no reason to leave it there either, so I’ve generally removed it when I know I’ll be near a trash can within a minute. I’m a lot more concerned with people who hang shit on their rear view mirrors: those are definitely blocking one’s view. If you track people who drive sloppily, those people dominate, followed by people who tint their windows very heavily.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is Intel becoming more and more like the feeling Boeing brings to people?
Answer: I don’t know what “feelings” other people have about Boeing. There’s a broad similarity in that both are declining, but the situations diverge rapidly. I’m a Chicagoan by birth and upbringing. When Boeing moved its HQ to Chicago in 2001, most people around me cheered that, but I saw it as a bad thing overall: I bet it was going to be the start of a long slide into mediocrity. That sequence has been repeated time and time again across corporate America. Nothing new here. If even a middle aged engineer like me knows that history, then Boeing execs had their heads in the sand. Intel’s situation is different. Their bread-and-butter (power hungry X86 processors) is doing okay and hasn’t killed anyone. And they’re doing okay in some of the things they’ve acquired (networking). But: They don’t have a management-engineering gap, at least not right now with CEO Gelsinger. The problem is that they haven’t been able to jump into fast growing areas while their bread and butter has been declining, at least in relative terms. It’s a common problem, but with known solutions: you set up teams that know what they’re doing separate from the existing cash cows and give them the resources to succeed, as HP did with inkjet printers and Apple did with the original Macintosh. The problem with that approach is you need the right people to drive it, and from stories I’ve heard from people who have worked at Intel more recently, they don’t have those people. So two different companies, two different situations. And two different sets of solutions.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Should I choose finance over computer science? I believe CS is oversaturated right now and so many people are jobless. What should I do?
Answer: Crap CS is oversaturated. Elite CS pays hundreds of thousands of USD a year. I’m assuming you’re Indian by your handle, “Hyderabad Kiraakz.” If you’re the kind of person who can get into an IIT and a top graduate program, then you don’t have much to worry about. If you can only get into a school that anyone can get into, you’re wasting your time and money.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: My prospective employer denied me the job even though I told him I got my PhD from Harvard. How am I not qualified?
Answer: If you actually had a PhD, Shane Kholbor , you would know that: As I do have a PhD from a school ranked much higher than Harvard in my area, I know I’m not qualified for most jobs in computer science/engineering. And I know exactly one person with a Harvard PhD who would be qualified to work at my current or previous employers. You’re not her.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What is the significance of the August 2024 Intel 15% layoff announcement?
Answer: I’m not sure it signifies anything. Intel has been sliding for a while now, and the layoffs are more an effect than a cause. The problems so far: Can they fix things? I think the foundry play is the correct one, but I’m not convinced they can catch up with TSMC. You have to get elite people and you have to pay them what they’re worth. Intel looked like they were going to do that in 2021, but then cut salaries in 2023.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What are some of the top and budget-friendly online MBA programs in the USA that offer great value for money?
Answer: As previous answers have stated, top and budget-friendly are opposing forces. The first MBA program (Harvard’s) was explicitly intended as a cash cow, and nothing has changed in the decades since. High ranked programs charge more. Much more. And there is no guarantee of a decent job afterwards. I’ve known people who went to schools in the #8–15 range who had a lot of trouble finding employment (and sometimes failing entirely). Online programs often don’t have a “top” reputation because the point of being online is to milk as many people as possible, which means lowering admissions standards as much as possible and graduating as many as possible. Which means any idiot can graduate, so there’s no prestige or guarantee of quality. On top of that, MBAs are usually laid off in droves in recessions. So when I realized these things, I gave up on the MBA and took the technical path.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: How hard is it to get employed in the USA? I will get my bachelors in Computer Science from Beaconhouse National University, Pakistan. Later, I plan on going for a job hunt in the USA. How difficult is it?
Answer: If you are a U.S. citizen, very difficult. If you are not a U.S. citizen, effectively impossible. U.S. corporations do not hire foreign nationals with foreign bachelor’s degrees. They have to pay more for those people both up-front (visa) and while they are working (required by law). It doesn’t happen even for elite foreign schools, and Beaconhouse is far too new to have established a reputation even if it were elite. Which it does not appear to be. Every Pakistani I’ve ever worked with has a graduate degree from a top U.S. university. If you aren’t good enough to get in that way, then you will probably not be working in the U.S.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What is the future of anyone studying computer science if major companies are laying off employees without any reason? Wouldn’t the students be jobless for a long time because of it and become doubted as a bad employee?
Answer: First, people weren’t students if they were laid off. They were workers. Second, companies aren’t laying off employees “without any reason.” There’s plenty of reasons. It’s just that the reasons are more likely to be something other than the quality of the employee. It’s less likely that people hiring will think you’re bad. The problem is that there are thousands of other people also looking for jobs, so competition is much higher. The future of computer science/engineering is fine for competent people. The problem is that there are lots of CS programs graduating people who didn’t actually learn much of anything.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I'm undecided on what course I should pursue in college. Do you have any advice on how to choose the right course?
Answer: College is generally a means to an end. Some people see it otherwise, but they probably wouldn’t be asking what to study. So figure out what you want your end to be: what job or position do you want to be doing for the next 40+ years? Then you can start mapping out paths that are likely to get to that goal.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is a double major in computer science and electrical engineering beneficial or is it more feasible to double major in computer science and computer engineering to focus on computing aspects?
Answer: They’re both a waste of time. Only high schoolers and other people without college degrees care about double majors. No employer cares, although recruiters might butter you up about it. Double majors don’t indicate any more likelihood of doing the job well. It’s a negative indicator if you don’t have personal technical interests, have low grades, or are from a school known to produce incompetent graduates: you’re a credential chaser prioritizing things that do not matter rather than someone that wants to do computer science/engineering. Many programs, including most of the top ones, do not allow double majors between computer engineering and either computer science or electrical engineering: they’re too close. Even if it’s allowed, it would be yet another signal that you’re a credential chaser. Employers are usually looking for more than just a generic major. They want to see deep interest in the projects they’re hiring for. I will not hire a generic computer science/engineering graduate: I want to see a deep interest in computer architecture, compilers, system software, and so on. The roles I hire for require that information. Other jobs will find that knowledge useless. Electrical engineering in particular has so many sub areas, you won’t be able to get a job in more than one or two. If you’re going to do computer hardware, do computer engineering. Go do a double major in something completely unrelated that you have a strong interest in and/or get a graduate degree in computer science/engineering. Those are a much better use of time.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I have a non IT related business. Will I get talented people if I opened my office in Silicon Valley?
Answer: I also have a non IT related business (health care) that I own with my wife in Silicon Valley, on top of my day job. We know a variety of other small business owners. I would generally not count on significantly better talent in Silicon Valley than anywhere else, especially compared to the cost. It’s probably not going to be worse, but I would not expect better. You don’t mention what kind of business you have, but I would not locate a business in Silicon Valley unless it was a true cutting edge tech company (not even “IT” businesses) or directly served the people in the area (medical in my case)

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Would getting a PhD in a STEM field (specifically computer science) and getting an MBA (like in finance) be beneficial for someone who wants to enter the tech industry?
Answer: Short answer: both, no. One, maybe. I know a handful of people personally with both a PhD in CS or engineering, and a MBA. My personal opinion of the degrees is: The tech “industry” is not a monolith: there are tiers, correlated with ability of the workers, and with pay. At the top, there are plenty of people with PhDs or MBAs that can’t hack it. I’ve rejected far more PhDs than hired, and the rejection rate goes up as the reputations of the schools go down. It’s less that reputation matters and more that reputation is based on the average ability of grads coming out of those programs. My point is that if you go to some no-name school, don’t expect it to be respected when you get out. All a degree really means is that you: No matter the degree, if you can’t produce what’s expected of you, you’re going to be out on your ass.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Do software companies in Silicon Valley like Facebook, Google and Apple compensate their employees fairly given the value they bring to the table?
Answer: There are a few important concepts here. All that being defined: yes, large Silicon Valley tech companies generally compensate their technical employees fairly, in terms of market fairness. One reason it’s “fair” is California does not enforce non-compete agreements, so labor can move around a lot more easily than in “pro-business” states where non-compete agreements are enforced: people are coerced into keeping their jobs in those places. Back to different value for different employers: when Apple, Google, and Facebook/Meta hit certain stages of (hyper)growth, they poached thousands of workers from other companies. They needed employees badly and were willing to pay for them, whereas the previous employers were not willing to keep up with pay. Over time, this effect results in top talent gravitating towards particular companies. Many of the top tech companies of 1995–2000 still exist, but most aren’t top anymore because of this effect. To wrap up: maybe what we have isn’t “fair” by your standards. But it’s certainly more free compared to many (most?) other places in the world. Those that work harder and have rare, valuable skills will generally be rewarded more than those who do not, which most people would call “fair.” It’s one of the reasons Silicon Valley still has relevance in the technical world, despite a huge amount of competition.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What is the ECE experience at UMich, UIUC, UT Austin, and Purdue?
Answer: Why do you think anyone on Quora would know the “experience” at four separate universities? No one except some professors would have spent significant time at more than two, and none of the professors I know personally at UMich or UIUC have been to more than one other of those universities. I doubt there are any truly important differences between those schools that matter in the long run. You find people from all of the who are at the most selective companies, and people from all that are perpetually unemployed.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Can someone with a master's in computer engineering get non-hardware-related software engineering OPT jobs?
Answer: Yes, but you would need enough software courses/background to be hired. I’ve rejected hardware engineers trying to move into software before, for lack of ability, and I will likely do so again.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Despite the cost of travel and living would it be better in the long run for me to attend college in a different country than USA, would a degree from a different country be valid in the US and would it be harder for me to find a job?
Answer: There are already good answers for this question, but as I have been asked to answer and have children approaching college application age, I’ll tell you what I would tell them. I’m assuming you’re a U.S. citizen. would a degree from a different country be valid in the US There are two separate issues here: validity versus acceptability. would it be harder for me to find a job? Yes for some jobs. Because those jobs have so many applicants, the recruiters are going to use very arbitrary metrics for pruning, which include school. They don’t care if you individually lose an opportunity: their job is to find anyone that fits. There’s also the problem that by going to a foreign undergraduate program, people will assume you’re a foreign national and throw your resume in the trash because they aren’t willing or able to hire those people. That’s an incorrect assumption on their part, but it does happen and I’ve seen it with my own eyes: a small slice of candidates are U.S. citizens by birth who spent most of their formative years in other countries. In general, don’t overestimate the intelligence, diligence, or respect of recruiters. They don’t care about you unless you count towards their numbers. would it be better in the long run for me to attend college in a different country than USA For my children, no. For most Americans, no. Too much additional cost, too many potential hiccups. If you want an international experience, lots of universities have study abroad programs. U.S. state universities are an excellent deal. The flagship schools are some of the best in the country and even the world. For many people, undergraduate is not a terminal degree. Graduate school abroad may make a lot more sense, when the world experts in your field are in a different country. Happens all the time across Europe.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: How far in the tech industry will an online degree in Computer Science from SNHU or Purdue University Global get me? Will I be able to land an advanced, high paying job in the future?
Answer: There are a few aspects to this, but it boils down to two things: And those two things are both strongly influenced by the following: So a university with very high entrance and exit bars will take very smart kids and train them hard. A university lacking those things will generally not produce the same quality graduates. That being said, the distribution is very wide, so you will find strong students at “weaker” schools, but they are not the norm. So you’ll have to examine the entry and graduating requirements for any given program to determine what you’ll learn and what kind of reputation the program carries. Online programs in general have the reputation of: It will be up to you to disprove any assumptions a recruiter or hiring manager may have. And you may not get the opportunity to do so.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is it a good idea to major in a subject you are passionate about?
Answer: I mulled on this on and off for a few hours. The major problem is that word: “passionate.” First, a few definitions of passion: If your passion is #1 or #2: effectively everything I’ve ever done that I’ve regretted in my life so far was due to strong emotions: I (and many other people) do stupid things under strong emotions. I wouldn’t make any decision under strong emotions. Even without that effect, strong emotions inevitably fade. What happens when (not if, when) that passion fades? The same can be said for a person’s love life, which is why the U.S. divorce rate for people married before 25, when they’re raging balls of hormones and emotions, is over 50%. So if your “passion” is #1 or #2, I would say it’s bad to decide your area of study based on that passion. If you’re #3, where your “passion” is an interest eliciting positive but not overly intense emotions, is it something that’s going to last? What are the conditions under which it cools? Is it going to last through the boring or tough patches? Because every life and every job has such stretches. That leads to the next item. The next problem is what information is your “passion” based on? By definition, what you know about college, your major, or where they lead is imperfect and incomplete: you’re going to college to learn about your major, and you haven’t had a job in your major. All you really have is personal opinions based on distant impressions. In the worst case, you might be making life decisions based on pure fantasy. As I have an engineering education, I saw a lot of kids enter math, physics, and engineering because they had “passion” and subsequently drop out. Their passion amounted to the salaries they thought they could get after school, or was based on the experience in a high school math or physics class. They couldn’t do four years of work towards a engineering’s bachelor’s degree, and college math and physics are very different beasts from high school. Finally: is college or the specific major going to pay the bills in the long run or otherwise sustain you? It’s easy to be “passionate” when you are approaching the end of high school, living in your parents’ house, with few concerns. It’s very different when you need to make your own living, when people you knew are apparently doing far better than you, when you can’t live the life you want to live. Some people stick with their passions and don’t regret their choices. Other people drop out of school, with little but the debt to show for it. The only thing I can say is that whatever you do, figure out how to apply what you learn to problems that people need solving. Sometimes the application is obvious, e.g. accounting or engineering. Sometimes, maybe for most college grads, it’s not so obvious. Your major does not determine your future, but some paths will be closed off to you with your choice of major. I generally recommend not closing off something that seems like a good option, and taking the opportunity to explore those options even if it means making “suboptimal” choices. For example, I did not apply to any technical schools like MIT because I wasn’t sure I wanted to stick with engineering. I instead went to my state’s flagship university, where effectively every conceivable major was available. Maybe I would have had a better result if I had applied to and attended a technical school, but I doubt I’m far off from whatever the “optimal” might have been. In summary, treat the college major decision, or even whether to go to college at all, as a problem where you have very imperfect information. You want to get as much information as possible about college itself and the paths it leads to afterwards, and base your decision on that. You should follow your interests, but don’t make decisions based on any emotions that will change significantly.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Does UIUC offer scholarships to out of state students?
Answer: I don’t know about UIUC as a whole: it’s a big and varied school. I spent effectively all of my time in engineering, mainly in electrical and computer engineering. But I would not expect any state university in the U.S. to provide scholarships to out-of-state students where it significantly offset costs. There has been a push for more scholarships and whatnot during the last ten years (I was asked to donate), but I would not expect any substantial scholarship to come until junior year, nor cover any more than in-state tuition.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is it hard to get an Android developer job in the USA for a computer science student who is studying a master’s in the US?
Answer: If you are not a U.S. citizen and not from Australia, Canada, or Mexico, you must meet a high bar and convince an employer to sponsor you for a work visa. Go look up the requirements on the H-1B visa on your own. If you are a U.S. citizen or one of the specific aforementioned countries, you don’t have to meet the same bar. However, the bar is still quite high, and if you don’t demonstrate performance in your first couple years of working, you will find it increasingly difficult to find jobs. Note that I haven’t said anything about Android development: these guidelines are general. I don’t know anything about the Android developer market. Since it doesn’t take a master’s degree to become an Android developer, I imagine a foreigner would have to be quite good to get a work visa.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Should I get a second master’s degree to get an SWE job?
Answer: Maybe. The big question is whether you’d be accepted to a master’s program that would enable a software engineering job. If you don’t have the relevant undergraduate degree, it’s a jump too far and many reputable programs would reject you immediately. If you have the relevant undergraduate degree, why bother with another master’s degree? I might look at an associate’s or second bachelor’s degree in computer science or software engineering instead. Without any details on country of residence, existing degrees, etc., I can’t say anything useful beyond that.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Why do they say STEM majors are the only worthwhile majors that lead to employment, but then you see "biology" on lists of the most worthless 4-year college degrees?
Answer: There are three important concepts for this question and for life in general. Just because something “leads” to employment doesn’t guarantee anything. Having two legs (natural or not) leads to being a world class sprinter, but two legs is hardly sufficient. A STEM degree is (often) necessary for a STEM job, but not sufficient. Next, if you have hundreds of thousands of biology grads applying to medical and graduate schools, but only a few thousand slots, what’s going to happen? The schools take the best graduates. What happens to the rest? Not only do they not get into med or grad school, the job market is flooded with such people: very high supply with low demand, resulting in low pay. It becomes “worthless” in the eyes of those graduates. But the degree has plenty of worth for those who became doctors. Finally: if you graduated with a C average from a diploma mill “university,” does that make you remotely prepared for a medical/law/grad school? Would you want your health or legal future dependent on such a person? Or would you prefer someone who was at the top of her class at the best school in your country? People want the best if they can get it, and they will often pay more for those people. Here’s how I would explain to my kids how think about college with regards to future employment in a STEM field: I’ll add to or restructure this as I mull on it some more.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is computer science oversaturated these days, and is there any other alternative degrees that pays as well or better than computer science in the STEM field these days?
Answer: Crap is oversaturated across all STEM fields. There is little tolerance for crap in any such workplace or industry. Even mediocrity will result in unemployment. Do you really want your medical staff having a 90% correctness rate? Your civil engineers being 90% correct? A lot of people are going to die with those sorts of people working. No one is expected to be perfect, but striving for perfection is expected. The difference with CS is that it’s a younger and less regulated field. So lots of schools are graduating people who can’t be trusted to do the work at a reliable standard. Just because you graduate doesn’t mean you can do the job. In the U.S., look at a CS bachelor’s degree the same way you would a bio premed bachelor’s. If you aren’t going to execute at the level that will get you into a MD program, the value of that degree drops precipitously. If you can execute at a very high level, you will be well compensated. The bonus being that a CS grad doesn’t incur medical school debt.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is it easier to apply for a PhD directly after a bachelor's degree than a master's degree?
Answer: Standards vary between fields and between countries. I don’t know how most countries or non-STEM fields operate. In my areas (ECE and CS) in the U.S., the bar is lower in terms of requirements when applying for PhD from bachelor’s. The reasoning is that most people drop out of PhD programs anyway. It’s like comparing venture capital investing, where most investments are expected to fail, versus standard retirement investing, where you avoid failures like the plague. So for bachelor’s grads, admissions casts a wide net for potential and expects most to fail. If you are a master’s graduate, you’ve had two years to demonstrate potential, so many admissions folks will want clear proof by that point. Some people would call that “harder.” I personally think that’s a brutal and possibly unfair attitude (it took me much more than two years to demonstrate research potential, and I’m not an isolated case due to the major shifts in my research area at the time), but that’s what some of them are thinking. It’s not a universal attitude, but it’s still a common one.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Should I double major something in computer science, and is it beneficial?
Answer: For the vast majority of people, you should not double major, and it will not be beneficial for the cost incurred. The double major credential in itself is of no value in job hunting. The content of the double major may be of value. But a double major generally requires you to take a slew of courses that are of questionable value, sometimes clearly no value. The additional cost of a double major, in time, money, and split attention (usually resulting in lower grades/academic achievement) is almost always not worth what you gain. As I’ve said in prior answers, a master’s degree in computer science/engineering is far better value and will likely allow you to take those courses that you would have taken in a double major. The master’s degree is table stakes for some jobs. And many schools will provide assistantships for master’s students, so at least you’ll get paid for attending the 1–2 years of school. With the jump in seniority and salary one often gets, it’s a no-brainer decision.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Why are branches of computer science born so quickly but many disappear in less than two years? Are computer science students tired of chasing changes all the time, and a lot of investment is wasted? It might be much better to study statistics.
Answer: I’m not sure what you classify as a “branch of computer science.” The actual branches of computer science are young compared to the “real” sciences and may diminish relative to other areas, but don’t disappear. Computer (micro)architecture, compilers, operating systems, databases: there are new developments and a lot of computer science students don’t study them, but those fields have been around for decades and haven’t left. What disappears are fads: the new hot thing which gets a lot of attention but is then dropped because it doesn’t make money for either individuals or corporations. Often some language is the new hotness, but languages come and go all the time. NoSQL databases were hot maybe a decade ago. What happens is that 20-somethings think it’ll change the world, but they don’t understand enough about what’s different and whether the new technology/tool is actually a displacing technology (generally not). Computer science curricula at top universities are set so that students study actual branches of the discipline and not fads. Learn the fundamentals and you can deal with fads as they come and go.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: How do I ask a tech company for one of their engineers to help my robotics club? We currently have no supervisor/representative that knows about engineering. And we wouldn’t need them every week just once a month.
Answer: I wouldn’t bother. Most such requests would be dropped on the floor. Your interests (finding someone to donate their time) run somewhat counter to theirs (getting as much work done and profit in as possible). Even if the person you contacted were interested, finding the right person would be a significant task and take away time from running the business. As previous answers state, you’re better off contacting local technical schools/universities: people whose job is to educate. The ideal is a parent with their own interest in robotics, or friends who have an interest, but presumably you’ve already tried that.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is a Bachelor's degree in mechanical Engineering or Physics more beneficial? I am interested more in Physics, but I am concerned about employment. Is it possible for me to learn physics through the ME curriculum? Thanks
Answer: What “benefit” are you seeking? Your personal education, or employment? Physics degree holders at all levels are often underemployed. There are a huge number of physics PhDs who work in something else. There are effectively no physics jobs for lesser physics degree holders. Because of the glut of physics PhDs, those folks get paid less than engineering PhDs. Despite all that, there are plenty of physics graduates who wouldn’t have changed their education choices. So again, what’s your goal? In any traditional engineering curriculum, you will be learning physics. Building things to work in the natural world requires knowing the rules of the natural world. However, you won’t be learning much of anything that doesn’t deal with your specific discipline. Go look at the schools you plan to apply to and do your own research on their degree content: the curricula of most physics and engineering programs are available online. Even most of the course syllabi is available at the top programs: you can find out what you’d be learning semester-to-semester and even week-to-week if you were a student at that school. If you are not capable of doing that research, you probably shouldn’t be applying to university in the first place.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I have seen a bunch of CS vs CE bachelor’s degree, but I can't decide yet because I have no idea of what I love. What degree should I pursue if I am lost?
Answer: A rough breakdown of the responsibilities: From the standpoint of prior education: If you are good at both, I would go into computer engineering to hedge my bets. You will get a basic software education, you will have opportunity to move more into software even before you graduate, and your hardware background will serve you in a variety of software engineering jobs, like writing device drivers. I was an electrical engineering student, but I ended up having a complete overlap with computer engineering by the time I finished undergrad, and I did mostly software courses/research in graduate school. I have worked only as a software engineer in my 16 years after PhD, on close-to-metal software such as compilers and device drivers.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: How do people who complete their PhD or master’s manage tuition fees with studies?
Answer: In general, graduate school should not be done unless one is financially compensated. So many degrees, undergraduate and graduate, are already worthless without digging yourself into a financial pit. Most PhDs I knew in school had assistantships: teaching or research commitments for which they were given a tuition waiver (it was paid for) and a stipend to live off of. All those teaching assistants for undergraduate courses are doing it for compensation. So those folks make a living while they’re in school. There are also fellowships to fund students with no work requirement, but are harder to come by. The National Science Foundation’s is possibly the best known one in the STEM areas. If you are a potential PhD student in the U.S. and are not offered financial compensation, run, don’t walk, away. However bad you want the PhD, you’re probably not going to get it, because the professors and administration are not invested in you. Some master’s degree candidates in engineering also have assistantships. The other group of master’s students I knew best were MBAs, and they almost always had to pay for the privilege, or had an employer pay in exchange for work commitments. But as shown in the above article, some people pay for the privilege and screw themselves over.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I'm planning to major in finance, and I'm not sure if I should minor in mathematics, data science, or CS. What should I do?
Answer: No one after school cares about your minors as a credential. Period. I had two and they were usually held against me. No one even cares about your degree after a few years: what you’ve done more recently matters a lot more. Employers do care about what you can do for them in the near future. Put the minor out of your mind and look (and ask) what coursework you can take, and what experiences you can have, that make you a better candidate than your classmates and people from other schools. In that respect, hardcore finance probably benefits from mathematics and data science/statistics. But since I only have friends in the area and don’t work in it myself, you should be asking verified professionals (and not unverified people on Quora).

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Can you start earning your bachelor’s at 33? Then your Masters, and afterwards, your PHD? Is this normal?
Answer: If you are contemplating this path, make sure you’re doing it for the right reasons (i.e. not showing off or thinking you’ll become a professor) and the economics work out. For the PhD specifically, most PhDs don’t pay off for the time invested even when you start university at 18. Having an estimated 15 fewer years of lifetime earnings doesn’t help.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What makes PhD candidates able to fill some of these higher up roles (specifically in software industry), such as subsets of AI? Don't PhD candidates primarily work on research? What makes them more qualified? Coursework?
Answer: Here’s a related example. Who should be the person in charge of making non-graphics programs run on GPUs? Maybe it should be the guy who did research in trying to run such programs on GPUs. Ian Buck did his PhD at Stanford on exactly that.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Should I study computer science or is the field becoming oversaturated?
Answer: Only the low-knowledge, low-skill “computer science” jobs are saturated. Which is why those jobs pay miserably. Most of my grad school friends, now in their 40s, make over $250k/year. Some make multiple times that. If the supply actually matched demand, they’d make a lot less. As for whether you should study computer science, I have no clue what your ability level is. The overall field is going the way computer engineering did: the top players get outsized pay, and the average and lower get little. If you have been a top student at math and science, then you stand a decent chance of being a top player. If you have been scraping by, not a great chance.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is it possible to work with AI and machine learning-related jobs with a computer engineering bachelor’s degree?
Answer: That depends on what you define as “machine learning-related.” I knew people with only a bachelor’s degree working at Cerebras and Waymo. A few were even working on machine learning directly. The likelihood of most computer engineering’s bachelor’s grads to get those jobs? Close to zero. Everyone came from a top-10 school, had excellent grades, and those that had previous work experience came from very selective companies. When people want to get into a hot field, only the top candidates get the jobs.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Will hardware engineering be taken over by AI? I am interested in getting that job.
Answer: Taken over completely? Not until some general artificial intelligence is developed. Parts of it replaced? Yes. Nothing new there. Hardware engineering today looks nothing like hardware engineering 20–30 years ago, which looks nothing like hardware engineering 50–60 years ago. Automation has eaten most of the easy/low-level stuff. There is an entire electronic design automation (EDA) industry with many billions of dollars of market cap and revenue dedicated to that task. Go look up Synopsys, Cadence, and Mentor Graphics (now Siemens EDA). Applying ML to design automation is just an incremental step in a decades-old progression. What already happens today is that if you’re really good, you will be put in charge of the automation to build what needs to be built. If you are mediocre, you will be out of a job. That’s why many people on Quora recommend you get a graduate degree if you are going into computer hardware engineering (because if you can’t, you’re probably not good enough).

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What are the most versatile bachelor’s degrees (like business administration/management) but without math?
Answer: The moment you cut out math, you’re so hamstrung, it’s a bit silly to talk about versatility. You might as well say, “If I’m missing an arm, what can I play in American football?” If you’re not American, the answer is “the kicker, some of the time.” Out of several dozen players. Business administration without math is garbage. How do you measure money or performance without math? Even some basic calculus is a useful tool, which is why it’s taught in top business programs.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is it better to have industry experience before getting on a PhD program? Can one work in the industry after doing a PhD or will they be stuck in academia?
Answer: I don’t know where you come from, but no one in the developed world is “stuck” in academia. The problem is staying in academia past a PhD: there are far fewer spots than candidates. Orders of magnitude less. As for industry experience, a lot of PhD areas have no direct applicability to any significant industry. I don’t know how one is supposed to get industry experience in those fields. No industry experience is the norm, but people working in applicable areas (e.g. computer engineering) may benefit from industry experience.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Anyone got tips to prepare to get a degree in computer sciences? I’m currently in 9th grade finally deciding where to go in my career but I don't even know how to code.
Answer: First, don’t worry about coding. I’ve worked at a variety of large tech companies and (successful) startups. I’ve made more money than I thought possible in high school. I did not code in anything meaningful until undergrad. I did not code seriously until graduate school. I’m actually discouraging my pre-teen children from learning coding because I don’t think they’re going to benefit much, and have a lot to lose. I’m prioritizing things like piano lessons (music has parallels with engineering) and sports. One of the most important lessons in life, which a few kids at least as smart as me didn’t learn, is that sometimes you have to work through obstacles and frustration to get to your goal. My coworkers and I were discussing the appropriate training for kids to become software engineers a week or two ago. And it boiled down to this: Do well in math → do well in geometry → do well in proofs in geometry class. It’s that kind of structured thinking that makes a good programmer. Does my code do the right thing for the right input? For all right inputs? Does it handle the “wrong”/unexpected inputs correctly? Shit programmers see that something works and call it done. Good programmers cover their bases and their asses. The second thing you can do is get used to thinking about complex systems: lots of moving parts. School generally won’t teach you that sort of thing, and I’m not sure where you’re going to get the exposure. Maybe some complicated puzzles, electronics kits, that sort of thing. Maybe buy a cheap, small computer like an Arduino or Raspberry Pi and build something that interests you. (Nothing kills a career plan like disinterest.)

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What are the extra facilities available in MIT, Stanford, CMU, UC Berkley over Georgia Tech for a Master’s in Computer Engineering?
Answer: Facilities aren’t the biggest factor when we’re talking about ranking or reputation of engineering programs. Especially when we’re talking Georgia Tech, which has spent significantly more per undergraduate student than similarly ranked schools for the last few decades. That act creates higher rankings, but not necessarily better outcomes.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Should you apply to a very good PhD before finishing your Master's (so to start the PhD the next year) or wait to finish your Master's and apply with your marks (increasing your likelihoods, but starting 1 year later)?
Answer: Your question shows a misunderstanding of the PhD. “Marks” (grades) are far less important than your ability to do independent research. That evidence is what you need to increase the likelihood of acceptance. Show you can do independent research (e.g., authorship in peer reviewed publications). Have nothing, you can count on rejection. If you have to wait until something is accepted, then you wait.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I really messed up my bachelor’s degree since I failed and repeated so many courses. Now, I got rejected from a master's admission and couldn't get any job either. What should I do?
Answer: You need to lower your sights. Someone who “repeated so many courses” does not belong in graduate school. Don’t waste time trying to pursue it. There are no shortage of applicants to graduate schools and any school taking you just wants your money. For jobs: you probably haven’t looked at jobs that don’t require a bachelor’s degree. You haven’t said what your major was, and I’m not sure it even matters. I don’t know if you simply aren’t fit for college or had some life issues, but if you aspire to a career, you need to find something you can perform at and/or get your life in order. Work on those things. You might be better off taking a menial job until you figure that out. I’ve known PhDs that waited tables to do the same.

Name: Shane Ryoo
