Question: Would it be easier for an international student who graduated from a more prestigious university such as UCLA or Pitzer to find a job in the U.S.?
Answer: I’ve never heard of Pitzer, but apparently it’s a Claremont College (which I have heard of). Which illustrates the most important point: each individual has their own opinion/standard for“prestige.” What you think is prestigious likely differs from your potential employers’. To answer the question: This is all talking about long term employment. There is also the optional practical training (OPT) attached to the F-1 student visa, but for most people it’s only good for one year. For certain STEM areas, it can be extended an additional two years. All this comes back to thinking about things from the employer’s perspective. I’m hardly a typical employer, but using myself for example: So if you want to work in the U.S. long term, study hard and work hard in an area that we actually have a shortage in.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Should I do a computer science minor or computer engineering master’s? I know there are significant differences between both, but from an industry perspective, what is more valuable?
Answer: Minors are effectively worthless as credentials. I had two (as a EE) and they were usually commented on negatively: the CS minor for being too close, the business minor for being a distraction. I left them off my resume and my interview results improved. The only minors I’ve ever found interesting in the thousands of resumes I’ve reviewed were in wildly different areas from science/engineering: history and classics come to mind. A few classes do not necessarily make you able to do significantly better engineering work for your employer. Your employer cares about what you can do for him/her, not your credentials past an undergraduate degree (if even that). What matters is whether the minor coursework allows you to get a job that you would otherwise not be able to get. A computer engineering master’s can have value, but if you don’t have an electrical/computer engineering or computer science undergraduate degree, you will not be prepared and will be rejected from most programs. Even other engineers do not have the prerequisites for a computer engineering master’s. Do not put credentials above knowledge, experience, and the ability to apply them to tasks that need to be done. Few people get paid to sit around spewing words. My PhD would be worse than worthless, as it is for some people I knew in school, if I didn’t have the knowledge and experience gained during the process or if it weren’t applicable to what I do day-to-day.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What was the topic of your master's thesis or doctoral dissertation?
Answer: Master’s: how to use microarchitectural features such as predication and speculation to reduce the amount of dynamically executed code on a microprocessor with the appropriate support (Intel Itanium). PhD: how to optimize “general purpose” (non graphics) code for GPU using CUDA on NVIDIA GPUs. Part of the content was reproduced from an earlier paper of mine, which was the first published guide for optimizing non graphics codes for CUDA devices. Funnily enough, the work I was most proud of from a novelty/technical perspective was in neither document. I did publish the work, though.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: How can I get a job any kind of job in the united states? I am from Nigeria and I studied biochemistry at my undergraduate level.
Answer: You probably don’t as a foreigner without advanced education. We have no shortage of people with biochemistry undergraduate degrees. If you are trying to move to the U.S., the options I see are:

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: With major tech companies like Oracle relocating out of state, are the boom days of Silicon Valley ending?
Answer: No, the boom days ended decades ago, either when we ran out of space or when we (finally) stopped being the only ones playing this game. We are now in a eat-the-weak phase: young companies eat the old and slow. Oracle is getting eaten and is moving to cut costs and not fight companies willing to pay more to their employees. Oracle missed the shift in how databases are managed in the cloud. Upstarts like Snowflake and Databricks are capturing Oracle’s market share and its ambitious engineers. AWS, Google, and MS Azure are the other players in that space: companies that know how to operate in the cloud. Top talent in Silicon Valley know where the top talent migrates. LinkedIn makes it trivial these days. Oracle hasn’t been a recent destination for top talent any more than IBM has. They’re not willing to pay for the talent. Like IBM, Oracle is still making plenty of money. Like IBM, they’re operating a cash cow which will peter out eventually. They’re past peak.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Should one consider emerging technologies when making career choices?
Answer: Yes, one should “consider” emerging technologies. However, how much they should be weighed is very hard to determine. You should gravitate to your strengths and interests before worrying about emerging technologies: nothing kills a career faster than disinterest plus incompetence. Technologies move both faster and slower than you might expect. These few cases demonstrate two major principles: The only thing I can really say for sure is that if you’re in your teens or twenties, avoid mentally easy things that will get eaten by ML or any other form of automation. Like manual factory work or manual coal mining, they will die. For example, I would not be surprised if fast food is fully automated before I retire.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What major should I study for my master’s with a bachelor's degree in business administration and no work experience?
Answer: You shouldn’t get a master’s at all. It’s statistically going to lack applicability to jobs, and you will end up with fewer job opportunities. Graduate education should generally be in service to jobs, especially when you have a business administration undergraduate degree. Figure out the job, then the education required.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Famous technology company founder are always from engineering background, regardles of America or China. Is accountant or business management CEO the weakpoint of technology company failure?
Answer: The premise is false. Several technology companies founders were not from serious engineering backgrounds. Steve Jobs is the most famous: he’s a tinkerer, not an engineer, with zero coursework in engineering. However, when the accountants or MBAs take over, that event is often the start of a slide to failure. Boeing is perhaps the most obvious contemporary example. It may take many years, perhaps decades, but ultimately management culture changes to care more about money and increasing profits rather than quality engineering.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Are the textbooks used for equivalent STEM courses the same or significantly easier ones at lower ranked schools like University of Idaho or University of Wyoming compared to HYPSM?
Answer: The textbooks are likely the same in at least a few cases. Introductory courses and the like. The amount you cover in the textbook almost certainly differs between institutions. Classes teach to the average. As I’ve said dozens of times previously on Quora, I once looked at the curricula of several introductory engineering courses at MIT, and those covered 30–50% more material than the introductory courses at schools ranked #8–10 at the time. The median engineering student in the U.S. wouldn’t be able to keep up at MIT. Classes teach to the average, and the average at MIT is far higher than the norm. And if you are an idiot that rages at any little thing, I received zero of my degrees from MIT and use it as an example because I have no horse in that race.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I have a bachelor’s degree of biomedical science. Can I get a master of biochemistry and then a PhD of chemical engineering?
Answer: If you aspire to graduate school, you should be able to do your own research. I imagine the shift from biomedical science to biochemistry is not too far. However, chemical engineering is about processes, and chemical reactors, and flows. As far as I know, biomedical science and biochemistry don’t touch those topics. You should be able to look at chemical engineering undergraduate curricula and graduate school prerequisites to confirm. If you are unable, you do not belong in graduate school.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: As a sophomore with a math-stats major and a bioinformatics minor, planning to apply for graduate school next year, should I pursue a dual degree in BME or continue with math-stats for my undergraduate studies if aiming for a master's in BME?
Answer: Thanks Professor Joshua Gross for the summons. There are so many issues with your question, Jacob Thompson. The biggest, and the reason I was summoned: why are you trying to get a BME master’s? Because if it’s to get a BME job, in the U.S. and several other countries, there are more BioE/BME undergraduates than BME total jobs. Not entry level jobs, not open jobs, ALL JOBS OF THAT CATEGORY IN THE USA. It’s beyond a glutted market. I was alerted to the issue by my former BME professor, who was trying to figure out why even his excellent graduate students couldn’t get BME jobs. He came across BLS and ASEE data which shows the discrepancy, and I looked up the same data for succeeding years to confirm his findings. Tiny market and the people in that market often make significantly less money than in other engineering disciplines. I don’t know why you want to pursue a BME master’s, but if it’s for a BME job, prepare to be disappointed. Other issues: If you are really dead set on BME, get a BME undergraduate degree. But I wouldn’t do it and my BME graduate wife I and I are not letting my kids do it.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Suppose 90% of males in s. Korea could get a score on today's Math GRE in the USA that is sufficient to get a PhD in math. Why does it make sense to create free PhD programs, even part time (while Koreans work) or distance, so they all can get one?
Answer: Ridiculousness up the wazoo, “Mr. TruthDaddy, the Truthseeking Man .“ Are you a North Korean? Even the Russian elites aren’t this disconnected from reality. The entrance requirements of a degree are different from the graduation requirements. Just because you can do well on the SAT or ACT doesn’t mean you can graduate from a bachelor’s program. The GRE is the same way, especially when we are talking about the PhD. It’s about independent research, not test taking. And the adjustment, speaking from personal experience, is very difficult. Which is why about half drop out. The idea of 90% of Korean men operating at that level is ridiculous. (I am ethnic Korean.) No ethnic population can. You need to select for ability and create such a population: you choose out of the graduate student population. And as I said before, only 50% of those people “succeed.” If you define graduation as succeeding, which is debatable. Finally, as Professor Joshua’s Gross’s answer similarly states, the Republic of Korea is in the midst of a demographic crisis unmatched by any other country in the world. Every year that goes by, the birth rate drops and is reportedly around 0.7 children per woman in 2024. The suicide rate is unmatched by any other developed country. What should be free is mental health care, child care, and child support. Then Koreans might survive and actually have babies. One of the most laudable traits of the Korean people is their commitment and drive. Unfortunately, it’s literally killing them/us.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Should I major in engineering or nursing?
Answer: I know a few people who have done both, so I’ve asked them to answer. Since I’m an engineer and married to someone who’s done both, I’ll give you my opinion as well. The fact that you’d ask this question means you don’t know what either entails, or your preference for either job. Effectively everyone I know personally would have a clear preference for one over the other. You need to arm yourself with data and facts, then make an informed decision.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is a biological science degree worth it if I don't want to work in health care in the future? Would it still be useful in terms of other job prospects with decent earning potential?
Answer: There are a lot of fields that use biology without being in (human) health care. Think anything that deals with living organisms. If you plan to target those careers, a biological science degree makes sense. Note that there may be more specific majors tailored to those careers, some of which are requirements (e.g. veterinary medicine). As for “decent earning potential,” many people I know in those fields make a livable salary. Others work jobs that don’t require a college degree, so their degrees were wasted as far as career selection is concerned. Always keep in mind that: Funny side story: I was on vacation with the extended family last week, and my doctor relatives were bitching about how thankless medicine is these days. Every idiot comes in thinking they know everything because they read it on a website or heard it from Dr. Oz and just wants the doctor to prescribe their drug of choice. The reason I went into computing is because computers and the people who build them are generally a lot more rational than the average patient.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Can I do MS in computer science after graduating from electrical and electronics engineering?
Answer: Depending on the school, yes. It’s a common path that has been walked many times in the past.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Should I major in computer engineering or electrical engineering? I don't care about the salary for the two majors, just which one has more growth for innovations in the future.
Answer: Both have potential for innovation. The form those innovations take are different. If you don’t get a graduate degree in either area, the odds of you making actual innovations drops to close to zero. While I received my bachelor’s degree in EE, my talents and interests ultimately were in computer engineering, so I shifted in graduate school.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Which university is better for a computer science degree? (for Bachelor) Purdue University or McGill university? (I want to do my master's in the USA after my bachelor's degree and live there)
Answer: As far as your stated goals of a master’s degree in the U.S. and potential work/residency, I don’t think it matters that much. I would balance cost and reputation. Doing undergrad in the U.S., everything else being equal, may give you a slight advantage. But if you don’t excel at Purdue, you’re not getting into graduate school. What will matter is: Note that the H-1B lottery has been oversubscribed for many years: you may not get it even if your employer wants you. Rich companies might employ you in a foreign office for a while until it goes through. Not-so-rich companies may give up.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I just graduated high school and I am trying to pick a major. I am deciding between computer science and mechanical engineering. I like computer science more but I heard it’s so hard to find a job. What do I do?
Answer: It’s hard to find a job in any major for some people. I don’t know which country the OP lives in. I’ll talk about the U.S., as that’s where I live. There are far more computer science jobs than mechanical engineering jobs. However, many (most?) computer science graduates can’t do those jobs. They don’t actually learn much of anything in school. They practice voodoo programming (go look it up). You don’t find many such mechanical engineering graduates because ABET imposes minimal requirements on what is taught and who gets to graduate. In the U.S., rigorous computer science programs will prepare you and except in major recessions companies will climb over each other to hire you. I haven’t known a top-15 CS school grad with a GPA over 3.5 that had any trouble finding jobs. Which means: If you go to a diploma mill or get barely passing grades, you’re going to have trouble getting a job in any major.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Would you love to get a new Tesla Cybertruck?
Answer: Nope. I see them daily, living in Silicon Valley near the factory. If I wanted an electric truck, I’d probably get a F-150 Lightning. I don’t trust Rivian to stay in business long enough to maintain service (had a few friends working there). But I don’t want a truck. Incidentally, the first car I test drove when I decided to replace my old car late last year was a Model Y. The road noise and ride quality were the worst I’ve experienced in recent memory out of any vehicle, including trains and school buses. I bought a different brand, even though I had to wait a few months for the exact features I wanted plus shipping.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: How is Purdue University compared to Georgia Tech and MIT in mechanical engineering?
Answer: As I’ve said hundreds of times before and will again, the variance in ability at those schools far exceeds the difference in their means. The top students at Purdue will easily be stronger engineers than the lower half of MIT graduates. The very top probably could have gotten into MIT or Georgia Tech, but were Indiana residents and saved their money. When you are coming from a state like California, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, or Texas, the local flagship state school should be a student’s default for engineering undergraduate study. The value cannot be beat unless CMU, MIT, or Stanford is offering a full ride. Most strong engineers will get at least a master’s degree after the bachelor’s. That graduate institution is the much more important one in one’s career. One of my friends went to undergrad at a school ranked over #100, then came to UIUC (#2 at the time) for his PhD. Successful startups, millions in the bank, and no one cares where he went to undergrad.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: How does a first-year computer science major decide between pursuing systems, theory, and machine learning?
Answer: You shouldn’t be choosing any of them, unless you’re choosing which course to take first. You are not in a position to do so. You should be taking classes in all of them and determining your aptitude and interests. That is why you’re in undergrad in the first place. Knowing the basics of all three will serve you in the long run.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Should I resist A-level math at university if I get a D? I really want a high paying job in economics in the future and I don’t know how this grade will affect my job prospects.
Answer: Do you understand how much math, both pre-collegiate and college-level, you need for professional economics? Let alone the “high paying” jobs? You need to rethink both your approach to mathematics now and your potential careers in the future. D-level performance now does not lead to your stated goal.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is a legal career more exciting in Silicon Valley then Wall Street? Gave NYC a try and it’s too lonely to live here for just a career and not social interaction too
Answer: If you find NYC lonely, I have trouble seeing why you would find Silicon Valley less lonely and more exciting. There are far fewer people and less going on. People are also extremely focused on their careers. I find a lot of single people are lonely here as well. The much ballyhooed departures from California, at least in Silicon Valley, are heavily fueled by such people. I think you’d regret moving here. Wherever you are, I would participate in more single’s activities and meet more people.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I have about 74% in a bachelor’s of computer engineering. What US university will accept me for a master's in data science?
Answer: If you didn’t finish any bachelor’s, none. Effectively all reputable master’s programs require a bachelor’s degree for admission. if you finished any degree, that would depend on what you finished in the computer engineering degree. The big requirement that comes to mind is linear algebra: you’re probably going to need it, and if you don’t have it, you’ll have to get it somehow. That plus good grades means most U.S. data science master’s programs will at least look at your application seriously. Barely passing grades likely means only diploma mills will accept you.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I was committed to Purdue as an integrated business engineering major but just got off the UCI waitlist as an undeclared major. I’m originally from CA. Which should I choose?
Answer: By “originally from CA,” are you a current resident of CA and still eligible for in-state tuition? And are you not an Indiana resident, and thus paying out-of-state for Purdue? That’s the real question. First, if you are an Indiana resident, take Purdue. No question, skip the rest of the answer. I had to look up the program: “integrated business AND engineering.” It’s fundamentally a business program with some engineering taster courses: you wouldn’t be able to get an engineering job, and the main benefit is that you’d know enough about reality that you wouldn’t be proposing unrealistic shit and the engineers working with you won’t think you’re a complete idiot. Other schools have similar mixed business/engineering programs: UIUC (my alma mater) has had one in a minor+ format since about 1995. The experience is not sufficiently unique that I would be paying $15k/year more for it (2024 tuition rates appear to be Purdue out-of-state $29k/year, UCI in-state $14k). While I am a fan of such programs and was in one (the aforementioned minor program), keep in mind that from a jobs perspective you’re competing with MBAs with engineering undergraduate degrees, and they will have more education in both the engineering and the business sides. The money they’d demand is likely a lot higher, but you’d be competing with them for jobs at some point. And there’s no shortage of MBAs, especially during economic downturns. In general, I would say that you should not be paying out-of-state tuition for any major unless: The specific example I’m thinking of is computer science: there are a decent number of Illinois high school grads who were not accepted into UIUC CS and their only competitive options are out of state. If my kids were looking at this decision and we lived in California at the time, I’d tell them to go to UCI. But I wouldn’t have let them apply as an undeclared either. I don’t know your odds of being able to transfer to the major of your choice in the long run. I might take Purdue just for the security: $29k/year is a lot, but maybe you can handle it. Incidentally, I lived in Illinois and Michigan for 30 years. I don’t want to deal with that weather again, and I don’t know if you know what you’re getting into. I’ve also been on the Purdue campus, and all the red brick would drive me insane. I’d take Irvine over West Lafayette.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I’m very confused as to what I should do in the future. Should I become a doctor or go into AI? Which is better, salary-wise and for the future, keeping in mind that I am interested in both of them?
Answer: Short answer: if you need to ask other people, you shouldn’t be making a decision. Be a big boy/girl/whatever and make your own decisions on your future, and own your career decisions. Because the vast majority of people who don’t own their decisions drop out of education before reaching those jobs. Your “interest” has no knowledge or experience backing it up. “Go into AI” in particular is an ignorant statement: AI is not a single, coherent field. You need to state your country of citizenship. Medicine education and requirements vary by country. Medicine is a calling. The fact that you consider it an option tells me that you shouldn’t be doing it. Most of the working adults in my family are medical doctors, and none of them seriously considered any other options, at least by the time they finished undergrad. (One did electrical engineering for undergrad study.) I’ve known people who failed that path even with doctor relatives exerting pressure: they weren’t committed. Lack of commitment kills the odds you will finish. The range of salaries and outcomes overlap and are very wide. If you are a top medical doctor, you will make a ridiculous amount of money until you retire. If you are a top computer scientist/engineer, you will make a ridiculous amount of money until you retire. If you are a shitty doctor or computer scientist, you probably would fail out before you finish the education, and you can still lose your job even after finishing education. Even my pre-teen kids know what it takes for either path: partly because they have family members in both paths, but mostly because I keep telling them “Go use Google, then explain it to me.” Go use Google, then explain each job and the pathway to that job to yourself. If you know yourself and know the job, the path will become clearer. If you live in the U.S., you don’t have to make a decision until end of undergrad: be a CS major with the prerequisites for the MCAT.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What level of education or training is typically required for the types of jobs you're interested in?
Answer: Required? Just a bachelor’s in computer science or computer engineering. The problem is that the vast majority of such people have never taken a single course in compilers and maybe one course in computer architecture, so they’re not qualified. Most entry level candidates for the jobs I’m interested in have PhDs, with most of the remainder being MS grads. People usually don’t get exposure until they get into graduate school. The sole exception I’ve worked with in the last 15 years had a bachelor’s from MIT.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Why does Silicon Valley investment in the 2024 T**** campaign seem to be transactional?
Answer: I would be surprised if the relationship of anyone with the Trump campaign is anything but transactional.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is it a good idea to double major in computer science and electrical engineering or computer science and physics?
Answer: Bad idea for most people. None of my double technical major friends thought the double major was useful after school, if they got a graduate degree afterwards. What do you think you are gaining by double majoring? The vast majority of your potential employers will not be impressed. At all. I didn’t do a double major and I see zero value in a double technical major today. You would be better served by doing graduate school and picking up courses and other information from whatever fields you need (or are interested in). The only double majors I personally find interesting are in wildly different areas. Get the other major in history, I’d find you interesting.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Why do big careers companies have jobs with hours so many a week 40+ that you usually don't get time to relax, and with high salaries. How come they don't hire two or more people with 20+ or about half hours each so it's easier for them and company?
Answer: And how do you expect someone to live on 20 hours/week of wages at current market rates? I know why your former employer (Walmart) would say such a thing, Mohammad Shuja: not to make the worker’s life easier, but to avoid paying them as a full time employee and thus avoiding per-employee costs and benefits. We’re not stupid.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is it true that you could forget everything you learned at university about your major if you don't work in your major?
Answer: Yes, certainly if you work in a job that doesn’t need a college degree. If you are in a job that actually requires a degree (as opposed to it being an arbitrary cutoff), kind of, as Professor Joshua Gross’s answer says. You could forget almost every fact. What you should be gaining in university is structured thinking within one or more domains. Certainly within your major. Maybe that thinking maps to other domains, and when that happens, I’d call that a useful education. Those are some basics. It shouldn’t take a PhD to think independently and flexibly.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Why is Oracle moving its headquarters from the Bay Area to Texas?
Answer: The benefits (lower taxes) outweigh the negatives (requiring HQ people to live in Texas). The negatives are negligible. Oracle still maintains many technical teams in the SF Bay Area. That’s where that talent has aggregated. But there’s no real reason for business folks to be in California, and Larry Ellison reportedly spends most of his time in Hawaii.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What happens if the new wave of tech jobs is too confusing for many people?
Answer: Technical jobs have always been too confusing for many people. There is nothing new in this regard for the next generation. The classic economic forces of supply (schools and training) and demand (the number of jobs needed/available), along with the wages they determine, will affect future supply and demand as people and institutions make changes. If there are lots of jobs, schools and bootcamps will train for those jobs, wages will increase until those jobs are somewhat filled, people will teach themselves and leave their own jobs for the new (higher paying) ones, etc. That’s why a centrally managed economy cannot keep up with rapid technological development: the market (via many different people acting in self-interest) is much more responsive at reallocating resources than a few people in an office, disconnected from day-to-day reality. It’s one of the reasons the USSR fell, and why Russia and China no longer follow that model.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: In computer science it's known that humans are more predictable than computers when choosing random numbers. In economics are computer systems causing more unpredictability than humans? Would computers being much simpler solve world''s economic woes?
Answer: Both questions are non sequiturs (they do not follow): This sounds like Isaac Asimov-style “Three Laws of Robotics” science fiction: it might make for an interesting story, but has no relation to modern technical reality.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Which is most promising, financially and other wise, for an undergraduate to consider for masters study; biology or life science, environmental science, nutrition, public health, business administration, data science or analytics, education?
Answer: As Professor Jeff Erickson’s answer says, you’re all over the place. I will go further and say that you should have chosen a field ahead of your bachelor’s and already know which master’s program you would be applying to. Stop doing things backwards and choose a field first. College degrees don’t have intrinsic value to employers: you are paid for applying what you know to a task that needs to be performed. Education determines a large portion of what you know. Most of those fields are reputed to be financially unpromising in the U.S. I don’t know where you live. Even the fields that could be promising end up not being that way for many people (business administration and data science).

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is it possible to get a master’s degree in computer engineering after getting a degree in agricultural engineering?
Answer: Possible? Maybe. Realistically? No. There is zero overlap of content between the two after basic physics and math. Around 2.5–3 years of learning that you would lack. Master’s programs in engineering are meant for people who did very well in the same area for undergrad. Curricula of engineering programs for just about any school is available online, and you can go confirm what I said by yourself for your own country.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Which international universities might offer me a scholarship for a bachelor's in software engineering after I have completed my A levels?
Answer: I don’t know about countries outside the U.S. Within the U.S., effectively no universities will offer you a scholarship: international students are income sources for U.S. universities. If you are operating at the genius level, there may be a handful of schools which may offer you a purely merit-based scholarship. These are rare enough as to be nonexistent.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Should I major in English since I love writing, or just major in Criminal Justice because English majors have a hard time finding jobs? I don’t really like law and government but want a high paying job and one that lets me write.
Answer: Why do you think either major would result in a high paying job? Your “reasoning” smacks of underpants gnomes. High wages are a result of low supply coupled with high demand. The ability to write English, and English and Criminal Justice degrees, are not in low supply or high demand. If you really want to write as part of a “high paying” job, write things that most people are incapable of writing. Such as technical documentation. Most such people I know personally are engineering or physics majors, since most English majors are incapable of understanding the terminology.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I am confused with life. If I don’t get into a good university in the USA, how can I get a good paying job there? I am willing to apply for a BBA in marketing.
Answer: If I don’t get into a good university in the USA, how can I get a good paying job there? Why is getting a job in the U.S. a goal? Are you a U.S. citizen or permanent resident? Effectively all foreigners studying undergraduate business in the U.S. will go back to their home countries, with the few exceptions being those that proceed to graduate study. Fresh undergrads are not worth the tens of thousands of dollars required to sponsor for a work visa. I am willing to apply for a BBA in marketing. You are “willing?” That’s a lackadaisical attitude. If you are a foreigner, that approach will not get you a job in the U.S. Bachelor’s degrees in marketing are more than plentiful: we have no need to import more. Information on how to get a work visa and apply for permanent residency are all online. There are hundreds of thousands of foreigners capable of researching that information and not asking this question, and have the education and work experience for things we actually need, like computer engineers and medical personnel. If you are a U.S. citizen or permanent resident, at least you don’t need to pass that immigration bar, but your attitude appears to be far too uncommitted. Almost half of undergraduate students do not finish, with little to show except student debt (which is not dischargeable in bankruptcy: you’re on the hook for life). I’d bet money you’ll end up in that category. Go find something you want to do, and will overcome all obstacles to complete the education and any other requirements. Until you do, don’t entertain the thought of college: it’s a waste of money and time. US citizens can join the military or enter a trade school if you want a path to education or money.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is a Masters degree worth it in the IT industry? I already completed my bachelor's degree in Computer Science. Does having a Masters matter salary-wise or when getting promoted? What are the advantages of having one in IT?
Answer: Outcomes depend on what you mean by “IT” and your role in it. Most people I interact with treat IT as the day-to-day digital information management of a business. Does the master’s degree help in that domain? Maybe: I wouldn’t know, as I don’t work in that area. I work in R&D domains: creating things that don’t already exist, or creating things that are much faster than what already exists. In my specific specialty and neighboring ones, a master’s degree is table stakes: bachelor’s graduates usually don’t enter the field because the core coursework and experience is gained during a graduate degree, not the bachelor’s. So the question is, what you are currently doing, or expect to do, versus what you want to be doing? Does the master’s enable anything for that difference? Does the 1–2 years of full time study pay off in lifetime earnings? It does for the fields I work in or adjacent to, but I don’t know what you do, or plan to do.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What could convince you as an immigrant family with a 3-year-old kid to move to San Francisco or Vancouver from Malmö Sweden if you have a decent salary and life as a senior IT specialist?
Answer: San Francisco or Vancouver proper? Nothing would convince me: I don’t want to live in a city. But that’s probably not the information you were looking for. Suburbs of those cities? I do live an hour outside San Francisco, but I’m not an immigrant: my parents are. However, I know a few Swedes, and a few Americans that spent some time in Sweden. My thoughts, based on what they’ve told me: It’s not a decision to be made lightly, as it’ll uproot your family. But it’s also a lot easier to move when your child is 3 years old and not 6 or older. I’ve only traveled through Vancouver, so I can’t knowledgeably comment on living there. There are some nice aspects to it that I’ve seen, but I would guess that someone from Malmö would find both cities dirty and heavy on petty crime. Which is why I don’t go into SF very often. But violent crime in SF is quite low compared to inland Californian cities and U.S. cities in general.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Should I double major in computer science and philosophy if it interests me?
Answer: You can if you want and the school lets you. Would I? No. People can (and I did) study philosophy on their own time, or with a smattering of coursework, without having the volume of coursework needed to graduate as a philosophy undergrad. There are large swaths of philosophy I haven’t touched as a result, but I’m not trying to be an academic. I followed one of my other interests (computing), make a lot of money doing that, and can spend my free time studying philosophy if I wanted to.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: How prevalent are psychedelics in the tech industry?
Answer: Some of the people who go to parties with “important” people are probably using them. A few of the low level workers might be using them. Particularly the youngest ones. The top experienced technical talent generally isn’t using them. Those people tend to be very socially conservative, sometimes outright boring: single marriages, no dangerous/thrill hobbies, nothing particular interesting about them. Even when they’re not at work, they’re thinking about work, and mind-influencing/altering substances degrade the ability to be hyper-rational. Even something like marijuana dulls the mental edge. I rarely drink alcohol myself. I buy OTC painkillers once every couple years: by the time I need it again, the old batch expired. I don’t touch anything stronger than those.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Should a Masters degree in a subject matter increase a person’s salary in a job directly related to said subject matter?
Answer: Not without including other factors. Salaries are established by supply and demand, at least in a developed country where the private sector is the dominant employer and the public sector takes cues from it. Presumably the master’s degree puts you in a slot where supply is lower. The question is, what is the demand? Demand comes from: In some (maybe most?) cases, the master’s degree provides inconsequential new capabilities, and you’re just riding on signaling and selection: most bachelor’s grads are incapable of being accepted to and graduating from a master’s program. You placed yourself above them by getting a master’s degree. In a few (technical) areas, the specialization afforded to you within a master’s degree enables you to work in a particular subfield, whereas the bachelor’s barely did, or didn’t at all. Moving to that subfield may create a salary spike. Or it might not, depending on the supply relative to the demand. In short, you can’t say that a master’s degree will universally result in a higher salary. It can, but it also might not, depending on circumstances.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Why are big tech companies leaving Silicon Valley for Texas?
Answer: For older companies that don’t require or use top Silicon Valley talent, the savings in corporate taxes and payroll outweigh the benefits of being in California. HPE and Oracle are the most recent ones I’ve heard of. Top talent moves around to the companies making waves and willing to pay for top talent. Oracle hasn’t been on the top list during this century. HP had a flood of its top Silicon Valley talent leave in the 2008–2010 timeframe (Google snapped up many of them). Apple had a surge around 2012, at the expense of Intel, corresponding with the design of their own processors. NVIDIA gained at the expense of SGI and Sun around 2008. And so on. If a company wants elite talent, they have to pay for it. HPE had most of its labor in Texas already. Compaq absorbed Tandem and then merged with HP 22 years ago, which put its headquarters in California. Then they started splitting off pieces: Agilent, then HPE. I consider the move a correction to a mistake. The sole potential outlier is Tesla, but they’ve been hiring quite heavily in California for engineering positions until the recent downturn. All this is natural flows of the corporate ecosystem. U.S. startups are still disproportionately founded in California, and as they grow they push out the mature companies that can’t afford or get the elite talent.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I have studied biology for five years but I failed to get admission in a medical college. Should I try once more, or should I switch my career to computer science?
Answer: Insufficient information provided. As you call yourself “Mishal Khan,” I cannot determine what country you reside in, and in any case I don’t know the rules for the South Asian countries where people with names similar to yours reside. In the U.S., medical school is a graduate program following an undergraduate degree. Failing to get admission implies either your grades, your MCAT score, or something else about your application is deficient. The MCAT can be retaken. The others cannot be corrected by the time you would apply for medical school. It does not follow that computer science would be an option for you. Nearly everyone in the U.S. that failed to get into medical school would not be a good fit for long term computer science study and career. In the U.S., I would look towards a career path in the same field but has less rigorous standards: nursing, physician’s assistant, or similar. As you have not disclosed your country, I can’t give you specific or tailored information.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: TX African American resident, 1530 SAT, 7/650 rank, 4.0 GPA and completed 19 AP Courses. I am a member of the National Honor Society, I'm an Eagle Scout. What are my chances of getting into UT Austin Computer Science or Texas A&M Computer Science?
Answer: I believe UT Austin has auto admission for your rank at Texas high schools. So if you actually exist with those credentials, 100% chance of admission. However, I don’t know about CS versus not. If you really are running those credentials, I would be applying to the top private schools (e.g. Stanford and MIT). You have a better-than-normal chance of acceptance (which is <5%, so that’s not saying much). And you are likely to pay less than the state schools, depending on your financial situation: much less if your family isn’t wealthy. However, depending on what your GPA means, your situation is not great for those schools. If most of the AP courses were Bs or Cs and your 4.0 is a weighted average, elite programs are not going to receive that well. You should prioritize mastery of material (A grade) instead of volume, especially going forward. CS grads with 3.0 GPAs are plentiful and not generally useful.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is taking an undergraduate in physics worth it? What kind of job can I apply to if I just graduated? Do I need to get a master's degree to get more high-paying jobs?
Answer: Short answer: by itself, no. As a prior answer says, most people who do physics plan to do it past undergraduate: to get a true physics job in the modern world, you generally need a PhD. My physics friends tell me that the master’s is a bail-out path for those that can’t finish the PhD. If a person doesn’t love physics that much, there are more applicable undergraduate majors, like engineering. Physics is a “go big or go home” path. Which jobs can you do? Jobs that require any undergraduate degree, of course, but that’s obvious. The interesting ones are those which are non-major-specific, but favor or require a technical education. Certain types of business consulting, like those done by Accenture and Deloitte, are relatively smooth avenues. Ignore the people who say physics is a gateway to engineering. That statement is not generally true in the U.S.: anything regulated or credentialed (especially civil engineering) requires you to have an ABET-accredited engineering undergraduate degree to work or to enter graduate education. Fields that do not have such requirements (some parts of computer engineering/science) are open to physics graduates, but such people are significantly hampered compared to people who studied the field full time.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I work a lot of extra hours and make good money doing that. Should I go to school to get a degree in the same field to work significantly less hours & make around the same/ slightly less?

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Will the Chip Act enable Intel to eventually compete with TSMC and Nvidia?
Answer: Two corrections: The big question for me with regards to competition is the talent pool at Intel. Intel management hasn’t kept salaries in line with the industry, and I would argue they’ve been cheapskates since at least the 1990s: “it’s a privilege to work at Intel, so we’re not going to pay as much as other companies.” They were going to raise salaries a year or two ago, then backed off on that and had layoffs. Given enough time, money, and talent, Intel is perfectly capable of beating any other company and has repeatedly done so in the past. We’ll see if they pony up the money for the talent.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Why does someone think computer engineering isn't the right job for me? I like computers and spend hours in front of one.

Liking and using something is very different from building something. Based on your “reasoning” and question history, Abdulla Sulaimani , you have some growing up to do before you’re ready to pursue an engineering education.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Are South Korea popular destinations for a foreign (non-western) software engineer?
Answer: I don’t know personally, as I am a western (American) ethnic Korean. If you’re talking about “destination” as a workplace, Korean workplaces are notorious for being high stress and sometimes abusive. It has never been a seriously considered option for me, despite (actually because) my being ethnic Korean. I am also not fluent in Korean, and since my wife is not Korean, I am not about to subject her or my children to the racism one finds there. Many Korean software engineers move to the U.S. and other “western” countries for better pay and working conditions.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Are there prestigious universities that allow computer science faculty members to work remotely 100% of the time, even if they reside in a different location in the world?
Answer: None to my knowledge. If a university allowed it at scale, it would be not-prestigious in short order. Even 100% remote software engineers or researchers are suboptimal. Faculty do not spend all their time doing research. Teaching, fund raising, outreach, mentoring graduate students, are all things that need some physical presence. If they are not physically present, you cannot force a meeting and create progress. When I’ve worked with professors who were on sabbatical or otherwise physically absent, it was a royal pain to get a hold of them. And when you can’t get a hold of them, work does not get done.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What do you think is the future of software engineering? Could advancements in technology eventually render it obsolete, or will these advancements serve as valuable tools that enhance the work of software engineers rather than replacing them?
Answer: The future will be different from the present. That fact has always been true in engineering. Software engineering changes more rapidly than traditional engineering. Software engineering today looks little like software engineering 50 years ago. Effectively no one is programming in assembly at scale anymore. The tools and hardware are tremendously more powerful. This trend is not going to change. Software engineering in a few decades will be different from today. Machine learning (“AI”) is one obvious technology that will give us new tools to work with. As Dallas’s answer similarly states, ML is crap at trying to provide things that require mathematical proofs for correctness, rather than statistical “accuracy.” That fact will not change anytime soon. Crappy software engineer wannabes will be even more out of a job. Good software engineers will likely be spending more time scrubbing ML-generated code for mistakes than writing code themselves.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Which job in the computer science industry has the best job opportunities and is safe from AI replacement?
Answer: Nothing. Everything is vulnerable to AI replacement. The blocker is cost of implementation relative to the savings: the same reason robots haven’t completely replaced humans in the fast food industry. Software engineers are expensive, but implementing the machine learning is really expensive. So AI is limited to much higher volume tasks at this time. “Best job opportunities” is something that: Nothing like that exists. There is nothing you can do that thousands of other people can’t also do, and will do in a hurry if the demand (and pay) rise up.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: How did you decide which branch of engineering you went in? How did it turn out, and would you have wanted to do something else? What made you think twice?
Answer: How did you decide which branch of engineering you went in? How did it turn out I didn’t stay strictly in electrical engineering: I moved to computer engineering and then computer science over time. But the EE degree was foundational to my PhD and my career so far, including multiple successful startups and stints at Apple and Waymo/Alphabet (where I worked mostly with Google engineers). I can’t complain. would you have wanted to do something else? Not really. Other jobs might have made more money, but they wouldn’t have matched the job security. What made you think twice? Nothing did.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Which alternatives to university or apprenticeship would you recommend to become an IT professional?
Answer: Define “IT professional.” For what I do, and everything adjacent to what I do, I would not recommend any alternative to university. There will be too many gaps in your knowledge otherwise. Even among many CS and software engineering graduates, they lack knowledge that I expect in a decent bachelor’s degree program. That’s why there’s a strong bias towards a very small set of top schools in recruiting: those people can be relied upon to have the fundamentals down. For example, the issue that’s come up for me recently is limits to representation in numeric types: the number of bits and what numbers can be represented in their encodings. Trivial stuff taught in the first or second year of a decent CS or computer engineering program. A lot of weak students never understood it when the subject was taught. The vast majority of “self-taught” programmers skipped that section of the curriculum entirely. All those people are useless when my team needs something done in that area.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Does it really matter which university you study at even when taking the same degree?
Answer: Kind of, but not in the way you’re probably thinking, and not nearly enough to care about a few spots in ranking difference. Most of my experience is in the STEM fields, so I’ll speak to that (the liberal arts are much “fuzzier.”) First, a top school cannot “fix” you. If you are a bad student at 18 years old, no school is going to magically make you better. If you bought your way into school and into a degree, reputation is only going to carry you to the first job at most. More colloquially, you cannot polish a turd. How does school does matter? So if you are a top student, you are probably better served by going to a tougher/more rigorous/more reputed school: you’ll learn more and benefit from the higher reputation. But the difference isn’t going to be anywhere as much as some people make it out to be, especially in technical fields where you are expected to get a graduate degree in the long run. As a prior answer mentions, there was a study done of outcomes of accepted students to the similarly sized top reject cohort of one top school, and they were statistically identical: the effectively same people produce the same results even at less selective schools. Personally, I have friends who went to far weaker engineering undergrad programs (some ranked over #100) who subsequently went to top-5 grad programs and absolutely destroyed most classmates during and after school. The undergrad institution didn’t determine their fates. In short, who you are matters a lot more than the school. An idiot cannot be fixed, and a genius armed with the fundamentals will figure out what (s)he needs to know on the fly, even if the material wasn’t taught in school. But there’s little point in going slow if you can go fast, and you might as well take advantage of the reputation if you can succeed at a school that has a good one.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is it a good idea to get a bachelor's in biomedical engineering and then a master's in mechanical engineering?
Answer: No. It may be a bad idea because you won’t be allowed in many mechanical engineering graduate programs. You won’t have the prerequisite background. The other way around is a safer bet, but in engineering it’s generally better to stick to one engineering discipline and pick the handful of courses you need in adjacent areas as necessary, without worrying about those credentials.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: My son wants to be a mechanical engineer or some type of engineer. Can someone recommend a good engineering field? What should he start doing? He’s going to become a freshman in high school.
Answer: Which country do you live in? That determines the path. In some countries (those with high school tracks), your son may already be mostly locked out of the engineering path. In the U.S.:

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What's the best dorm at PAR UIUC? Is Global Crossroads worth it?
Answer: I’m not familiar with Global Crossroads: it didn’t exist when I was in undergrad. It appears to be a relatively low-time program, so if you want to do it, fine. I found living that far south as an engineering student taking several engineering courses and evening/weekend extracurriculars to be annoying, so I moved to ISR after my first semester. Your priorities probably differ, so you should make different choices.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Why should you choose the USA for your studies?
Answer: Undergraduate: because you were born and raised in the U.S. As a natural born American, I didn’t consider anywhere else. Foreigners should generally stay in their own countries for undergraduate study. It will generally be much cheaper and no worse in quality. The three people I’ve met who I believe were justified in coming to the U.S. for bachelor’s degrees all received bachelor’s through PhD at MIT: exceptional even among exceptional people. Graduate: the leading researchers in my desired field are mostly in the U.S. So I stayed. Foreigners should do so because you want to continue your studies, or want to work in the U.S. immediately after via the optional practical training (OPT) attached to your student visa.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: As a foreigner, what major should I study in the US that would get me a job there after graduation?
Answer: Since you say “major,” I’m assuming you’re talking about undergraduate study. Almost nothing will reliably get you a job after undergrad. The vast majority of foreigners spend their money on an U.S. undergraduate education and go home. As Professor Joshua Gross said in his answer, displaying immigration intent when applying for a student visa will get you automatically denied. Those are the rules.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What are the chances of getting a job in the USA with a PhD certificate issued by an American online university?
Answer: Assuming you’re not a U.S. national getting a “PhD certificate” from a fully online university? Effectively zero. First, many online PhDs are effectively fake. No effort, no value. Every significant employer knows this fact. Second, PhDs aren’t rare compared to the demand for them. There are thousands graduated every year and very few (faculty) slots that actually need PhDs. The question is whether the employer will actually get use out of the PhD that they wouldn’t get out of someone else. The answer is usually no. You have to be a top graduate from a top school in a high demand area for which work visas are issued (e.g. engineering or computer science) to have a reasonable chance. A PhD in an area of study that isn’t useful to employers (which is most areas) has effectively no chance. Fully online programs also have the problem, the last time I checked, of their graduates not having even a limited right to work in the U.S. (the optional practical training attached to the F-1 student visa). That’s one of the major benefits to studying in the U.S., and you wouldn’t have that.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What inspired you to pursue your current field of study or career path?
Answer: The only thing that “inspired” me was seeing the exponential growth of computing as I was growing up, and playing with computers. So I figured I would get into computing. Note that my undergrad internships were in marketing, not engineering, despite being an engineering major. The original plan was to get a MBA after undergrad. Studying electrical/computer engineering through PhD and going into my specialty wasn’t driven by inspiration. The decision was a question of: I lucked out in that demand for my specialty (compilation for non traditional computer microarchitectures) spiked when I graduated, after a steady decline and many people leaving the area several years prior. So the financial compensation has been quite good.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is it possible to be interested in a career but disinterested in studying the degree regarding it?
Answer: Possible? It’s very common. There are two extremes that occur to me. In highly technical fields and/or fields that require a lot of background knowledge, those people are often called “wannabes.“ “I want to become a theoretical physicist/philosopher/medical doctor/software engineer because it’s glamorous/pays me a lot of money but I don’t feel like putting in the work required.” Effectively all such people will never get on that career path. In areas such as the arts (e.g. film, drama, music), studying the degree doesn’t mean you can do the work, and doing the work doesn’t require the degree. The degree may help, but it may be meaningless. This isn’t limited to the arts: for example, I find that the people who study entrepreneurship are mostly disjoint from people who do entrepreneurship. That case is actually wannabes in the other direction: they study but can’t do it. The question, if this situation pertains to you, is what your career interest is, and whether there’s a weak or strong relationship between study and practice.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I’m a freshman Computer Engineering student. I couldn’t get any internships My parents started yelling at me that I would waste my summer breaks. Im so lost what do I do to make it productive and something that would help me?
Answer: Your parents are ignoramuses. It is irrational to expect an internship after your freshman year. Frankly, you don’t know anything useful yet. I could not get one despite coming into college with >60 hours of credit, because I still didn’t have enough engineering coursework. I wouldn’t be surprised if you couldn’t find one after sophomore year: that is all too normal. Make your summer productive by producing something. Get some kind of job, or take summer classes. I did both the summer after my freshman year. I am still gainfully employed in my late 40s, so evidently it wasn’t a career-killing decision. I felt a bit burned out because of it, so I wouldn’t go too hard on both. And I would work on writing cleaner, correct English, if you plan to work in an English-speaking country in the long term. Written communication is important and your question as written would disqualify you in a competitive job market, which computer engineering has.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is it worth going back to complete my degree if I’m a successful technology professional at 51? I’m a little concerned about job security and being singled out with ageism already playing a part. But it’s a difficult and expensive decision.
Answer: Which degree? Bachelor’s degree? In this situation, think like a hiring manager. You need to be the cost- and time-effective hiring decision. If you were presented a 51-year-old without a degree and a 53-year-old just out of a bachelor’s degree, would they be meaningfully different, all else being equal? I wouldn’t think so myself. You’re not hiring people for the degrees they obtained in the past. You’re hiring people to do specific work now and in the future. The defense against ageism that I see working for people (a few current and former coworkers are over 70) is having knowledge, experience, and ability to do things that extremely few people can do. And if extremely few people can do it, ML can’t do it, since it doesn’t have the training data, and the cost of setting up the system to self-learn will be prohibitive for at least until my retirement age. A PhD might do something, but it also might not: capabilities matter far more than credentials. I’ve seen a few people do it later in life, and it works for a percentage of them. That sample size is so small, I can’t draw any useful conclusions from it. And I doubt you want to be spending the next 7+ years in school.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What are the job availabilities after studying an MS in exercise science in the USA?
Answer: By saying “in the USA,” I’m assuming you’re not a U.S. citizen and do not have the unrestricted right to work in the U.S. In that situation, you can exclude jobs in the U.S.: you cannot get a work visa with that educational background. Work visas are limited to certain fields with high demand and low supply, notably engineering and medicine. You mentioned in the comments of another answer that you were looking at a physician’s assistant program. That program would open up possible opportunities in the U.S. for you, but getting a work visa even with that is apparently quite challenging according to a quick search on the Internet. Since my experience is limited to medical doctors (MDs) and engineers, I don’t have any useful information in that regard.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: If I am majoring in Electrical Engineering, is it worth it to second major in Computer Science?
Answer: Double majors are usually a waste of time and money as far as jobs or academia are concerned. Double engineering majors even more so. EE+CS is nearly always so: the computer engineering major exists for a reason, and several of the best U.S. engineering universities have a combined EECS department (MIT, UC Berkeley, Michigan). Most people who would do EE+CS would be better served by doing computer engineering and graduate school (where you are often paid) afterwards. If you wanted to do something that combines relatively disjoint aspects of the two, say, resilient software systems for managing electrical power grids, two undergraduate majors might be justified, but you have to look at the specific case. For the example I just gave, two undergrad majors is not going to accomplish your goal because resilient, fault-tolerant computing systems generally aren’t studied in undergrad in either major. I would do one major and pick up what I needed in graduate school. In general, graduate study is an avenue for an EE student to move into more CS-adjacent/oriented fields. I and several of my friends did so. Or you can go to a school with a single EECS department and pick and choose exactly what you want to do. Ultimately, people care about what you can do, not your credentials. Don’t get hung up on the latter. Focus on what you can do.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: It’s my first year of software engineering at university. My uncle wanted me to pick electrical engineering, and he said I will be unemployed because software engineering won’t be in demand in the future. What do you think about it?
Answer: I think your uncle is wrong and/or overgeneralizing, but he knows you personally and I don’t. My undergraduate education is in EE, and I have a lot of friends in the area. There isn’t much demand for mediocre engineers of all stripes, and in many situations a mediocre software engineer may have less job security than a mediocre electrical engineer. If you are generally a mediocre student, then I can see where your uncle is justified in claiming you’ll be unemployed. If you are generally a top student and are going to a top school, I don’t see how your uncle is justified at all: top software engineers make a ridiculous amount of money, and the best EEs often move into finance to get similar compensation. The solution is to not be mediocre, specialize in an area with high demand and low supply, and be a person who decides what the future of software engineering looks like. That’s hard to predict, but it’s usually obvious what has high supply (the easy stuff). Work hard.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is doing a double major of biomedical engineering and mechanical engineering worth it in college? Does it help with employers? Are salaries higher for double majors? How much is it better than single major?
Answer: * No. * No. * No. * None. Possibly worse, if your grades are poor.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Does double majoring or getting a dual PhD really boost your career salary opportunities?
Answer: No. As I’ve said in hundreds of other Quora answers, multiple majors/degrees at any level do not provide tangible benefit to employment. Especially if you have poor grades (representing lack of mastery of the material and prioritization of credentials over mastery). Yes, there are people with double degrees who are successful, but you have to look at the many people who aren’t, particularly the ones that drop out and thus aren’t included in graduate statistics. Selection and survivorship biases are your enemy in this situation. I’ve never personally met a person with two PhDs. It’s bad enough that you’re basically in your 30s after one PhD: people have to eat. I have met plenty of PhDs that move into other areas. In any case, PhDs are not all equal: the higher ranked programs achieve those rankings by having very high standards for admission and graduation, and even at those high ranked programs, there are people who are clearly several notches ahead of the rest. In the tech industry, you often see mediocre PhDs who cannot outperform top BS and MS grads. The point being that more is not universally better for degrees. If you are hearing about supposed benefits of dual degrees from an individual, I would actively distrust that person in the future.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Can I pursue 2 completely different degrees in university? Is it possible to do a double major in 2 very different areas such as film and science?
Answer: Can I pursue 2 completely different degrees in university? If the school lets you, yes. It varies by school. Is it possible to do a double major in 2 very different areas such as film and science? If the school lets you, yes. However, what is your intent and goal by splitting your attention and taking more time (and thus money)? As Professor Joshua Gross’s answer implies, it’s a waste of time when it comes to finding a job in industry or academia. A double major/degree undergraduate credential isn’t useful for predicting future job performance. In general, degrees are impressive only until the ink is dry on the diploma. If the following work performance doesn’t match, then they’re worthless. As a high schooler, you find them impressive, but once you have one, what you’re currently doing matters a lot more: it’s far more predictive of future performance. I understand that some countries have a reputation for people coasting after getting their degrees, but that’s not generally true worldwide. Regarding the specific majors in the question: in most of the pure sciences, you cannot get a job in that field unless a) it is menial, or b) you have a PhD. I don’t know much about film, but plenty of film makers don’t have degrees in film, if they have degrees at all. Your education is your own, but don’t fall into the credential accumulation trap.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Would you recommend studying at UC Berkeley or Yale for a double degree in my graduate studies in terms of student life (partying etc.) and quality of education?
Answer: Well, “D,” since you ask something resembling a troll question, I’ll give you a corresponding answer. Several years back, I was living in CT and met with my friends in New Haven when they were traveling from NYC to Boston. We decided to drop by the university's visitor’s center, where Yale’s rankings were proudly displayed. And as we consisted of one Stanford economics PhD, two UIUC electrical/computer engineering PhDs, and one Michigan MBA, we looked at each other and said, “Yale is ranked inferior to each one of our graduate institutions in our fields of study.” UC Berkeley, on the other hand, is generally on the other side of the rankings. More serious answer:

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is an EECS degree from Berkeley still worth it in 2024? What can I do during my time there to ensure employment or admission to a top graduate school like Stanford?
Answer: Is an EECS degree from Berkeley still worth it in 2024? Absolutely. Especially for California residents, it’s by far the best bang for buck for EECS education. Maybe you hate the campus or the atmosphere, or you prefer a smaller school or a more idyllic setting: everyone has their preferences and UC Berkeley isn’t my “ideal” either. But California residents will generally not get EECS education of equivalent or better quality at a cheaper price anywhere. My daughter has declared that she will likely be pursuing an EECS degree. As a California resident, I told her to target UC Berkeley as #1, over my alma mater UIUC or other highly reputed schools such as MIT and CMU. What can I do during my time there to ensure employment or admission to a top graduate school like Stanford? Why would you want to go to Stanford if you’re already at UC Berkeley? This is not a rhetorical or sarcastic question: graduate programs specialize in different things, and Stanford is an illogical choice in general for the areas I operate in (compilers, computer architecture, computer microarchitecture, electronic design automation): there aren’t professors actively working in those areas. UC Berkeley, on the other hand, is often considered the #1 choice for several of those areas. What should you do? You certainly should excel in classes. You should try your hand at undergraduate research, which will hopefully inform you whether graduate school is a reasonable path. In EECS, go to the appropriate graduate program with a critical mass of professors working in your area of interest. Don’t chase prestige alone: I know a few people that went to Stanford seeking the label, and it stops having an influence as soon as you get the first job after grad school. Maybe you’ll impress people without an EECS degree, but the people you actually need to impress are the people you work with and the people who will hire and promote you. We all know somebody who went to a top school but is a mediocre worker.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What makes platforms like LeetCode and HackerRank unsuitable for interview preparation? Is it true that competent developers can ace interviews even without preparation?
Answer: I don’t have a lot of experience with those resources, but by the time they were available, I was already specialized enough that people hire me for my specific domain and ask me domain-specific questions. I doubt those sites go anything into the detail that I usually get asked. I imagine those sites might be good for undergraduate students or new grads.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: If all team members equally contributed to a project's success, but many members including you didn't receive promotion, stocks, or bonuses due to stack ranking used by the company, what would you do in this situation?
Answer: See other answers talking about self-promotion: maybe it feels a little sleazy, but it’s necessary if you want to get recognition. I’m mediocre at it compared to other people, and I don’t push it past what is strictly true, but I can show clear ownership of projects and code and that’s usually enough to get what I want.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I have a 1330 SAT score. Which colleges are best for an undergrad in mechanical Engineering?
Answer: Short answer: the ones that will take you, where you feel comfortable at, that will prepare you for a mechanical engineering career and not fail you out. Longer answer: first, determine which country you will be getting an education in. If you are not a U.S. national, you probably should not be studying in the U.S. If you are getting a 1330 SAT, you will be paying a lot of money for an education that can be matched in most other countries for far less money The following is assuming that you will be studying in the U.S. Rankings are correlated with admit test scores, by design. So to find the set of schools most willing to take you, go get a rankings list and go down the list to see roughly where the average student has a similar score. Many schools publish or otherwise release a “middle 50%” bracket: they give the scores for students at the 25% and 75% marks. If you are below the 25% mark, I probably wouldn’t bother applying. In the U.S. and many other countries, test scores are insufficient: college admissions will look at your high school grades (they’re a better indicator of how you will do in school than a single exam score). And they will look at other aspects of your education and your extracurriculars. (I suspect a person who only studies is more likely to fail out of school, but I don’t have data to back that up.) As for preparation and assistance: the bigger the school/program, the more likely they won’t give a crap if you crash and burn. If you think you’ll need assistance, you’ll want to avoid those schools, such as large U.S. state schools. There are schools which actively assist you with internships and cooperative learning experiences: you may want those.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Do engineers actually work 40 hours a week? What do they do? Is it very stressful? Is it worth it to get a degree in engineering?
Answer: Do engineers actually work 40 hours a week? As most of the prior answers state, most full time, salaried engineers work more than 40 hours a week. People who work significantly less tend to accomplish less and are more vulnerable to firing and layoffs. One of the reasons I’ve done so many startups is because if I’m going to work hard, I want a potential big payoff. What do they do? That depends on their field and their specialty. You can read other answers to get an idea of what they do. I moved away from traditional engineering in school and have only worked as a software engineer. I write computer code, generally to compile human or machine-generated code into formats that are optimized and usually closer to/at machine level. Is it very stressful? What are you comparing it with? It’s stressful compared to growing plants in my garden, which is why I garden in my off time. It’s not stressful compared to getting shot at (at least for me: see other answers). And it’s certainly an easy life compared to my extended family in North Korea. I can’t afford to slack off if I want to keep my job, but I have absolutely no worries about having a roof over my head and food to eat. I could retire now if I was okay with moving to a cheap part of the U.S. or the world. Is it worth it to get a degree in engineering? “Worth” is subjective. I’d say it’s worth it, by my standards and values. And my pre-teen kids are saying that engineering is their primary choice for now. But we like building things and making them work. If your motivation is money and not building things, I would recommend looking elsewhere to make a living. There are easier ways to make money. I can understand doing engineering if you are trying to immigrate to another country: most countries can use more engineers, but otherwise restrict immigration.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What PhD can be after an MBA?
Answer: I have heard of business (process) PhDs graduating after obtaining a MBA, but they’re evidently rare enough that I haven’t met one personally. The overwhelming majority of MBA grads have it as their terminal degree.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Do you think it's crazy to make a career switch after getting laid-off with just two years of working experience?
Answer: For something to be “crazy,” it has to come from an irrational decision. So the real question is, “Is it rational to make a career switch after getting laid off with two years of work experience?” The answer to that question is “It depends.” In the 2001 dot-com bust, over a third of my engineering undergrad classmates lost their jobs. Many took the opportunity to switch careers (notably teaching) and have subsequently stuck with those careers for over 20 years. I don’t see why they should be called crazy.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Are engineers in the same intellectual league as theoretical physicists and mathematicians? Are engineers not smart enough for those professions at the highest levels?
Answer: You evidently don’t operate at those “highest levels.” Many of my EE professors had joint appointments in physics and vice versa. Like the guys who invented the transistor, LED, etc. Many of my CS professors had joint appointments in math. Sometimes they co-publish. They’re doing the same things where they overlap, so by definition they’re in the same league. The vast majority of engineers can’t operate at the highest level because they aren’t capable of doing PhDs or top level research. The exact same can be said for all the physics and math students who couldn’t get a PhD. The difference is that while an engineer with a bachelor’s degree can still be an engineer, a person with a physics or math degree without the corresponding job (most of them) usually doesn’t have the gall to claim being a physicist or mathematician. Even PhDs in physics and math often have to go work in a different area after graduating. When physics and math grads do get physics or math jobs, the supply glut of people relative to the demand means their pay is significantly lower than engineers’.
