You can talk about “intellectual league” until you’re blue in the face, but money talks and bullshit walks. Sarcasm aside, ultimately engineers build tools and other things, often for the use of physicists and mathematicians (e.g. particle colliders and supercomputers). Engineers have to get things working consistently within the constraints and randomness of reality. It’s not the physicists or mathematicians building large, complex systems of physical things that have to work with high reliability. The oversimplified idea is that mathematicians and physicists find/discover something once, engineers have to get it working all the time. Engineers build things like the Channel Tunnel. Or the International Space Station. Or the chips that provide compute power. Yet engineers generally don’t claim that physicists or mathematicians are below them. Everyone has a different focus and each field makes their own contributions.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: For computer science, is it worth getting a master or a PhD?
Answer: Depends on the level you operate at and who you compete/work with. The PhD is table stakes for academia. Enough said, move on. If you plan to work in industry, I would generally not get a PhD. My personal experience is that it only works out for top PhDs who are lucky with how their specialty interacts with the state of the industry. There are lots of mediocre CS PhDs who cannot compete in industry against top bachelor’s grads. They dug themselves a deeper hole by getting the PhD. The master’s is usually a win, in that you’ll specialize in your area and get a stronger foundation in theory. But again, there are plenty of master’s grads who cannot compete in industry against top bachelor’s grads. In general I warn against getting a graduate degree thinking it will “fix” something, unless you excelled at a weak undergrad and are going to a much stronger graduate school. If you are having trouble obtaining a job, for example, going to graduate school is generally not going to fix that fact.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Why doesn’t each real estate agency make a website like Zillow for themselves? What is Zillow's unfair advantage since the beginning?
Answer: Companies used to doing things the same way for years almost never put together what they need to change the industry themselves. Taxi companies could have made an Uber/Lyft app, or standard retail could have made a website like Amazon. They lacked the foresight and the skills.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: How can I transition from the defense industry to the tech industry?
Answer: Depends on what you were doing before. Technical people in defense have no trouble doing the same things in commercial/consumer tech. If the same things don’t really exist (e.g. certain kinds of radar systems), then it gets harder the bigger the gap, from my limited experience. Non technical people in defense have a bigger gap to bridge, but depending on your background, your clearances, reliability, teachability, etc., there is a place for you. I even know of a few former enlisted rank folks working in the Waymo motor pool.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I have always gotten good grades (mostly A’s), but I never seem to be able to get any higher no matter how hard I try. I wish to rank in the top ten. Is there a problem with me?
Answer: It’s a “problem” if you haven’t admitted that your “wish” is a fantasy. Your question exhibits potential causes of your lack of performance relative to your “goal.” You say “top ten,” but ten of what exactly? Ten percent? Ten students (out of what size class)? You made an assumption that “top ten” means something to the rest of us. It does not. That kind of fuzzy thinking and communication is what causes mistakes. Multiple mistakes cause non A grades. Do you analyze every single mistake you make on homework and exams to figure out why you got it wrong and make sure that you don’t make the same mistake, or similar mistakes, ever again? If you’re not, then you’re not working very hard or very smart. You say you’re trying “hard,” but that’s a meaningless opinion. The fact that you’re of school age on Quora means your life is a lot easier than most of humanity’s. Are you working “harder” than those people? Probably not. Be more precise in your thinking, work smarter, work harder, and get off of Quora. Or admit that you’re not willing or able to operate at that level and give up on your wish.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is it accurate to suggest that the layoffs in the US are primarily driven by companies aiming to enhance quarterly earnings revenue, rather than being tied to employee performance? If not, why?
Answer: No, because of the definition of revenue. Revenue is what you bring in with the sale of product or services. Revenue is independent of cost, and firing employees is reducing cost. Maybe income is increased, because revenue minus cost is income. In the tech industry, enough unemployment benefit is being paid out that I wouldn’t expect income improvement in the same quarter. Certainly in future quarters. There is a possibility that who gets cut is tied to performance, but as Josh Osborne’s answer states, it’s a lot more opaque than one would think correct or fair. I talked to some of the people laid off in 2023, and some of the reasons were very questionable. Frankly, I had less issue with the stated reasons for my own termination in the same period (not enough code volume and perceived “complexity” to justify my pay).

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: VC giant Andreessen Horowitz says that half of Google's white collar staff does no real work. Is it correct to say that most Google engineers are incompetent and they are only good at solving Leetcode questions? If not why ?
Answer: I would claim a16z is exaggerating if they’re actually claiming “half,” but they’re not completely off base. For Meta, I wouldn’t be surprised if it’s more than half. It’s not that Googlers are incompetent: they would be fired in a heartbeat if they weren’t producing solid code (been there, seen that). It’s that many Google projects are ultimately meaningless: the projects do not contribute to Google’s bottom line, future income, etc. Fiscal discipline at Google has always been weaker than most large companies, and while it’s improved greatly under CFO Ruth Porat, it’s still weak. My impression, based on my unscientific survey of people I know at Google, is that management is dominated by a clique of MBAs, heavily drawn from management consulting firms like McKinsey, with their pet projects. My unsubstantiated guess is that upper management is more worried about maintaining their relationships in that clique rather than swinging the axe more regularly. If something disrupts Google’s business, the prioritization of those relationships is a significant weak point that can cause the company to stumble or fail. This effect is not unique to Google at all: one can say the same general things about many large corporations, and especially Boeing in their current situation. Yet another internal MBA with personal connections sucking up to the board of directors and becoming CEO, rather than people making hard decisions based on reality. When bean counters run engineering companies, things inevitably drop from their peaks. Note the qualifications in the above paragraphs: I only hear whispers and side comments from third parties, so my opinion is hardly based on quality intelligence. More like George W. Bush “WMDs in Iraq”-level intelligence. So maybe it’s complete crap and feel free to disregard me if you feel that way, but the effect is so common to large corporations, if it’s not true now, it will be in the future.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Which private housing hall of UIUC is best for an electrical engineer freshman?
Answer: Hendrick House is the default, but it depends on your priorities. Mine was being able to walk to engineering classes and (evening/weekend) engineering extracurriculars in a minimal amount of time. Since Everitt Lab was the home of ECE at the time, ISR or Hendrick were the options. With ECE now being further north, I would be even more incentivized to stay north. If you are not coming in with a lot of AP and community college credit, correspondingly more classes will be on the Quad, so being further south and west may be desirable. You’re going to be taking only 2–4 ECE courses your first year. If your priorities are different, you should consider different options. If you were doing a lot of music activities, for example, being closer to those is of value. (Trying to get down there with a large instrument was a pain in the butt.) If you want to meet non engineers, you’ll want to get further away from engineering campus.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Which is better for mechanical engineering, UIUC or UCSB (in-state)?
Answer: UCSB in-state for the vast majority of people. Excel there, go get a graduate degree somewhere else. If you don’t do well and can’t get into graduate school somewhere else, UIUC wouldn’t have helped you.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is it possible to emulate an "Ivy League" experience at a state school like UT Austin?
Answer: UT Austin is currently in the Big 12, transitioning to the SEC this year, both of which most college sports aficionados would say is superior to the Ivy League. The point I’m making is, strictly speaking, the Ivy League is an athletic conference comprising eight schools in the Northeast. Everything else said about “the Ivy League” is a generalization of those eight schools and/or the opinion/imagination of humans. What are you imagining an “Ivy League experience” to be? To me, despite having several good friends who graduated from those schools, the distinguishing factors of the eight schools in the Ivy League are low acceptance rates, social elitism, and nearly a third of the undergraduate student body being accepted on legacy or sports instead of merit. I would be very disappointed in UT Austin, Michigan, or Berkeley if they approached anything like the latter two situations. Go to a work field that is meritocratic instead of operating on old money and cronyism, and especially outside of the Northeast, you find precious few Ivy League grads in positions of power. So no, you’re not going to find much social elitism or old money buying spots at state schools. But if you want high selectivity, the top flagship state schools have similarly high admissions requirements, especially in high demand majors such as engineering. Acceptances in computer science at the top state schools are on the order of 5% or less, similar to the top schools in the Ivy League, Stanford, and MIT.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: As an undergraduate that is in the biology major, why do you still have to take physics?
Answer: Biology is applied chemistry, and chemistry is applied physics. Classic xkcd comic: One of the big consumers of computing power is computational biology, and since I work in high performance computing, I’ve supported such efforts multiple times in my career. Molecular dynamics is elementary physics. If you’re going to make a career out of biology, physics will be useful. Personal story: one such effort was trying to understand why a molecule was able to get through a cellular gate: experiments showed it did, but did not explain why, because the shapes were so different. By using physics simulations running on new-at-the-time GPUs, the researchers I was supporting showed that the forces between the molecule and gate contorted them into spiral shapes that allowed the molecule to wriggle through like a worm. I believe it resulted in a Nature article, and capped at least one PhD. Yay physics.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What are ways to self study to learn equal to the knowledge in a major, as in the way you can save tuitions, and show on resume, then how could I prove my learning experience?
Answer: There is no “equal” way to learn at the same speed and quality as a good undergraduate program, and thus no proving anything. By self-studying: Can people learn better by themselves than from a bad teacher and fellow students? Sure: been there, done that. But in the aggregate, the only way you’re going to beat a full undergraduate education by yourself is by using a really crappy undergraduate program as your standard.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I want to get a double major in physics and philosophy. Should I do this, and what jobs will be available for me? I am a high school student. What can I do now to prepare me for this?
Answer: First, read Professor Joshua Gross’s answer. That’s how you prepare. Second: You don’t have to treat college as a trade school where you have to major in something that leads to a specific career path (e.g. accounting or engineering). But you need to make somewhat realistic plans and do job preparation while you are in school. Interns are far cheaper for companies than full time hires, so your goal should be to do internships well before you graduate.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Why is it not easy to get jobs after majoring in bioengineering?
Answer: The jobs aren’t there. In the U.S. and a few other countries, there are more bioengineering undergraduate students than total bioengineering jobs. All jobs, not just entry level ones. Basic supply and demand dictates that most bioengineering students aren’t going to get bioengineering jobs, and the ones that do get jobs are going to be paid less than engineers of similar ability in other fields. It doesn’t take an engineering degree to figure that out. I was alerted to this gross imbalance by one of my former bioengineering professors, who was wondering why his students weren’t finding jobs. You can look up the same numbers via ASEE (graduation count) and BLS (job count). The money imbalance wasn’t as bad as it was several years ago, but the job availability still isn’t there. My wife was biochem + chemical engineering majors and I was an electrical engineering undergraduate. We’re not letting our kids major in bioengineering: they’re better off being in the area which has bioengineering applications, so they have options. EE, ME, materials science, CS, whatever.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I recently started my PhD and the postdoc working on the same project (enzyme) has already made a lot of progress. There aren’t significant questions left to be answered in this project. I feel useless and frustrated. What should I do?
Answer: I don’t think you appreciate the opportunity you have. You have a resource many people wish they did: a mature researcher to learn from, who has the time to talk to you (unlike many advisors), and a project approaching an “end” as an opportunity to learn about an entire research project from the “end” backwards. Figure out where the project started and how (s)he got from something unknown to something known. The individual result is less important than the research process. And you can drill into the details of this particular project and start determining the general principles on which you can do your own individual research. If you do enough work to publish, that means your name on a paper before you presumably hit year 2. Be grateful. Some of us (me) didn’t get our names on papers until year 3–4. No first author publication until year 6. Year 1 is generally the worst for PhDs, but you haven’t seen “useless and frustrated” yet. In any case, go talk to your PhD advisor and ask him/her about his/her intent on what you should be aiming for in this experience. I’m just a guy on the Internet who hasn’t done academic research in 16 years, not your research supervisor.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What should I do if I have a bachelors degree in Art but I want a career in computer science/programming?
Answer: I would investigate an additional bachelor’s degree in computer science. That’s the most reliable way to enter the field. There are master’s degrees in computer science for non-CS undergraduates, but those are usually meant for people with STEM undergraduate degrees. Probably a bridge too far.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Which is more difficult and requires more brain, medicine or computer engineering, and why?
Answer: While I am a computer engineer, most of the rest of my family is medical doctors. They are different kinds of difficult. “How much brain” they use is meaningless. A few points that immediately come to mind: In summary, they are different. Most humans will be more inclined to one than the other.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Which should I commit as an international student, UIUC CS (40k), or Rutgers CS (30k)? My dream school is UMich (60k, accepted), but the cost is not it for an undergrad.
Answer: $10k/year is a lot of money, but based on what I see in my section of the job market, I would pay the extra $10k for UIUC, assuming you’re at the top of your class there. If you are not, it’s not worth the extra money. $20k/year on top of that for Michigan is not worth the money. Be warned that undergrad is often not the terminal degree for people working in CS fields. However, people pursuing MS and certainly PhD are often paid to go to school, in the form of assistantships.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Can I become a chemical engineer even though I took biology and chemistry in my IBDP program?
Answer: “Engineering” is regulated by country, and you haven’t said which country you reside in. In most developed countries, there is no way you could become a chemical engineer without additional education. Go look at chemical engineering curricula at accredited schools in your country. In the U.S., curricula diverge quickly from biology and chemistry into processes and flows. For example, here is MIT’s requirements: You probably don’t have any of the following, let alone the technical electives following them.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What is the future of biomedical engineering, biotechnology and computational biology? Would biomedical engineering be better that any other field of engineering if I really want to make healthcare devices?
Answer: You haven’t said where you live. Biomedical engineering is extremely oversubscribed in the U.S. and several other developed countries. There are more undergraduate students than total jobs. Not entry level jobs; all jobs. If you are not good, you won’t get a job in the area. If you are good, you’ll be making less money than similarly capable people in other engineering disciplines. Those areas will grow, but not at an extreme rate.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What is the best way to make the transition from industry (engineering) to a PhD program (STEM)? I am worried about my upcoming decision (having doubts), and am curious to know if anyone has made this transition.
Answer: PhD in engineering, or something else? “STEM” is overly broad. I don’t see how an engineer is going to make an effective transition to science or math PhD study. I’ve known a few people that worked in industry for a while and then did a PhD. It’s a small sample size, but the results are bimodal: either they don’t do well (and drop out), or they do very well, with a disproportionate number becoming professors. The question is whether you can make the adjustment, not only back to being a student, but also being a PhD student (which is a very different animal from every prior stage).

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: If someone has no particular passion for a subject but wants to pursue a career in academia and pursue a Masters and PhD in the future, which of Civil and Environmental Engineering and economics would be more beneficial as an undergrad major?
Answer: I don’t know where you live, but in the developed world, you don’t survive bachelor’s through PhD, let alone enter the tiny percentage of people who become professors, without passion. However smart you think you are, you haven’t competed at the undergraduate or graduate level yet. Go find something you are passionate about, then talk about academia.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What makes the University of Arizona more special to study computer science?
Answer: Its enormous undergraduate student body: if you want a boyfriend/girlfriend, there’s almost certainly someone out there for you. Only a handful of schools are larger, although one of them is ASU. In terms of computer science education, there’s nothing too unique to differentiate it.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What is a recommended RN program in the Bay Area?
Answer: First, here are the requirements to become a RN in California. The best bang for buck is to get an associate’s degree through a community college. The problem with such programs is that the waiting list is reportedly several years long at this point, and you’ll need a bachelor’s degree anyway if you want to advance your career in certain directions (e.g. nurse practitioner). The next option is to get a bachelor’s degree in nursing through one of many four-year institutions. Some programs are more reputed in general and it’ll probably benefit you if you can attend one of those, but I don’t have personal experience with any of them. If you already have a bachelor’s degree, there are two options I’m aware of.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I'm a software engineer with a mechanical engineering degree who writes efficient code better than many software engineers. How much is the potential for me to grow in this field?
Answer: Not very much, Ahmed Kaleem. Not without an attitude change. How do you define “efficient?” It’s almost certainly different from how I define it, and I’ve been working as a software engineer for over 20 years, with the last 16 in Silicon Valley. In any case, efficiency is not the primary goal in software engineering. It’s readability and maintainability. After correctness, of course. Which “software engineers” are you comparing yourself to? Students at Ghulam Ishaq Khan Institute of Engineering Sciences and Technology? Most computer science and software engineering graduates, let alone students, never become competent software engineers. I would compare myself to software engineers who have been working at top tech companies longer than me. Assume you know nothing and that your standards are weak compared to professionals’ standards. Then you might get somewhere.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: How can we encourage more women to pursue careers in STEM (science, technology, engineering, and mathematics) fields?
Answer: That question is the wrong one to be asking. Let’s assume we’re talking about the U.S., since I live in the U.S., Quora is a U.S.-based company, and we’ve got a lot of data. Women already equal or outnumber men in many STEM areas. Source here. I don’t see why we need to further encourage women to enter STEM in general. However, for specific areas, they’re underrepresented. If you want to correct those imbalances, yes, we can talk about encouragement, and I would say that encouragement is a possible solution to the imbalance. The biggest problem is the bootstrapping program: with few women in the field, women do not have many female role models, have a smaller network, etc. It will require men to pitch in and support the effort. Also important is removing sources of discouragement. It’s no accident that “brogrammer” is a known term. Just like racism, if you’re not actively squashing that behavior, you’re letting it flourish. There’s also the career ratio imbalance, and the wage and seniority gender gap. Those issues are not fixed by encouragement.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Will birth control ever be 100% effective?
Answer: Which kind of birth control? At what cost? Glib statements are meaningless for medical situations. We can remove the organs responsible for reproduction and it’s 100% effective at preventing future children. No magic there. Destruction of certain tubes is a 99.999% guarantee, if you have a competent doctor. (A friend’s doctor was not competent, so they had a child without trying.) It’s not like cancer where you have to kill the patient to 100% guarantee death of the tumor. If you want to keep your organs, nothing will be 100% effective before the fetus is created. Pills, physical barriers, whatever. Any kind of artificial intervention has a chance of failure. Individual human bodies and environments are unpredictable.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Do companies actually hire people? How do people get jobs?
Answer: Do companies actually hire people? Yes. Effectively every company I’ve worked for (about eight at this point) would hire the appropriate people if available. Note the emphasis. How do people get jobs? People apply for jobs. Some of them get the jobs. Companies want: For whatever reason, most humans can’t understand things from the company’s/employer’s perspective. I find it’s the small business owner with the toughest job: they have to deal with these clueless people the most, while being all too sensitive/vulnerable to labor issues.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Why is engineering such a competitive line of work? Is it simply supply and demand meaning only the best are needed, or that only the best are ever seen as worthwhile, or the special interpersonal skills required to be respected in a diverse way?
Answer: Is it competitive? Compared to what? The competition for engineering jobs is nothing like what you’d see in music, the arts, or professional sports. The supply and demand curves would imply that getting an engineering job is not that competitive: otherwise wages would not be as good as they are. Engineering is difficult, to be sure, and requires a lot of study followed by work that isn’t considered easy. And there is competition. But it’s more about making sure that:

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Isn’t engineering a good field? My teachers/friends say it's not an in demand field. Is that why they chose CS?
Answer: I don’t know which country is your reference point. Compared to CS, engineering might be less in demand, but engineering is far more in demand than most college areas of study in the U.S. Which is why engineering graduates get paid more than most college grads. In computer engineering, the bar is a lot higher to get a “true” computer engineering job, with the good jobs generally going to people with master’s degrees and no few number of PhDs from top schools. Most of the middle-aged computer engineers I know personally in Silicon Valley are making at least $250k/year. Sometimes double. Software engineers could make that kind of money, but many (most?) people don’t make it to that level.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Can one come out skilled at software engineering after a minor in computer science or information systems?
Answer: No. Unless you use the word “skilled” a lot more loosely than I do. Most computer science and information systems majors do not “come out skilled at software engineering.” Not enough to lead a project of broad scope and large scale. A minor is a puny fraction of the content of a major. Incidentally, I do have a computer science minor. Knowing what I know now, it wasn’t sufficient to be even a mediocre software engineer. Thankfully, I entered graduate school and took many more computer science classes and wrote much more code before I entered industry.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What advice can you give us students if we want to pursue the exact work you have now?
Answer: Stop. Don’t even think about doing it. The world continuously changes. The tech world in particular changes very fast. The “exact work” I’m doing today didn’t exist five years ago, and it won’t exist five years from now. Compounded on that is most students cannot achieve the education necessary to do my job. It does not take a PhD, but it seems that most people capable of the job have PhDs. Go get an education with a solid theoretical foundation and be open to new opportunities. The opportunities available now will not be available in the future.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Should I major in a STEM field even though I’m terrible at those subjects to get a job, or major in something I’m good at?
Answer: The point of college when you are not talking about fields that teach specific knowledge and skills required for the job (engineering) is to show you have discipline and the ability to learn. That you can do something that someone who is a dropout or never attended cannot accomplish. So maybe you can be better at other things in the same way. Think about how you can leverage what you are good at to develop yourself in a way that makes you more capable than most people.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: How do I study to be a brilliant engineer? What is your real life experience?
Answer: You don’t study to become a brilliant engineer. You do. You build. You learn from the experience and get feedback from solid people. You build again, something new. Iterate, repeat, as fast as you can. If you’re not doing and learning, you’re falling behind. The ageism one hears about is a result of some people not learning and developing as they get older. But the people leading teams in industry are generally not in their 20s. They kept growing.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is 2,000 hours of studying software engineering enough for a student to land a good company job?
Answer: Mostly necessary, may be insufficient. Most people who try to study on their own will not have rigorous standards and will probably not get decent feedback.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Which college should I choose for pre-med? My options are University of San Diego with a 60% scholarship, or UC Irvine with no scholarship and minimal aid, I am also an out of state student.
Answer: You really should have applied to more schools within your home state, assuming you’re a U.S. resident. The costs of both schools is excessive compared to what you get. Given these two choices, I would go to USD. But I would have stayed in state. You might even want to do a year or two of community college and transfer instead. I would seriously consider that option. Ideally you should have applied and been accepted at programs that have early assurance or some other guarantee of medical school admissions, as Arnold’s answer states. Many, many people fail to get into medical school. Given that the typical admit at the listed universities has a SAT score around 1200–1300, maybe such programs are out of reach.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Why did you choose the USA for an undergraduate program?
Answer: I am a natural born American citizen. I lived in the suburbs of Chicago, IL at the time. As I was not and still am not an adventurous person, I decided to stay within my state, so it never occurred to me to look outside the country, at all. Looking at the distances today, I’d have to travel at least 500 km to get to good schools outside the country (Ontario, Canada). Other countries are much, much farther away. In contrast, there were two elite U.S. universities within 60 miles (Northwestern University and the University of Chicago) and the #2 ranked U.S. electrical engineering undergraduate program at the time (UIUC) less than 200 miles away. Once I decided that I would try electrical engineering, I applied to UIUC on early admission and didn’t bother applying anywhere else once I was accepted (in October, if I remember correctly, well before any other application deadlines). Two other factors were in play: From a cost-benefit analysis, there isn’t a better choice that I can see now, let alone back then. Now that I’m in my 40s and lived in various states of the U.S., and visited much more of the world, I’m not as adverse to living elsewhere and I’m going to be taking my kids around the U.S. to get them used to the idea of going to school elsewhere. They’ve inherited my lack of adventurousness, so I doubt they’d want to live outside the country either. [A few days after writing this answer, I asked my kids if they want to live on the other side of the country for college. They said no. Hopefully they’ll change their minds.] As I ended up with a PhD in computer engineering (also from UIUC, usually ranked somewhere around #5 for its graduate program), part of me regrets not applying to other highly reputed engineering schools. But I doubt I would have done any better in my life or career: I probably would not have done as well under a different PhD advisor, and I also met my wife of 14 years at UIUC.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I have a friend who is 60 and wants to go back for his PhD. He went to a top school years ago. Is there a chance he can get into a good program in computer science?
Answer: There’s always a chance. I’ve personally known people in their 50s pursuing PhDs. If I were a professor looking at such an applicant, my questions would be: I just remembered one guy that finished his PhD when he was about 60. Sir Brian May, born 1947, left his PhD program to be lead guitarist for Queen. Went back and finished in 2007. Astrophysics from Imperial College London. Not something I could do, at any age.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What are some of the cheapest universities for international students that offer a computer science degree in the USA?
Answer: Wrong question. International students are cash cows for universities. Any school finding out that they’re “cheap” is going to raise its prices. Any particularly cheap school likely does not have a computer science degree worth paying for. Foreigners should generally get undergraduate degrees in their own countries and come to the U.S. for graduate school if they’re good enough.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Due to me being unsure with careers, I have been accepted to Berkeley and UCSD for physics. I now know that I want to do engineering should I study engineering at cal poly Pomona, or take the risk and try to switch to engineering at Berkeley or UCSD?
Answer: I’m pretty sure you can switch to most engineering majors at Berkeley or UCSD from physics. You’ll want to check that there are no barriers to doing so. A quick email or call to a dean at each school’s engineering college should be sufficient to confirm. Some schools now prohibit transfers into certain majors because of capacity limitations (usually CS), but most engineering majors don’t have the same restrictions. Most people change their major. I think the median number of major changes is close to two, so if anything it’s the common case. One guy I know switched at least five times. He ended up an engineering professor at Georgia Tech before making a crapload of money in HFT, so I can’t say it hampered him all that much.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What's more difficult, earning a PhD or attending law school?
Answer: They are different beasts. Different people will find one harder than the other. The problem with statistics and drop out rates is the base rate fallacy: there’s very little overlap between the people who attempt each degree, so you’re trying to compare two separate groups of people. Take those statistics with a large grain of salt. The difference between PhD and professional degrees is that in the PhD, you can do everything you’re told to do and still fail. For the JD, MD, and MBA, you meet the school’s requirements and you get your degree. For the PhD, you can meet all the school’s requirements, but unless you publish innovative research, you fail. Some people graduate in a few years, some take much, much longer. Despite the ambiguity and the moving target of the PhD, I would probably find law school harder, simply because I wouldn’t be motivated.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Which school should I go for my undergrad, UIUC or UCD for electrical engineering? I live in California.
Answer: That’s a tough decision to make. UIUC is a more reputed program, but if you aren’t close to the top of the class there, it’s pointless to go and pay the extra tuition. If you think you’re around the top (e.g. your GPA and test scores exceed the 75% mark for admits), I would go there. It would probably be worth the extra money. If UCSD was an option, I’d probably take that over UIUC: the gap is smaller. If my kids had to make the choice between UIUC or UCD, I’d push (and pay) for UIUC. Solely because I figure they should be able to hack it, since my wife and I both went there.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Do parents with degrees in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) have better kids in terms of their children's education and future career choices than those without such degrees?
Answer: I wouldn’t claim that in general. But I would say yes for STEM careers, because of what the degree indicates. As a result, what you’ll find in both engineering and medicine is that a disproportionate portion of the people pursuing the field have a parent or other older relative in the same field. I don’t have the same exposure to the sciences, but the few people I know who make a living in that area also have a parent or relative in the area. As for guidance: effectively no one slacks off the first eight or twelve years of school and magically catches up later. The fundamentals and foundation have to be solid before you can build on them. That’s why guidance is important. I pay relatively close attention to my 9 and 11-year-old’s class performance to make sure they don’t slip. By the time they’re in high school, I expect I won’t need to supervise. I also expose them to engineering concepts: two weeks ago we were going through a rural area, and they were asking me what a water tower was for. Not really my area, but that means I can explain it in terms they’ll understand.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Where should I go? I got accepted into UCR, UCSD and Berkeley, each for either biology or molecular bio. I am on the pre-med track and I am not sure what school is better for pre- med.
Answer: First, there are several very similar questions linked to this one, covering two of the three schools. Look at the answers to those too. I’m going to assume that your goal is medical school, otherwise I have no idea why you’re a pre-med. It’s more important to knock it out of the park wherever you go, rather than worry about school reputation. Get a 3.0 GPA at any school and you can kiss U.S. med school goodbye. Get a 4.0 and you’ll be competitive at the vast majority of schools. The important thing is to prepare for the MCAT and get top grades. As some of the answers to related questions state, you’ll want to go to as reputed a university as possible (Berkeley) if you want a chance at the ultra elite med schools or the academic route (PhD). I don’t know where those options weigh in your mind. Many people change their minds about med school, or find that they can’t hack college and disqualify themselves. Do not slip up, slack off, have a meltdown, or anything else that will derail your performance. Been there, saw that. But don’t forget to live your life and enjoy yourself either. Either extreme is bad. Finally, I should mention that the reputation of your med school isn’t the final determinant of your medical career. The residency is where the real training is done. And people do jump from solid (but not necessarily top) medical schools to highly reputed residency programs. The medical doctor road is a long one. I personally would go to Berkeley out of the three, since I don’t have a preference for campus environment, and I like to throw myself into the toughest academic situations I can find. But that’s my preference alone. My wife eschewed Berkeley for Illinois, which I thought was insane for the out-of-state tuition alone, but she wanted to get away from her parents and all the other Asians. (And ended up meeting me and coming back to California.) That’s her preference. You’ll have to decide based on your own preferences. I’ve only passed through Riverside, but Berkeley and La Jolla are very different towns in some respects.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I am interested in pursuing these degrees: business and economics, psychology, mathematics, and natural sciences. Which one do you think is more in demand (US and worldwide), and why?
Answer: You’re making a high schooler’s mistake. Having a degree doesn’t make you truly in demand. What employers are demanding is exceptional people who can do exceptional things. Degrees are one way of filtering them, but they aren’t a perfect filter. I know people with degrees from Stanford and MIT, all the way up to PhD, who have trouble finding a job because of repeated evidence that they cannot produce value. You can bet there are such people at all levels, from all schools. Also, those aren’t degrees. Those are areas of study. The commonly accepted degree levels (with their typical lengths for full time study) in the U.S. are associate’s (2 years), bachelor’s (4 years), master’s (+2 years), and PhD (+5++ years). With the exception of business, every area listed in the question generally requires a PhD before you get to do “real” work in the area. Meaning you’re maybe halfway through your formal education, if you’re currently in high school. Some areas give more transferable skills than others.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Where should I realistically go for electrical/computer engineering? I am a junior in HS with a 3.9 GPA, 1400 SAT, and have taken AP calc AB, AP Physics NM and EM, AP CSA, and will take AP chem, AP calc BC, and AP stat next year.
Answer: Short answer: whoever will take you. Longer answer: the major ding in the information you provided is your SAT score of 1400. That score puts you out of reasonable contention for the “top 12” ECE programs (according to US News). Well over 75% of admits at those schools have a higher score. Raising it 50–100 points would put you in a much better position. As it’s April, you’ve got a couple months. As a first cut, I would go down the US News electrical and computer engineering rankings and look up statistics on their quartiles/”middle 50%.” That will give you an idea of who typically gets into that program. For example, MIT’s quartiles are 1520–1570: they effectively require a perfect math score and a near perfect verbal. Once you have a couple profiles, then you start targeting “reach, “reasonable,” and “safety” schools based on where your stats lie in their admissions ranges. If you have no activities outside of classes, you’ll probably have to discount your chances.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is it a good idea to move to the United States to get a university certificate and then look for a job?
Answer: In general, no. Bad idea on top of a bad idea. I don’t know what you mean by “certificate,” but it’s degrees we value in the U.S. University “certifications” are mostly meaningless. As a foreigner, you will be paying for the privilege of attending university in the U.S. There is effectively no financial aid for you, so it will be a very expensive proposition. I’m guessing you’re from Italy by your name: it is far more effective to do an undergraduate degree in Europe and come to the U.S. for graduate study. Second, getting a work visa to live and work in the U.S. full time requires that you be well above average in a high demand, low supply field like computer engineering. Even if you satisfy those requirements, the H-1B visa lottery has been oversubscribed for several years: it will take at least several months and possibly years to get it. Meaning that you need to leave the country until you get it. Not as big a deal as it used to be, with modern telework tools, but still an annoyance. The point is that you need to be planning a job well before you graduate, not after you finish your degree.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I'm a student who's been accepted at UIUC and NYU for engineering, and I'm having trouble choosing. What is the career placement like at UIUC, and is the quality of their program as good as its ranking indicates?
Answer: Which engineering? Your career outcomes can vary wildly at UIUC. The bottom can and often does drop out of engineering entirely, even if they graduated. The top has no ceiling. Flag rank in the military, lots of successful corporate founders, a few billionaires. The school is not going to be your limiting factor. A bunch of my friends and former classmates are multimillionaires. I’ve personally done multiple successful startups (I don’t generally count my financial assets). As for quality, I don’t know how to define or quantify it separate from the students. A lot of UIUC’s ranking and outcomes comes from its selectivity, as do most other top engineering schools. I’ve been looking at SAT scores: when a school around #20 has a middle-50% range of 1100–1400, and UIUC engineering’s is 1470–1550, that’s a huge gap in general academic ability that cannot be made up with “better” teaching, more equipment, etc. MIT is going to have the best technical students as a whole because their admissions standards are higher: rankings are a self-fulfilling prophecy. The reputation is established by not letting crap in, and not letting crap graduate. What I can say is that high admissions standards, whatever the school, result in high output standards and people who work hard and smart in industry. Most of my high performing school friends are at Apple, Alphabet, and startups. People with significantly lower grades got significantly less prestigious/well paying jobs. At my previous job at Waymo, the three most represented undergraduate programs on my team were MIT, Seoul National University, and UIUC. Good company to be in. As a UIUC undergrad student in EE who was effectively a CompE double major, I thought the course quality was generally good. There were a few weaker teachers, but the only one I thought was bad was a new professor teaching a grad class (he did not get tenure). I can’t speak to other disciplines.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Which school should I pick, UCSC Computer Engineering, UC Merced CSE, or SJSU CS?
Answer: It’s impossible to say definitively without knowing you and your goals. If you’re gunning for a future that includes graduate school, UCSC is probably the appropriate choice: it has the highest admissions standards and thus the strongest cohort. All three schools have standardized exam score distributions significantly lower than the top ten CS/CompE programs, so wherever you go, don’t lull yourself into complacency. Classes are taught to the average, so students at the higher ranked schools will be used to learning more at a faster pace. Whether you can outperform them in grad school or work is up to you.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I'm a freshman in high school but I am planning on going to PFW and doing an art major and a music major. Would I have any free time? How much? How many classes would I take?
Answer: First, I have no clue which school “PFW” is. Is that Purdue Fort Wayne? I don’t know anyone who’s been there as a student or teacher. Second, calculating workload is impossible without knowing you personally and knowing how many years you plan to use to graduate. Undergraduate students typically take 5 courses a semester, maybe more. Assuming it’s on a semester system. Finally, you will probably change your mind about your majors or drop out, because most people fall into one of those two categories.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What do I major in? I am between computer science, computer engineering, electrical engineering, and mechanical engineering. I want to work with software, renewable energy, robotics, embedded systems, satellites, semiconductors, and/or rockets.
Answer: Based on what you listed, I would start out in electrical engineering and start exploring the actual practice of building those sorts of things. Then adjust as necessary.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is it actually strange that I want to learn? I am a sophomore in HS and I am learning physics and other engineering stuff on my own. People call me weird and a freak, I just want to be ready to be an electrical engineer and follow my idol, Tony Stark

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I have heard doing a PhD has a very low ROI. Under what circumstances is this true and not true?
Answer: Short answer: true under effectively all circumstances, depending on your definitions. If we’re trying to measure ROI, keep in mind that it stands for “Return On Investment.” What is 5–8 years of your life worth? That’s the investment. What are you getting for the prime of your life? That’s the return. Individuals get to decide what their own lives are worth in any country with unfettered access to the Internet. (My condolences for those from North Korea, Russia, China, etc.) That answers the first question. What are you getting in return? Note my emphasis on “you:” the money issue touches something that makes effectively all degree comparison statistics I’ve ever seen, frankly, crap for a person’s decision making. If you are capable of finishing a PhD, all bachelor’s or master’s grads is not the appropriate comparison group. The appropriate comparison group is people who could have done the PhD but chose not to: the people most like what you would have been if you didn’t chase the PhD. No one breaks that statistic out because no one can, but trying to pretend that the statistics are useful for an individual’s decision making without that breakout is crazy. My area is computer engineering/science, so I can only comment on that area. I am in my mid 40s now, so I’m 15+ years past PhD. I’ve known people who left after a master’s, people who dropped out of PhD, and people who finished their PhDs. The people who only did a master’s, but who I thought were PhD material, are doing the best on average. They were making six-figure salaries after two years of graduate school and compound interest was tremendous. Their aggressive attitudes and clarity of thought served them very well. So I would claim that at least 99% of all PhD attempts are worse than stopping at a master’s or earlier: the PhD has inferior monetary ROI. Even if you finish, the several years of lost income and lack of compounding interest cripples your earnings compared to a good master’s graduate. The only people who maybe caught up are exceptional even for PhDs. People who publish widely used introductory textbooks, people who get jobs only available to PhDs in lucrative engineering industries, etc. They were exceptional people with or without the PhD. If you are considering pursuing a PhD thinking that it will “fix” something or improve your reputation, stop and walk away. It will not. I’ve known plenty of crappy PhDs that cannot outperform the aforementioned master’s graduates who could have finished a PhD at a top engineering program. All that being said: the vast majority of us who pursued PhDs didn’t define our investment and return in terms of money. I wouldn’t change my decision to pursue it, although I would have changed my initial research topics.

Question: Do you believe chemical engineering is the most innovative field in science?
Answer: Hardcore theoretical and experimental physics is both in science and truly innovative: they’re figuring out the building blocks of existence. Engineering is not science and is innovative only when considering its (many) constraints: building usable things at reasonable cost to last a useful time.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Which school should I pick if money isn't a big factor, UCSC EE major or SCU ME major? I am living in the Bay Area.
Answer: You should put where you’re currently living out of your mind and decide: First, I would have applied to more schools in the first place and had more options. Second, I would choose based on the major first, environment second.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Do you believe that chemical engineering is underrated compared to other engineering fields?
Answer: Given that chemical engineering is one of the higher paid engineering disciplines, especially when you include petroleum engineering, I’d say it’s rated quite highly by employers. Do students underrate it? Maybe, but I don’t give a crap about the general opinion of students, a third of whom will drop out of engineering before they graduate, another third won’t last more than a few years as engineers, and nearly all of whom outside of chemical engineering will never take a chemical engineering class. Opinions based solely on ignorance and ego. I’d rather base my opinion on where the money flows. Note that I’m not a chemical engineer, although I’ve dated a few.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: If studying CS to be a software engineer no longer has a future, what majors and careers will have more prospects?
Answer: The premise of the question is false. Shit CS graduates have even less of a future than before, but they never had a long term future to begin with. The people defining the future still have CS and engineering degrees, and will do so for the foreseeable future. Go big or get out.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Which one gives me more chances of immigrating to the US: civil engineering or environmental engineering?
Answer: Both give you effectively zero chance. We have no shortage of either engineer. Both are relatively low paid compared to engineering areas that do give a chance of immigrating: U.S. supply is better at meeting demand in the former fields, so we don’t need to import them. You’d have to be an exception among exceptions and probably get a PhD in the U.S. and be aiming for a professorship to have a reasonable chance.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What are the cons of doing a non-traditional major for pre-med such as physics or engineering?
Answer: In the U.S., the only real con I can think of is that the courses you need to prepare for the MCAT and thus medical school might not all fit into the physics or engineering curricula. So you might need to take longer or have a busier schedule. But if you came into undergrad with some extra credits, it probably won’t be an issue. The positives outweigh the cons, in my opinion: I would prefer engineering over bio-pre-med and have known quite a few doctors with the former background.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: When comparing biomedical engineering to software engineering, which offers more opportunities? I am starting college soon and I am interested in becoming an either a software or a biomedical engineer.
Answer: They can be wildly different. If you have a clear passion and/or talent for one area, commit to that area. Biomedical engineering is very heavily oversubscribed in the U.S. and a few other developed countries: there are more undergraduate students than jobs at all levels (not just entry level), according to BLS and ASEE data. The odds are you won’t be getting a job in it if you major in it, especially if you are a weak student or if there aren’t many jobs in your country. But the top people are getting jobs in the area. There are far more software engineering jobs, more than computer science or software engineering majors. However, many grads do not learn the principles and cannot last in industry for a long time. Again, if you are a weak student, you won’t have many opportunities. The top people can make very large amounts of money. You have to be a strong student and a productive worker if you want to make a career out of either.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Would you choose U Wisconsin Madison or Rutgers New Brunswick as a NJ resident going into Computer Engineering? Is it worth paying extra for a better program? Does UW Madison have a better brand name, and will employers think more highly of it?
Answer: I would choose Rutgers. I would make absolutely sure I was at the top of my class there. Then I would go to graduate school. If you are unable to get into graduate school from Rutgers, going to a supposedly “better” school, whether it’s Wisconsin, or UIUC, or MIT, will not help you. As Konstantinos Konstantinides and Professor James Leland Harp have implied in their answers, if you want to do “true” computer engineering and be a leader in that space, most such people under the age of 45 have graduate degrees. The people deciding what happens with hardware at Apple, at Google, at NVIDIA, etc., mostly have PhDs from the very top institutions. Maybe there are exceptions, or maybe you can get by without a graduate degree at a company that doesn’t build technology (e.g. finance and HFT firms), but I wouldn’t count on it. Aim for a graduate degree. If you don’t want or plan to be doing that kind of work, then I can’t give you useful advice and you can stop reading. The curricula of engineering programs at state flagship universities aren’t significantly different: ABET accreditation requires that they be similar. It’s the admissions standards which are the primary determinant of undergraduate program “quality”: on average, the input determines the output. You are not an average and it’s up to you where you end up. Using SAT scores as a proxy for general academic ability: Rutgers SAT quartiles (25%-75%) are 1190–1410, Wisconsin-Madison’s are 1370–1500. I don’t have engineering-specific numbers for them. Wisconsin-Madison takes better students as a whole, but that’s as far as it goes. The range is much higher than the difference in the means: you have to go a ways up the ranks before you get a student body that’s significantly better as a whole. Being a top student at Rutgers will put you in a better position than the vast majority of Wisconsin grads. Undergraduate “brand name” isn’t a thing if you’re well above average. It is understood across the tech industry that a state flagship university is the best bang for buck for undergraduate engineering education. If you are in the top 10% at either school, you will have a lot of options. And you should be going to a graduate school with a bigger reputation, which will make your undergrad irrelevant. If you are in the lower half, you’re operating in an area I have effectively no experience with: most such people I know from higher ranked schools drop out of engineering entirely.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I’m a computer engineering student, and I want to go down either the biomedical engineering route or the mechatronics route, but I’m not sure which to pick yet. My school offers minors in both fields. Which minor would be better to take and why?
Answer: Neither. The mistake you’re making is letting the existence of a minor make you think it has employment value. It may not, and probably does not. The real value is in your major. Minors are fluff and won’t give you enough knowledge to do real work in the area. I don’t know about mechatronics, but biomedical engineering as an industry is highly oversubscribed: there are more students than total jobs (not just entry level). As you’d be a computer engineering grad and not biomedical, you wouldn’t be in the same situation, but I would not count on getting a job in the area. Most computer engineering grads move to software. You haven’t mentioned which country you are from, but that software likelihood increasing dramatically if you aren’t in a country that produces a lot of computer hardware. I would prepare for that likelihood.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Are computer science technical interviews (e.g. having applicants solve algorithmic problems in leetcode) actually useful for tech employers? Don’t savvy applicants simply cram-study just for the interviews and then forget everything later anyway?
Answer: “Useful” means there’s benefit. The benefit doesn’t even have to outweigh the costs. Relatively simple technical interviews serve as a useful screen to match the impression gained from what a candidate describes on their resume to the actual person. So yes, technical interviews are useful, in that they have a use. Can applicants cram-study and forget afterwards? Sure. But is that a bad thing? (Note that I’m playing devil’s advocate to most of the prior answers.) The pace of coursework at the top engineering or computer science programs can only be called cram study by most humans. Does anyone remember everything they were taught in undergrad? I certainly don’t. Everyone forgets things they don’t use regularly. That’s why we used to have shelves of reference books on our desks until the early days of the Internet, and why we have bookmarks to reference pages today. So even for qualified software engineers, we can’t remember everything all the time, and there’s a legitimate need to cram study for interviews if we’re interviewing for a job that might require, or at least test on, something outside our recent day-to-day experience. However, if you know the principles of the topics, your brain can pick those things up again quickly in the future. And an interviewer can easily go beyond the ability of an untrained person to be able to cram or look up on Google. So even if someone crams, interviews, and then forgets “everything,” they’ve demonstrated that they can get the right solution quickly even if they don’t know it right now. Not knowing and forgetting is the normal mode of operation. If you’re not operating on the edge of your comfort/knowledge zone, you’re not growing. Which in the tech industry meaning you’re falling behind. When I am personally interviewing people, two sanity check questions come to mind: There’s always a point at which you can’t fake experience for an experienced technical interviewer. You just need to get really down in the weeds. One tangential thought: some people get awfully offended when a medical doctor uses Google to go to NIH, Mayo Clinic, or some other site to check their knowledge of something. But every doctor I know personally (which includes most of my family members) does it from time to time. Again, no one remembers everything they’re ever taught. Even, and especially, at the highest levels of academic achievement.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Should I go to Carnegie Mellon or Princeton for engineering? Currently interested in electrical engineering but not quite sure. Also have smaller interests (minors?) in Entrepreneurship and Business Management.
Answer: Let’s assume you got into both. If you haven’t already, then you probably won’t have that choice, since the vast majority of people who apply to both will get rejected by at least one (and usually both). The primary determinant of success in this situation is going to be you and how much you like the environment. Pittsburgh and Princeton are very, very, very different. If you hate one, it’s going to affect your performance. Both programs produce top EEs. The variance is far greater than any difference in the means. If you’re barely passing, the money and effort you spent on admission will have been a waste. Don’t waste your opportunity. There’s always idiots who did well in high school that fell apart in undergrad. As for entrepreneurship and business management: I also had an interest in it. I did some coursework and a minor. Don’t prioritize it over your technical studies. Take whatever’s available, but you can pick up anything you need in passing. It’s your technical skills that are going to give you entry to the world of entrepreneurship, and if/when the company fails, they’re what will keep you on your feet. Speaking as someone on startup #4. If you ever plan to lead a business, basic accounting, finance, and marketing courses are useful, but the courses that will be worth your time are those in business and entrepreneurial law: that’s not something you can just wing or rely on hearsay. Most of those courses will teach you the basics and you’ll realize that the principles between engineering and law are very different. Then you’ll realize that you’ll need a competent lawyer for anything but the most trivial things. My wife and I have started two businesses, and we would have been burned badly, possibly killing the business, if we hadn’t gone to a lawyer at the right time. Lawyers are expensive, but a few hours with one can save tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: My major is civil engineering, but my dream is to become an architect. Should I change my major to become something I want or stay an engineer because this is what my dad wants?
Answer: If your dream had good job security, I would say go with that, but it generally doesn’t. You’ll have to balance your desires with practicality, keeping your family’s desires in mind (especially if they’re paying the bills). At least there’s a relationship between architecture and civil engineering (of buildings), and if you have architectural engineering as an option, that closes the gap significantly. Depending on your school, you might have the ability to take some architecture courses that count towards your major, or at least electives of some kind. I would dip my toe in and see if it’s what I dreamed it to be before committing. Many people’s dreams are actually delusions with no basis in fact, so you’ll want to make sure you’re not one of those people.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Why don’t all Silicon Valley firms outsource their engineer tasks to India for cheaper labour costs?
Answer: Many tech companies have teams in India: full members of the overall team, and more importantly, full ownership. Outsourcing engineering is often deleterious for both speed and quality, no matter which country where that outsourcing is occurring. You only have to look at Boeing’s screwups with the 737 MAX aircraft to see the results of that. Software changes much more rapidly than physical assets. Silicon Valley software changes much more rapidly than generic software: otherwise it’d be in a far cheaper part of the U.S. in the first place. Outsourcing software to another company is usually worse for speed and quality because the outsourcing company: My personal experience with Indian outsourcing firms is that many such firms are out to drag out the process of specification and development, milking money instead of building good software. I have no clue whether that’s the norm, but it’s happened to me enough that I won’t use one. Being late to market costs far more money than anything saved with cut-rate labor. The British have a very old saying for this: “penny wise, pound foolish.” Software engineers in India should be part of the team and be held to the same standards. And most Indians, like most Americans and most humans in general, do not measure up. Incidentally, a friend was talking about his experience with a South American outsourcing company. It was no better than any other outsourcing company. However, when that outsourcing company folded, his company hired on a few of the former employees and cut out the middleman. As a result, the code quality is higher and the delivery speed is faster (with fewer people!), the new employees get paid more even though overall costs are less, and everyone (except presumably the former outsourcing bosses) is happier.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is it convenient to do a bachelor in physics while PhD in electrical engineering? I have studied bch. and MS. in electrical engineering? What is the best approach to be a theoretical physicist in this situation?
Answer: What do you mean by “theoretical physics?” Do you know if anyone alive is doing what you define as theoretical physics who’s entered a PhD program in electrical engineering? If no one like that exists, that’s your answer: you don’t. If you really want to go down that path, you need to get off the current one. Incidentally, most schools will not let you pursue a bachelor’s degree when you already have a master’s. If your definition of “theoretical physics” falls under some auspices of EE, e.g. semiconductor research, you operate in that overlap zone as a EE student. It’s not my area, but I have several friends in that area. They weren’t going to be doing astrophysics, or gravitational physics, or stuff that’s similarly distant.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: For at least several decades, the engineering majors at UC Berkeley have been 'impacted' (that is, there are more students who want to major in engineering than there are available seats). Why doesn't UCB just expand the number of engineering seats?
Answer: Short answer: money and incentives. I asked a similar question when I was in undergrad at UIUC. As I made my way up the academic ladder and got involved in teaching, research, and fund raising, I got a better look into state universities as a whole, particularly the financial aspect, and some of the differences between UIUC and UC Berkeley and Michigan (where most of my collaborators were) in particular.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Are there more PhD grads than jobs that require one?
Answer: Yes. That’s also true for effectively every degree level: associate’s, bachelor’s, master’s, MBA, JD, and so on. We rarely produce exactly or fewer than what we need. The exception that comes to mind is medical doctors (MDs), but even that’s arguable, as DOs and physician’s assistants fill most of the gap.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: People who lied on their resume and ended up getting the job, what ended up happening?
Answer: I don’t know about other countries or industries, but in the U.S. civilian tech industry, there is a tendency to trust, then verify via performance. For technical roles, it’s usually blatantly obvious in interviews if someone falls significantly short of their resume. When I’ve been the interviewer, I cut it short and reject them. The few cases I know of where people got the job, then were caught lying on their resume were because: If they get the job and can do the job, almost no one’s going to be checking their resume for the foreseeable future. But when someone lies about their experience, they’re usually lying about experience they don’t have, and lacking that experience often means they lack some ability to do the job. That’s when people start checking your credentials in depth. If your job doesn’t directly require those credentials, you might not get caught for decades, e.g. sports coaches or the MIT Dean of Admissions about 20 years ago. But then people might start asking about how they can achieve similar longevity/success, which is when those lies come to light. School attendance and graduation are easily checked, and the aforementioned people lied about their schools. If you lied on your resume when they start looking into you in those situations, effectively 100% of the time you’re fired in the U.S. It generally doesn’t matter how long ago it was: that former MIT dean lied on her 28-year-old job application. Some idiots might try to sue for wrongful termination (e.g. discrimination), but that will likely backfire. The only person I’ve ever met personally (but didn’t know) lied about their managerial experience. She wasn’t hired in as a manager, but was promoted at one point. It was obvious in short order that she had never managed anyone. If she hadn’t lied in the first place, she probably would have been demoted rather than fired. For jobs that involve security clearances and the government or military industrial complex, the scrutiny of your resume is going to be repetitive, and the results of lying are going to be much worse. I’ve only heard stories, but they make the above sound like a vacation.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: How is ECE at Princeton University?
Answer: I have a few friends who graduated ECE at Princeton, both undergrad and grad. It is a top program. You will not lose to anyone other than by your own deficiencies. Depending on your area of interest, it is superior to other schools’ programs generally ranked higher.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What major (CE or CS) is better with BME minor in terms of job flexibility, demand, and skills? And is the combination of CS/CE major with BME minor a good choice? How much work will it demand to major and minor in both?
Answer: Minors are fluff, just 4–5 courses. Don’t expect them to get you a job. I’ve never personally seen or experienced a situation where minors mattered in a positive way. (I have two of them.) BME is extremely oversubscribed in the U.S.: there are more BME undergraduate students than BME jobs at all levels, according to ASEE and BLS data. Your BME minor is worthless in that context: there are plenty of cheap graduates who actually specialized in the area. As for effort, who knows? 95% of engineering graduates would fail out of MIT, because the latter has a brutal pace and workload. (No, I did not go there, but I compared syllabi of MIT courses with schools ranked around #10. 30–50% more material.) At an easy school, it will be easy to add a minor. At a tough school, it will be hard to finish in the same time you would have without the minor. Choose an engineering major because you want to do work in that field. Ignore minors as far as useful credentials go.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Should tech companies skip coding interview rounds for older experienced candidates? Don't you think it's very rude & insulting to reject older developers just because they couldn't pass a coding test? What's your honest opinion on this topic?
Answer: If the older developer is going to be developing, then (s)he should be tested on coding. It’s part of the job. I’m in my late 40s now, so a lot of fresh grads consider me “older.” I still punch out code. Not always similar volumes as I did before, but my code is far more stable and long lasting than when I first started out in industry. And I don’t think it’s rude or insulting to ask me a coding question. Those are trivial compared to what I have to work on day-to-day. Bang it out, move on. I’ve known developers in their 60s. They’re still hammering away. If you don’t want to be developing, move into a non development management role.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Out of UCSB, UCD, and UCSC, which have the best CS academic program and internship opportunities/job security after a degree?
Answer: Schools do not give you internship opportunities or job security. That’s your job. A more reputed school may get a few more eyeballs on your resume, but it doesn’t make up for crap grades, complete absence of evidence of interest in the field, or a lack of substantial projects inside or outside the classroom. In the industries that CS graduates work in, the world keeps changing. You get job security by keeping up, or ideally being the person who defines the future: people have to keep up with you.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Will Rust replace C++?
Answer: Rust will not completely replace C++ unless the latter goes completely off the rails. I’ve been using Rust full time for over a year now. I’ve been using C++ for over 15 years before that. For certain kinds of graph manipulations, especially for control flow or dataflow graph optimizations in compiler backends, Rust at best gets in the way and at worst requires huge amounts of copying to implement the same functionality as C++. All while not fixing the core problem with compilers, which is whether the transformations are actually correct. Rust is certainly better at some things and I’ve encountered those situations, but that performance hit in the pursuit of safety is not something people are willing to incur for compilation. Not even for the Rust compiler, which uses LLVM (written mainly in C++) as its backend. I’m still a Rust novice, so I might be missing a good way to do my work in Rust, but I haven’t seen it yet.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I got accepted into UCSB, UC Irvine, Chapman, and Santa Clara. Which school is the best?
Answer: Which major? What’s your goal? It’s impossible to say unless we know these things. For something like computer science or engineering, I don’t think any of them is wildly better than the others. I’ll assume you’re in California and would be paying in-state tuition for the UCs, since all four schools are in California. Undergrad will not define your life. What it does is give you opportunities. There are plenty of opportunities at any of those schools.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I have been learning C++ for a year now, and I am fully prepared. Can you please guide me on how to start earning with it?
