Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What field of engineering/computer science should I do a master’s/PhD in when trying to learn AI chips?
Answer: Most graduate programs cannot teach you about AI chips specifically, because most designs of AI chips are not available to the public. The companies designing the chips will give out some details at conferences, but not enough to get a good understanding of the chips. If you want to design AI/ML chips, then the appropriate graduate programs are in electrical and computer engineering, and computer science. Specifically, you want coursework in logic design and computer microarchitecture. That’s a small subset of all the topics ECE and CS cover. You can look at who publishes in the International Symposium on Computer Architecture (ISCA) and the IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Microarchitecture (Micro) to see which schools tend to be stronger. However, there can be a disconnect between who publishes in academia and who does good work in industry, so you shouldn’t use those publications as some source of “truth.”

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I have good ML skills which I get from watching tutorials and taking online courses. Can I get an internship without a degree? How?
Answer: You think you have good ML skills. The fact that you’re looking for an internship means you don’t actually know whether people in industry share your standards. Most likely they do not. Most people I’ve met doing ML internships already have bachelor’s degrees and are in the process of getting master’s or PhDs. Second, internships are for current students. Not for people after receiving their degrees, and not for people who have never had a degree.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: How much of a threat to Nvidia is Cerebras Systems?
Answer: I’ve worked for both NVIDIA and Cerebras. For consumer graphics or automotive applications, Cerebras is irrelevant to NVIDIA. It’s only in the domain of parallel computing and machine learning in particular where Cerebras is a potential threat to NVIDIA. Cerebras is a non zero threat to NVIDIA. However, the fact that each Cerebras machine is on the order of a few million USD and requires power not generally available in a house or standard office setting makes it very specific in its purchase and usage model right now. I would say Cerebras is not an immediate, overall threat to NVIDIA, but will likely eat NVIDIA’s lunch in very specific cases. Like the following. As I’m on the software side, I get requests from recruiters for those jobs, and something I’ve been noticing is a lot of companies trying to virtualize/abstract away which hardware is being used for neural network training. If one or more of those efforts succeed, then Cerebras becomes a much bigger threat: people can rent training time on the cloud and the software can choose the appropriate hardware. If Cerebras hardware is better for the money, then cloud providers will buy much more of it.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: How do I know if I really want to start a tech company?
Answer: If you’re asking, you don’t really want to. Most people I’ve know who’ve founded tech companies were compelled to do so. They did so either because they will not do anything other than start and run tech companies, or they had an idea that they had to make sure got brought to market. That’s my standard for starting a tech company, which is why I haven’t done so even though I’ve worked for four startups. I’m not the first kind of person, and I haven’t had any ideas I needed to bring to market.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I recently got admitted to Berkeley, CMU, Georgia tech, UMich, Princeton, USC, and UIUC for EECS/ECE/EE. If I want to specialize in application specific accelerators, which university should I go to based on the academic strength in this area?
Answer: Are you talking about undergraduate programs? It doesn’t matter much. As Professor Joshua Gross and Konstantinos Konstantinides both said in prior answers, ASIC/accelerator work is done almost entirely at the graduate level. Been there, done that, got my PhD and made a living off of it for 16 years, four startups, and counting. GPUs, FPGAs, ML accelerators both tiny (for phones and self-driving cars) and huge (Cerebras wafer scale processors). And a bunch of work on “standard” processors too. I live on the software side now, but work with hardware folks all the time. Don’t choose a school if it’s going to be ridiculously more expensive than the others, otherwise visit their campuses and go with your gut. I’ve been to most of those campuses, and they’re all different. Incidentally, congratulations: that’s an impressive admit list. You’ve got every top undergrad program besides MIT and Stanford (which have ridiculously low admit rates). If my kids get half of those, I’ll throw a party (which I don’t do for birthdays). You should be proud of your accomplishments that enabled your acceptance. Just remember that it’s a brand new game at the next level, at which point your past accomplishments might as well not exist. Second, most of those schools have professors working on application-specific acceleration, or did at one point. I went to UIUC and worked on accelerators in graduate school. I had collaborators mostly at Berkeley, UMich, and Princeton. The three UIUC professors I would say were most focused on application acceleration when I was in school have all left academia (two are currently at NVIDIA), so I wouldn’t choose that as the default option. The academic world changes all the time, and by the time you graduate, the world will have changed. Even more likely is that you and your interests will have changed. So keep an open mind. You might be able to learn GPU programming (probably using NVIDIA’s CUDA) towards the end of undergrad at certain schools. But I wouldn’t be in a hurry to get to that point. Which touches something important: You need a strong foundation and fundamentals before you start diving into specifics. I can’t stress that enough. I return to those fundamentals all the time. That’s why undergraduate study is important. The problem with some CS folks is that they have no grounding in the physical reality of computing, then propose structures that can’t exist in reality. You’re not going to be able to make a living off of your knowledge if it runs off into fantasy land. Hope that helps. Good luck with your studies. It’s an interesting (and lucrative) time to be working in the area, and that fact is not going to change by the time you graduate undergrad.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Can I transfer from a community college in CA to UIUC? Does anybody have experience transferring from a community college in California to UIUC?
Answer: I spent 12 years at UIUC. The only person I met who transferred from a CA school to UIUC did so from San Jose State, not a community college. See Professor Joshua Gross’s answer for all the reasons you shouldn’t bother applying. The only things I’m going to add are: Back to the person who transferred. I thought she was insane for paying out-of-state tuition when she was also accepted to UC Berkeley and would be paying in-state tuition there. And I thought she was crazy for wanting to be in the middle of freezing cornfields when her birth country has a subtropical climate and she grew up in an urban area. But she wanted to get out of California very badly and was willing to pay for it. On the other hand, I didn’t think she was crazy enough that I shouldn’t marry her or have children with her: we’ve been married 14 years. However, I wouldn’t rely on having that luck.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What is the better route: Bachelors and Masters (CS) in 3+1 years or Bachelors with double major (CS and Math) in 4 years? The reason for math is to gain skills in reasearch and possibly PhD post graduate.
Answer: The first. No one gives a shit about double majors when it comes to graduate school or employment, especially if your grades aren’t effectively perfect. The recruiters might lie and say they’re impressed, but that’s their job: don’t believe them. Once you’re out of school, almost no one cares about graduate degrees either, again excepting recruiters. You can take a crapload of math towards your major in most CS curricula. You don’t need a double major. If you’re going to do a PhD in CS, do research in CS. If there’s any math you need, pick it up on the way. Math research is not CS research. Choose what you’re going to study, focus on that, and get to your goals beyond a degree. A degree is just an enabler.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Which martial arts are considered fake?
Answer: Define “fake.” Most hand-to-hand martial arts are considered relatively useless compared to a few hours training in firearms. Ignoring availability and legal issues, a gun and the ability to use it is far more useful. Most empty-hand martial arts are effectively useless against multiple armed assailants, and that’s an all-too-common case in “civilization.” Hunting in groups with weapons is what put us on the top of the food chain, after all. The point is that martial arts may have limited use and effectiveness, but that doesn’t make it not real. Maybe it doesn’t even have a combat use: it’s still “real” as far as bodily motion and exercise go, which is something much of America badly needs. All that being said, I’d say the use of playing cards as weapons is “fake” in that it cannot do real damage. Anything that can reliability put mass behind a blow, or the opponent on the ground and/or unable to move, is real enough.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: After doing a BSc in Physics, if someone does an MSc in any engineering subject, can he practice engineering? Does he get the status of an engineer? Will it be the right decision?
Answer: Depending on the country, you will not be admitted to a graduate program in classical engineering fields if you don’t have the appropriate, accredited bachelor’s degree. Even another engineering degree, definitely not physics. Civil engineering is the classic example. There’s at least two years of coursework that are disjoint between most engineering fields and physics. Otherwise, most fields don’t care what your earlier degrees might have been. I think two of my computer engineering professors had undergraduate degrees in mechanical and aerospace engineering, respectively. No one cared.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What are the differences in academic rigor of the biggest state schools: Berkeley, Michigan Ann Arbor, Minnesota, Wisconsin Madison, and Texas Austin? Are all of them about the same or Berkeley stands out head & shoulders above the rest?
Answer: “Rigor” is a bit difficult to define, but I would claim it’s roughly in line with admissions standards. So UC Berkeley will generally lead, as it usually has the highest admissions standards. (Admissions standards are used in rankings, so those are correlated.) Schools teach to the average student, so when the average student is more capable, there’s more material at a faster pace. I once went through course syllabi of introductory electrical and computer engineering courses at MIT and several schools ranked around #10. MIT taught 30–50% more material per course. If you had the same “rigor” at the lower ranked schools, I’d bet at least half of the students would fail out. Note that I did not attend any of the aforementioned schools, including MIT.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What are some of the promising jobs in the USA one can get with regards to having a degree in language, specifically English?
Answer: If you are not a U.S. citizen, permanent resident, or otherwise have the unrestricted right to work in the U.S., stop. First you should be asking whether you can work legally in the U.S. with an English degree. Getting a work visa to live and work in the country is generally reserved for professions in low supply, and getting that visa requires that the person be paid above the average. English degrees are not in low supply. Unless you are coming in via some other mechanism, you are not going to be getting permission to work. Second, because neither English degrees nor the skills they provide are in short supply, most such people do not have “promising” jobs available to them. The jobs available to all college graduates are the primary market for such graduates.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Should I just major in physics? I have heard bad things about it and how there is little to no jobs and honestly I really can’t see myself studying anything else. Is physics a good starting point to branch out into other careers or industries?
Answer: I think you’re probably best off starting in Physics, but I would also explore and be ready to change my mind. As a high schooler you don’t have the experience to know what’s out there, and most undergrads change their major at least once. A lot of people with Physics (graduate) degrees have already weighed in, and you should read their answers. But keep in mind that most of them got their degrees decades ago. The world constantly changes, and you should take all advice (including mine) with that in mind. Doing physics will lock you out of some paths, but all majors lock you out of some paths. Since engineering shares a decent amount of coursework with physics, I’ll talk about that. If you want to be an engineer in the U.S., you may be locked out of paths that require an ABET-accredited engineering degree. However, most jobs involving computers do not require an engineering degree, and that’s where I’ve encountered a lot of physics graduates (often with PhDs). Experimental physics often uses supercomputers, which is a transferrable skill. And that’s what you want to be picking up in the course of your studies. You might be disadvantaged in some jobs compared to a specialist, but life and education are not only about the job market.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I might want mechanical engineering/aerospace in university, but my family is afraid I can't get a job. My mother suggested I become a teacher, father suggested learning software since I already know Python, I'm not sure what to choose?
Answer: What country do you live in? Effectively every country has a need for mechanical engineers. Except maybe for a few Western European countries, my impression is that teaching is a more unpleasant profession in terms of pay and treatment. Knowing Python is insufficient for a good software engineering job, so I’m assuming that you’d be studying computer science. But CS is not necessarily any more in demand than mechanical engineering. Mechanical engineering talent is sufficiently scarce that you may be able to immigrate if your country doesn’t have enough jobs in that area. If you don’t do what you have intrinsic motivation for, it’s probably not going to go well. I might give different advice if you wanted to study dance or something similarly less practical, but mechanical engineering is a solid profession in most places.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Can you get fired during an internship if you don't perform well?
Answer: I’m only familiar with internships at tech companies, almost entirely technical internships. Other companies and industries may vary. Normally (ideally?) the hiring bar for interns is high enough that gross incompetence is caught before an internship is offered. So even if an intern doesn’t do too well, there isn’t a need to fire them ahead of the ~12-week end of the internship. The only cases I’ve heard of interns being fired were at least in part due to awful attitude. Unwillingness to learn, insistence on doing things a different way from mandated, or general disagreeableness.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Can Japan make Silicon Valley?
Answer: No. Not today’s Silicon Valley. Three reasons: First, immigration ease/policy. As a natural born American, I have almost always been in the minority of Silicon Valley teams: it’s mostly foreign born. We want top talent and Americans are less than 5% of humanity. When you cut second generation Americans (e.g. Nisei) like myself, the percentage is really small. The sub issues are: Second, culture. Japan has the wrong culture for Silicon Valley style innovation, as exhibited by differences in our popular sayings. A Japanese saying goes, “the tall nail gets hammered down.” But in the USA, we have an opposing saying: “the squeaky wheel gets the grease.” Take this man: This man is Shuji Nakamura, inventor of the blue LED. He doggedly worked on a hard problem for a very long time. In Japan, his company tried to shut him down multiple times and awarded him a pittance for his invention. He needed to get a PhD to be taken seriously. In Silicon Valley, you don’t need a PhD (although I do have one). And we don’t shut people down for crazy stuff. Stuff like the wafer scale computer my third startup, Cerebras Systems, created. (There were no PhDs on the initial team and two of four were foreign born.) Plenty of answers on Quora from supposed “experts” said it couldn’t be done. They had all heard it from someone else and didn’t know why it had failed. (Most such answers have been deleted by this point.) The point is that Dr. Nakamura would be (and is) treated bigger than a rock star in the US technical world, even before receiving the Nobel Prize. Which is why he lives in the USA now, rather than Japan. Other cultural differences: Finally, Japan’s domestic software industry, while large, does not generally innovate. And today’s Silicon Valley is overwhelmingly software. I recently came across a video explaining why Japan’s software industry is underperforming compared to the rest of the world’s, so I’ll just link it here. Since my Korean grandparents grew up during Japanese occupation and lived in Japan for over a decade, I’ve been to Japan more times than I can conveniently count. It’s a lovely country, and I’ll visit again. But I also work in Silicon Valley and I’ve been a part of four startups so far (along with Apple and Alphabet). The first two were acquired, the third will IPO in the next few months, and I’m an employee of the fourth now. That kind of work history would be looked upon with suspicion in Japan, and even in slow moving areas of the USA. But in Silicon Valley, I’m a reliable worker who gets stuff done in a hurry and delivers value to my employers. Japan can’t get people like me to live and work there compared to the USA and Silicon Valley in particular.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I received offers from Georgia Tech and Michigan Ann Arbor for an ECE master’s. I want to focus on digital IC and analog IC. Which one should I choose?
Answer: I would lean towards Michigan myself: I went to UIUC for my degrees but know quite a few people on Michigan’s faculty. However, my area isn’t strictly ICs: you’ll want to see which professors align with your interests at both institutions and choose accordingly.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I’m 20, on placement year at a really good company/field and have 1 year uni left (chemical engineering). I want to get a graduate job/move to the USA as soon as I can, any advice?
Answer: Realistically? Assuming you’re not from a nation with special status (e.g. Canada, Mexico, Australia): Watch out for people promising a shortcut or special treatment for bribes. People from more corrupt countries sometimes try that route. I don’t know where you come from, but when it comes to immigration, that approach tends to backfire badly. You will most likely be banned for life. Trying to get a work visa as a fresh undergrad graduate is effectively impossible. You’re not worth the extra cost. Don’t be an idiot and presume that you can work an engineering job without the legal right to work in the U.S. You wil be filling out Form I-9 for every and any job proving you have the right to work in the U.S. No company employing engineers will employ you illegally, because they would face potential prison time.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What are some of the best certifications I can get online as an undergraduate computer-science student?
Answer: Nothing. Certifications are for cookie cutters. There are no certifications for the ability to build things from scratch, and to jump into projects and quickly contribute in a meaningful way.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Incase my plans to go to an ivy league do not work out, how do I be sure that I'll be surrounded by intelligent people throughout college? I'm tired of people who resist thinking deeply/learning in highschool. Will majoring in physics be enough?
Answer: Frankly, if you want to have the majority of people around you be those who think deeply and constantly learn, you’re going to have to wait until graduate school. That’s how long I had to wait. Even at a top undergraduate program, there will be people there who only want to pass and graduate, not expand their minds. There’s an answer somewhere on Quora from a purported Princeton grad who had Cs and Ds throughout undergrad. But you can prune out much of the bottom by going to a program/school with high admissions standards. The Ivy League (athletic conference) schools are selective, but so are many others. It is insufficient to look at acceptance rates, because the base rate/population of each school is different. Most schools publish their admit quartiles: the GPAs and test scores of the admits at the 25%, 50% and 75% marks. The same major at different schools may have wildly different statistics. I guarantee some of the admits will fail, even at the most selective schools, because some always do. Their parents won’t be there, they’ll get hooked on alcohol, drugs, or some other distraction, and so on. But the percentage of idiots will still be a lot lower.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is working at a tech company with their own programming language/low code develop platform a good career choice and bring good future opportunities?
Answer: The question is too vague to give a useful answer, but the default answer is no. Just because a company has its own programming language or low code platform doesn’t mean you are going to be using it. Google has its “own” programming language(s), although open sourced and adopted externally over time, and its own low code platform for use mainly by customers. Most people would say that Google is better than most companies as a company to spend part of your career at. If no one else adopts the language or the platform? You’re spending time potentially working on stuff that isn’t transferable. Generally not a “good” thing. Finally, I don’t know what you consider a “good” career choice or “good” future opportunity. That’s subjective. I know people who don’t think Google is a good place to go. I think they’re in a very small minority and I don’t align with them, but that’s their opinion.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Do medical schools place a lot of emphasis on the undergraduate school the student attended?
Answer: Undergraduate institution matters. I have no clue how you define “a lot of emphasis.” Very little has a hard cutoff for medical/graduate admissions. Think of it from the perspective of the medical school. They want good, smart people. If Undergrad Program A has consistently produced such people, the med school will favor such a program for future candidates. If Program B graduates mostly people who cannot perform in med school (e.g. diploma mills), the med school is going to mostly ignore that program/school. The MCAT serves as a calibration tool, and most medical schools have been around for decades, so they have a lot of data to work with when choosing admits. So if you and some other person are being compared, and the other person went to a school/program known to be more selective/rigorous/competitive, you may need to get better grades, have more accomplishments, or do something similar to be accepted to the same graduate institutions. But the school will not save you if you have below a B average, and a school known to hand out degrees will kill your candidacy. There are far more candidates than spots, so no reputable graduate school needs to lower admission standards to that level.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Which university? U-Michigan OOS with scholarship of honor or Harvard? I want to study robotics and create a startup.
Answer: Have you already been accepted at both, Blake? If not, don’t count your chickens before they hatch. Apply first and see if you get in. Nearly all people who apply to both won’t get into at least one. If you have, congratulations. The next questions are: I didn’t go to either school, so I have no horse in this race. Unlike effectively all of the prior answerers, I actually have some startup experience: four of them, with no failures yet. If my kid said (s)he wanted to study robotics and create a startup, I’d tell them not to even bother applying to Harvard. The dream list would be MIT, CMU, Stanford. Followed by Michigan and several other top engineering schools. Most of them have acceptance rates in the single digit percentages, so spread your net really wide.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I am planning to apply for the computer science field in college. I have ECA activities that are more like leadership and event organizing. Is it going to negatively affect my acceptance into a good college?
Answer: No, it’s a positive. Maybe not the most positive thing you could do, but still positive. And I’m not sure what would be definitively better, off the top of my head. Kids who code before college aren’t necessarily a good fit for computer science study.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Can I get a job in the US as a software engineer, when I don’t live in USA?
Answer: Theoretically yes. But you need a work visa, and it’s difficult to get one unless you’re a world class engineer or did your education in the U.S. There is effectively zero possibility of working illegally as a software engineer.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Waymo just deployed 50 robotic taxis in Los Angeles. Are there legal ways people could fight against them?
Answer: Theoretically yes, but it requires political and/or legal system approaches, and their lawyers (including one of the CEOs) are almost certainly better than anything you or a small group of citizens could afford. Interfering with the cars themselves isn’t legal. I don’t know why you would bother, even if your income was from ridesharing. It’s the inexorable march of technology. Waymo cars are safer than humans, especially in a place like LA, so once the cost to the consumer falls below Uber or Lyft, people are going to take it. I’d take it, even though they laid me off last year.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Do FAANG companies hire at the entry level software engineering, or do they tend to hire more experienced developers for higher positions?
Answer: Moa, the answer as your question runs is “yes.” They hire at the entry level, depending on the state of the company, and they also hire more experienced developers for higher positions. If you’re asking whether they’ll hire at entry level for higher positions, the answer is no. Why would they? They’ve got competent people within the company already, so those would be promoted and new hires will be entry level. There have been times where certain companies do not hire fresh grads. When they’re relatively small and the bulk of their tasks are specific work to be done by specialists, they may hire few or no new grads. Apple and Netflix generally didn’t hire fresh software engineering grads in the early 2000s (this is before even iPod or movie streaming were out). As the workload increases, at some point a large tech company needs to build its own talent pipeline, rather than rely on others, even if it lowers overall efficiency. The U.S. airline industry has the same issue: when the U.S. military can’t supply enough pilots, they have to take civilians from schools and other avenues.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Should I go to the University of Washington, UIUC, or UC Santa Cruz for an engineering major? I am living in CA.
Answer: Which engineering? UCSC is probably the best bang for buck with in-state tuition. However, if you’ve aiming for CS and U-W or UIUC has accepted you into their CS program, I would try to go to one of those schools, even with higher tuition. If you stop at undergrad with CS at UCSC, you may be limited in your future. Note that UIUC does not allow transfers into CS anymore, if you were thinking about trying to do that. For whatever school, work hard and excel: that will determine your future far more than the school.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: As a freshman CS major with no significant projects, should I minor in accounting to have a backup plan for getting an accounting job after graduation while applying for CS jobs, given the potential difficulty in landing a CS role right away?
Answer: You seem to misunderstand what an “accounting job” is. That’s not something you get with a minor, unless you’re talking about doing basic bookkeeping. Just about anything of substance is done by a CPA, and that usually takes five years of education. Not 4–5 classes. And it’s one of the harder business majors, looking at how much my friends in the field studied. It is not that difficult to get a CS job out of school. Find internships during undergrad, do well in them, and they’ll want you back.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Assuming equal cost of attendance, should I attend Columbia University or The University of Michigan? I want to study robotics and ultimately start a robotics company (which would probably start from a product that I develop throughout uni)
Answer: As someone who’s visited both but not associated with either, I don’t think it matters too much, but I would lean to Michigan. My impression is that there’s more focus on student-started startups at U-Mich, as Ann Arbor doesn’t have all of NYC competing for attention. I’ve been to Michigan’s startup fair myself and it was a remarkably big thing. I saw VC firms such as Andreessen Horowitz attending, so there’s no lack of capital.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Should we, as American citizens, apologize and pay reparations to the people and nation of Japan for the horrific atomic attack in 1945?
Answer: This is a picture of a memorial at Hiroshima. I’m going to save its explanation for later. As you aren’t a question spammer, Jack Rea, I’ll assume you’re asking an honest question and aren’t familiar with all the history. Other than the fact that the Japanese attacked us first at Pearl Harbor, without a preceding declaration of war (a violation of the Hague Convention of 1907, which the Japanese were signatory to). Which is enough reason for most Americans to say “they started shit, we’re going to end it.” The reason we (the U.S.) sanctioned Japan in the first place was the horrific things they were doing to the Chinese, our allies. That war is called the “Second Sino-Japanese War” by most history books. The Japanese killed eight million Chinese, mostly civilians, before Pearl Harbor was attacked. News of events like the Nanjing Massacre in 1937 got out to the rest of the world. The Nazis wouldn’t commit that kind of butchery for several more years. So if some idiot says “the U.S. provoked Japan into attacking,” I have nothing to say to them. Except “go help de-mine a minefield in Ukraine by walking through it.” During the war, the Japanese committed quite a few atrocities. End the war quickly, end the inhumanity, and definitely don’t waste American servicemen. Back to that picture. That’s the Monument in Memory to Korean Victims of the A-Bomb at Hiroshima. And while I’ve been saying “we” as a natural born American, my grandparents were residents of the so-called “Protectorate” of Korea, occupied by the Japanese, when the bombs were dropped. Over ten thousand Koreans were collateral damage of each bomb, before the term was invented. That’s war: people die, civilians die, and even people who don’t want to be there die. So, to answer the question: before talking about apologies and reparations to Japanese people, let’s first get apologies and reparations to Koreans who survived or died. The Korean survivors have gotten little help from any government in getting treatment. It took over 60 years to even get the limited recognition they have today. As for the Japanese? I’ve spent a lot of time in Japan and been to Hiroshima. We (the U.S.) already helped rebuild their country, and it was our (Korean) war that gave the stimulus to rebuild their country. All three have been allies since WWII and share common adversaries. It’s hard to forgive, but we should try. Being mired in the past prevents you from looking at the future. However, we should never forget, lest we repeat the same mistakes.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: How do I get an invitation to visit Silicon Valley?
Answer: You can pay me $10,000 US and I’ll give you one. In seriousness, Silicon Valley is not an official name or place. It’s a geographic area where a bunch of companies are based. So you come the same way you enter any other public place in the United States of America: if you’re not a citizen or permanent resident, you probably get a tourist visa and visit. However, there’s very little to see in Silicon Valley: just the outsides of buildings. For safety and security reasons, you’re not going to be let inside the buildings, and even if you did, 99% of it is just nerds at desks staring at screens. You can watch a similar scene on TV and save yourself the trip.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Would it be doable to double major in electrical and chemical engineering?
Answer: Doable? Yes, theoretically. However, it is a waste of time, effort, and money. Your mother might be impressed, but no engineer or recruiter will be. I would even say it’s a red flag for many of us. I had a few friends that completed double undergraduate engineering majors. All of them thought it was a waste of time in the end. At most they would have taken a few courses in the other area, e.g. my EE+ME friend did MEMS for his Ph.D. research: he did need a few ME courses, but found most of his ME degree to be a waste of time. He could have graduated undergrad earlier and not paid that extra tuition.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: My son is looking at UCSD or Washington for computer science. Does this limit work opportunities versus schools closer to Silicon Valley? Would a Santa Clara have better internships and work opportunities post graduation?
Answer: As I constantly repeat on Quora, the variance in ability at a school is far greater than the difference in the means between schools. If we are talking a company like Apple or Google, they want the best, and the best comes from everywhere. Think of top tech companies like a top sports league where the sport is played across the world, like the NBA, MLB, or Premier League. No team at that level recruits only locally, or even nationally: they recruit worldwide for top talent. Anyone who limits themselves geographically is disadvantaged when we’re talking worldwide competition. Santa Clara U is a solid university these days, but on average the UCSD and U-W grads are better, and hiring managers at top tech companies know that through their own experience. You will find more UCSD and U-W grads than Santa Clara U grads at top companies. You will find even more UIUC and U-Michigan Ann Arbor grads. In fact, the most represented undergraduate schools on my former team at my last employer were MIT and Seoul National University, which are arguably the top technical schools in their countries, and definitely not local. High pay and perks and interesting projects draw the best talent.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I would like to migrate to the US or Europe, but I would also like to work as a professional. I am an economist with 8 years of experience. What should I study, and what is the best way to do it?
Answer: I don’t know much about immigrating to Europe, so I’ll comment on the U.S. If you want to migrate permanently, you need a visa. The State Department provides information here. Some options I know of: There are a couple different types of work visas, all of which are listed on the State Department’s web page. Unless you’re already internationally renowned as an economist, you almost certainly can’t get the “exceptional talent” O-1 visa that would let you come in straight away. lThe majority of U.S. work visas are provided only where we have a relative labor shortage. Economics is generally not one such area. As a prior answer mentioned, engineering and medicine are two common areas. A quick aside: the U.S. has special trade status with a couple other countries. So if you’re from Canada, Mexico, Australia, or a few other countries, the bar is significantly lower, with special visas. You’ll have to do your own research on what’s required. Assuming you need new study/training to get a work visa, the next question is where you should get your training: the U.S., your home country, or somewhere else.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Would it be possible to major in computer science with no background? I am told that I will be a failure.
Answer: Who’s telling you that? Maybe you shouldn’t be listening to that person. Especially if they aren’t already a professional software engineer. As other people have said, you don’t have “no background.” You know how to use a computer, because you’re on Quora. If you’ve gotten As in high school math, that’s sufficient background. The ability to do things rationally and methodically is all you need. You do not need to be able to program in a production-level programming language before undergrad. In fact, I would argue that it usually causes people to pick up bad habits. I had no knowledge of production-level programming languages before undergrad. I was still a novice when I entered graduate school. Even when I entered the workforce, I knew basically C and little else. I’ve had to pick up several other programming languages since then. Three successful startups plus employment at Apple and Alphabet would suggest that I haven’t been a failure. So lack of knowledge of programming languages won’t cause one to fail, if that’s your issue. Work hard, learn fast. Most people are so damn lazy, especially mentally, those two things will get you far.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Degrees have deteriorated and becoming a commodity, they have adopted toward their student as “consumers", like they're being dared, how much further will it go? The delusion of the primacy of a four-year degree is falling, it's going to go splat?
Answer: Are you asking a question or writing poetry, Cess Romer? I’d give you at least a B for that in the appropriate poetry class. As for bachelor’s degrees, sure, some of them are effectively worthless. The problem with degrees is that the quality of the output is mostly due to the input, not the school. Crap in, crap out. But if you look at the top engineering, accountancy, or other programs where there are correct answers and you can’t bullshit your way through, the degrees are the opposite of deteriorated: the standards for admission have only risen over time. The fact that you can post something on Quora with a computer or smartphone means you’re using the results of a lot of work of my friends and colleagues. Most of them took their four year degree, added at least another two and sometimes eight years of education on top of that, and are making a crapload of money. So the bachelor’s degree with actual standards of admissions and education will be just fine. And the people with crap degrees won’t be able to get into the same doors.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: How is it possible to believe in stronger border security but not the prosecution of American employers who consistently hire undocumented workers?
Answer: How is it possible? The words “logical inconsistency” or “hypocrisy” come to mind. Railing against illegals crossing the border is like Hamas calling for a Palestinian state. The slogans rile up the uneducated, but the people in power don’t actually believe in it, because they don’t take the necessary steps to accomplish their purported goals. Some people like to hear what they want to hear, even if it’s lies.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: If a person wants to pursue a master's degree or a PhD in a mathematics related field, would having been a high school math teacher look good on their application? Or would the teaching experience be perceived as virtually irrelevant?
Answer: Mostly irrelevant. Teaching is not research. Even at the collegiate level. Better than an absolutely unrelated job, but I suspect that many schools would prioritize fresh undergraduates with clear desire for a graduate degree over someone that didn’t commit to the path as early as possible.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Should I just major in physics for pre-med given that I can’t see myself majoring in the traditional biology or chemistry?
Answer: You can, but as far as backup plans go, physics is no better than biology or chemistry in that you need a PhD to get a “real” physics job. Even more so, if anything: a bachelor’s or master’s in biology or chemistry is probably more likely to find a job in a lab somewhere. My personal preference would be to go to as broad/general an engineering discipline as possible over physics. There are more job options in case you decide not to do medical school, or don’t get accepted. Depending on the program, you can get the entire set of pre-med prerequisites to count as technical electives and not spend any extra time or money on undergraduate. You might feel like you have all the time in the world now, but realize that you’re not going to be making real money until your 30s, maybe even your 40s, if you go down the medical path. Time is precious and money is valuable.

Question: I don't have knowledge of mathematics but I have passion for AI and data science. I am in college right now but want to pursue a bachelor's in any of these fields. What are some suggestions?

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What makes working for FAANG companies seen as a gold standard? Why do some FAANG developers view those who haven't worked for such companies as tier 2 talent?
Answer: Short answer: the person doing the seeing has constructed that “standard” in their head. The vast majority of people with that opinion which I’ve encountered have either never worked in the tech industry, or have worked for one “FAANG” company and no other companies. Meaning young, inexperienced people. In my personal experience, I don’t think most people at “FAANG” companies look at that group of companies as any kind of standard. I certainly didn’t/don’t. I learned about the “FAANG” acronym from Quora, not from anyone actually working at any of those companies. The people I know who actually work at Apple or Alphabet would not voluntarily work for at least one of the other companies. It’s not something they/we strive for. Additionally, more than a handful of years in, most developers specialize in a domain and a skill set, because they’ve been working on a particular set of projects, and that means they can’t get a job at a company that doesn’t do that work, or doesn’t value that work. So, for my immediate friends and acquaintances: There’s no unity, and thus no “standard.” For the second question: in my personal experience, every FAANG developer I’ve met who views people who haven’t worked for the FAANG companies as lower tier has never worked for a non “FAANG” company. It’s about boosting one’s ego and having limited experience. I haven’t encountered such a person over the age of 45 (not that there are many of us), since we usually have a wider variety of experience and the “FAANG” companies mostly didn’t exist when we first started looking for jobs. Tech companies rise and fall: Apple in particular is living proof of it. You’d have to be completely ignorant of tech industry history to not have that in mind when you look for a job. Not that ignorance is in short supply among humans. If you aspire to make your way into an elite tech organization, don’t use an acronym that includes individual companies. By the time you’re heard about them, at least one is past peak. It’s like surfing: if you’re a bystander watching waves, by the time you see them it’s far too late to do anything significantly positive and a whole lot of ways to screw things up. You don’t have to do a lot of startups like myself, but catching companies as they fall is a good way to get crushed.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: What makes studying in the USA a top choice for international students seeking higher education?
Answer: Most U.S. institutions offering undergraduate degrees are willing to admit foreign students. So unless you are illiterate or mentally disabled, there will be a school somewhere in the U.S. willing to take your money and graduate you. Higher education is an industry in the U.S. At very elite institutions, foreigners are there for the same reasons as U.S. citizens: to get a quality education and expand their experiences. At my last job, I worked with three people born in three different countries who all did bachelor’s through PhD at MIT. They wouldn’t lose to anyone. As one goes down the admission bar and rigor, I’ve encountered many foreigners using a U.S. undergraduate or MBA education as a status symbol. Mostly it indicates that someone had money to begin with. A few of them are dumb enough to assume that a random, casually dressed ethnic East Asian (me) is a foreigner and doesn’t have an education. Their attitudes shift tremendously when they find out what my education and work experience are. It might be the most profound thing they learn in the U.S.: unlike their home country, we don’t feel obliged to impress people with our clothing and other material objects all the time.

Question: Why do a lot of East Asians in America complain about racism directed at them when their countries are some of the most homogeneous immigrant restricting nations in the world?

Why is an immigration policy of a country they’re leaving behind have anything to do with them? Maybe they left because the place was too damn homogeneous. I couldn’t care less about the immigration policies of East Asian countries. I do care if a racist person gets in my way or attacks me. Thankfully, no one’s taken away my gun rights yet.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Is it possible for me to double major in civil engineering and psychology, working as a engineer then getting my doctorate and transitioning to a psychiatrist?
Answer: Theoretically, it’s possible. But I would say it’s not close to a rational choice. If you are in the U.S., “psychiatrist” requires getting a MD and doing the appropriate residency. If that’s your goal, you need to get to that goal as quickly as possible. Four years of medical school and four years of residency only gets harder and more expensive as you get older, while your money-making years shrink. Medical school is a full time anti-job (you’re working a full time job and paying as much money as most people wish they were making). If you wanted to be a “psychologist,” that requires a PhD or PsyD. Still many years doing full time study, although you should get paid to do a PhD. If you were trying to accumulate money by being an engineer, civil engineering is the last engineering discipline I would choose. There’s no overlap with the biology and chemistry MD prerequisites and the pay is one of the lowest in engineering. People who are actually committed to civil engineering are busy acquiring the Professional Engineer designation so they can move up in their careers (and make more money). I would focus on a single major/degree and excel. Splitting your attention is probably going to kill your opportunities in both fields. Every PhD I know with a double undergraduate major regretted it in the end, and most double majors don’t make it to a doctorate.

Question: If I study in a university online, does the certification differ from on-campus certification?
Answer: It depends on the university, but many schools will distinguish them. Even if the university doesn’t distinguish the two, recruiters and corporations might, especially if they notice a distinct difference in the quality of graduates.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Who would you prioritize hiring for a senior software engineer position and why would you hire: a candidate from prestigious universities like MIT, Ivy League schools, or state universities, or a candidate from less prestigious universities?
Answer: There are two parts to my answer. The proportion of effective people coming out of MIT is much higher than most schools. The average capabilities of graduates are roughly in line with computer science/engineering rankings. It’s a statistical result of admissions standards and rigor of program. So I might prioritize my time by going to more reputed schools for recruiting: on average, I get better quality. However, I hire individuals for what they can produce today and in the near future. Automatically applying a generalization/stereotype to individuals is an “-ism”: racism, sexism, ageism, whatever. Even the average MIT grad is not a good fit for anything I’m looking for: I am trying to find outliers, not warm bodies. I make hire/not-hire judgments based on quantitative metrics that I apply to every candidate. I distinctly remember one candidate at my last job that knocked it out of the park. I don’t remember which Canadian university, and it didn’t matter. But he clearly beat all sorts of people with more degrees and more reputed universities. Of course I said hire. (Incidentally, he wrote tests before he wrote functional code. That was unusual, in a very good way.) Second, a senior software engineer has previous experience, or you’ve got a company that hands out titles far too easily. The school doesn’t matter at that point unless their experience was at school (e.g. they are a fresh PhD graduate). Work is not school. What matters is the content and performance at the last few jobs. I’ve known people from no-name universities that were excellent software engineers, and people from MIT that couldn’t code their way out of a paper bag. I’ve met people who looked great fresh out of school that fell apart several years after. They stopped being able to hold a job. No one cares about the institution, or even the degree, after a couple years. If they did at one point, they stop doing it, because experience shows that school doesn’t correlate strongly enough with future work performance. People usually perform like they most recently performed in a similar environment, not necessarily how they performed in a different context many years ago. They deviate from that generalization far less often than generalizations about schools.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Which degree will be better for embedded software engineering, a BSc in computer engineering or computer science? Is knowledge of hardware compulsory?
Answer: Depends on your definition of “better.” Either can work, and either can be insufficient if you don’t get the proper coursework/education. First, keep in mind that the point of a science/engineering degree is to give you an education in the area, not set you up for one relatively specific subindustry or role. You never know when that subindustry or role might crash. Case in point, the percentage of jobs that are considered “embedded software” is either smaller or shifted compared to decades past, depending on your definition of “embedded”: much of what used to be called “embedded” devices are now full blown computers. You don’t need hardware knowledge to the depth of a computer engineer’s core curriculum: I have that but don’t use it. In particular, you don’t truly need to know about the analog world that underlies digital electronics, much less actually design hardware that abstracts it away. So in that respect, you could consider it wasted effort, but again, read the previous paragraph. You may also not have enough software education to be productive, but plenty of people learn software on the job. On the other hand, many computer science graduates don’t even have a basic understanding of digital hardware necessary to usefully program embedded systems. Even in top programs that require computer architecture coursework, and definitely at weak programs. A CS program that doesn’t teach you that knowledge will effectively lock you out of embedded software, especially systems software, unless you find a way to train on the job. And again, there will be chunks of the CS program which don’t apply to that specific job, and that’s the point of the program. So the “ideal” bachelor’s degree for working on embedded systems software might be a computer science degree with enough logic design and other digital hardware coursework that you could design digital logic circuits if necessary. It’s those people and their designs that you’d be interfacing with as an embedded software developer.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Can I become a software engineer with a math degree? Would it be recommended that I pair the math degree with an MS in CS or would it be better to try and go into the industry?
Answer: Both “the industry” (FYI, it’s not a monolith) and grad school admission standards run a very large range of prestige and abilities. Your options depend on your current state. If you have poor grades (certainly below a 3.0 GPA, as high as 3.8 depending on the team/company/school), you’re not getting a job at a company with competition, nor going to grad school. If you have no experience writing software, you’re not getting a job writing software. I would take some basic computer science courses during undergrad, especially data structures and algorithms. While some people who call themselves “software engineers” don’t have that knowledge, you won’t get very far or long without it. Address those issues, then we can talk about options. In general you shouldn’t be going to graduate school unless it significantly improves outcomes, because it costs time and possibly money. A MS might improve outcomes if it also beats your undergraduate institution in prestige/rigor/connections/whatever. If you don’t already have some CS knowledge going in, you’re probably going to gravitate towards the math parts to keep you afloat, which does you no favors when it comes time to look for a job. Go look at at specific companies and jobs and see what their requirements are for entry level jobs. There is always some wiggle room to ignore “requirements” if you can do the work. Since corporations are, amazingly, willing to tell you what they’re looking for, you can aim for those targets.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: I understand this may come off as a weird question, but does anyone recommend any good degrees for pre med other than biology and the other sciences that offer job opportunities say if I don’t gain admission to med school?
Answer: It’s actually not a weird question at all for anyone that knows how medical school admissions works. I wish everyone targeting medical school asked this question. Too many people think they’re a shoo-in for medical school, not realizing that they’ve been big fish in very little ponds until it’s far too late to hedge bets. I’m going to assume you’re in the U.S.: other countries have different systems and I can’t give advice on those. Some context: my father was and my cousin is a med school professor. My wife interviews applicants to Stanford Medical School. The majority of the working adults in my family are medical doctors. So this topic is something I hear a lot about, even though I didn’t go through it myself. In the U.S., med schools take effectively any undergraduate major, as long as you satisfy prerequisites and do well on the MCAT. So you can take just about anything, but unless you want to be spending significant extra time in school, doing something in STEM tracks is more time efficient. So if you’re excluding the sciences (and it usually takes a PhD to get a “real” science job these days), I would recommend engineering. However, if you’re trying to improve job opportunities, that recommendation excludes bio(medical) engineering, despite the obvious subject fit, and that’s because enrollments are way out of whack with the job market: there are literally more current undergraduate students than the entire BioE/BME job market, which also depresses wages relative to other engineers. You can check ASEE and BLS statistics to confirm. The last time I poked around, it seemed like general/systems engineering had the most flexibility in which to fit in your medical prerequisites, followed by industrial engineering, but any is fine. My aforementioned cousin was an electrical engineering graduate and has worked at both Stanford and UCSF, which have two of the top medical schools in the country.

Name: Shane Ryoo
Question: Can an industrial engineer pursue masters and work with embedded systems?
Answer: What aspect of embedded systems? Hardware design: no, you wouldn’t have any of the core technical knowledge to design hardware. Most IE programs don’t even require a circuits course. You probably wouldn’t be admitted into the appropriate graduate program, and you’d never get hired. Maybe there’s a remedial master’s program that will teach you the appropriate skills, so look for something like that. Software: maybe, but again, you’re lacking the core technical knowledge. Unlike the hardware design, computer science programs and software jobs don’t have the same expectations of prior education, so you could make your way there. However, most people who try will fail.
